# ModernTex

A native macOS LaTeX editor for researchers, not a programmer's IDE with LaTeX bolted on. Multi-file editing, synchronized PDF preview, and the full academic manuscript workflow in one app.

Download the free 7-day trial

Refunded if you email within 14 days of purchase. Updates are included forever.

From the studio behind Scholar Utility Belt, which 1,000 researchers use and the Chrome Web Store rates 4.5 out of 5.

The trial is the full app for seven days, no account, nothing to enter. Buying is $19.99 once, with all updates included, forever (terms); the receipt email includes a permanent license key. After the seven days the app asks for it. Not useful? Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase and it is refunded. Already using the trial? Choose Enter license key in the app, paste the key, and the copy you have unlocks straight away, with no reinstall. Version 1.4.0 · 18 MB disk image · macOS 14 or later · Apple silicon and Intel. Requirements. Also in the Mac Suite with Outbound Veil, Legroom, Keyfeel and Vitae Plus for life, $54.99 once. First ten minutes: install and first build.

## Sixty-five seconds, start to submission

A mistyped command caught as you type, TikZ and tables built visually, a searchable symbol palette, revision snapshots, and the submission checker. Real footage of the app on a sample manuscript.

Play the tour on YouTube

In the app

## Source and PDF, always in sync

New in 1.3

## Two things nobody enjoys writing by hand

A TikZ diagram and a results table are both perfectly capable LaTeX, and neither is a pleasant place to start from a blank line and a syntax reference. ModernTex builds both visually and drops in the real source underneath: nothing hidden, nothing you couldn't have typed yourself.

### TikZ Designer

Drag boxes and arrows into place, pick colors from a swatch, resize by the corner, connect two shapes by dragging between them. Start from a flowchart, pipeline, state machine, or tree preset, or a blank canvas. Reopen an existing diagram from the Figures menu to keep editing it instead of redrawing it.

### Table Editor

Paste a range straight from Excel or Google Sheets and it lands in the right cells, growing the table if the data is bigger and leaving the rest untouched if it's smaller. Return moves down a row, ⌥Return breaks a line inside a cell, and dragging a column edge resizes it, the way a spreadsheet does, producing booktabs-style tabular underneath.

Read more about both on the blog →

Features

## Everything the manuscript needs

### Multi-file manuscript navigation

Navigate complex projects with root file detection and a structured sidebar. Jump between chapters, sections, and bibliography files without losing context.

### Three compile modes

Fast, Live, and Full compile modes let you move at the speed you need. Live mode keeps the PDF in sync as you type. Full mode does the deep pass before submission.

### Synchronized PDF preview

Forward and inverse search: click the source to jump to the PDF, click the PDF to jump to the source. Side by side, always in sync.

### Citation management

BibTeX autocomplete that searches your bibliography by author, title, or key, not only the keys you have already cited. Cite-as-you-type with smart suggestions from your .bib files.

### Plain-language error diagnostics

LaTeX error messages are hostile by design. ModernTex translates them into clear explanations with suggested fixes, reducing the debugging spiral that breaks flow.

### Submission readiness checks

Automatically check anonymization, page limits, required sections, and submission packaging before you hit send, so formatting problems are caught before a journal returns the paper.

### Version snapshots

Take a snapshot at any point: before a major revision, after peer review, before resubmission. Diff between snapshots with meaningful context.

### Live TikZ figure editor

Build flowcharts and diagrams by dragging boxes and drawing connections on a canvas. ModernTex generates the TikZ code as you go; insert it at your cursor when it's ready.

### Table editor

Paste a range from Excel or Google Sheets straight into the right cells. Resize columns by dragging, set a table-wide font, and generate clean booktabs-style LaTeX underneath.

### Native macOS experience

Built in Swift for macOS 14+. Native dark and light mode, system fonts, proper keyboard shortcuts, and performance that doesn't make you wait.

Plain-language errors

## From a cryptic error to a fix

LaTeX reports a mistake in its own terms and leaves you to work out what it means. ModernTex reads the error and says what went wrong in plain language, with a suggested fix.

What LaTeX prints

! Undefined control sequence.
l.42 As shown by \citeauthr
{smith2024}, the effect holds.

What ModernTex tells you

LaTeX does not recognize the command \citeauthr on line 42. This is usually a misspelled command, or a package that defines it is not loaded.

Suggested fix

- Remove: \citeauthr{smith2024}

+ Add: \citeauthor{smith2024}

An illustrative example, not a capture from the app; the wording varies with the error.

Who it's for

## For academic authors

### PhD students

Writing dissertation chapters and conference papers across multiple files, with deadlines and a committee watching over your shoulder.

### Faculty & researchers

Managing journal submissions, coauthor workflows, multiple concurrent manuscripts, and the full resubmission lifecycle.

### Technical coauthors

Jumping into someone else's LaTeX project and needing to understand the structure, fix compilation issues, and contribute without breaking things.

Not the right fit if several co-authors need to type in the same document at the same moment (keep Overleaf for that draft), you work on Windows, Linux or an iPad, or you would rather not have a TeX distribution on your Mac. ModernTex is also new, first released in September 2026, so it has less of a track record than TeXShop or Texifier. The comparison of Mac LaTeX editors covers the alternatives.

Comparison

## ModernTex compared with Overleaf

Overleaf pricing is from its plans page, checked September 29, 2026.

TopicModernTexOverleaf

Price$19.99 once, after a free 7-day trial. No subscription.Standard plan: $199 per year. A free plan is also offered.

CompilingOn your Mac, so there is no server compile timeout.On Overleaf's servers. The free plan has a compile timeout.

AccountNone.Required.

Where it runsNative macOS app. Files are ordinary .tex and .bib files in a folder on your disk.In the browser.

Co-authorsNo real-time co-editing. Get Changes and Send Changes sync with a co-author.Real-time collaboration in the browser.

Manuscript toolsMulti-file navigation, synchronized PDF preview, plain-language errors, submission-readiness checks, revision snapshots, BibTeX completion.See Overleaf's own feature list.

Prefer Overleaf when several people edit the same draft at the same time, or when you work on Windows, Linux or an iPad. Prefer ModernTex when you write mostly alone on a Mac and want no subscription, no account and no compile limit. Moving over is a zip download or a Git clone; see the FAQ.

Before you install

## What ModernTex needs.

A Mac running macOS 14 or later and a TeX distribution. MacTeX or TinyTeX both work, and you do not have to set either up first: if ModernTex cannot find one when you compile, it offers a one-click TinyTeX install right in the editor. After checkout you get a signed disk image: open it and drag ModernTex to Applications. Bookmark the download page; it always hands you the newest version.

First ten minutes: install and first build

Want one email when a notable version ships? Leave your address. No newsletters, no follow-ups.

Your email is used for release notes and nothing else. Privacy Policy · Why ModernTex →

## Frequently asked questions

How do I get updates?

ModernTex checks for a new version once a day and offers to install it in place. You can also choose Check for Updates from the ModernTex menu at any time. Updates are included in the purchase, and each download is code-signed by Purplelink LLC.

What macOS version is required?

ModernTex requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later.

I lost my license key. How do I get it back?

Enter the email address you used at checkout on the Find a purchase page. If that address bought ModernTex, a new license key and your download page are emailed to that address. Any key you had before keeps working.

Is there a free trial?

Yes. The trial is the complete app for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account and nothing to enter. When it ends, the window shows a notice and a Buy button; your .tex files are ordinary files on disk and are not touched. When you buy, the receipt email includes a license key: choose Enter license key in the app and paste it, and that same copy unlocks, with no reinstall. There is only one download, and it updates itself. If you bought before version 1.4.0, your copy keeps working with no key.

What does it cost?

$19.99, once, after a free 7-day trial. That covers all updates, forever. There is no subscription and no account; the optional AI features run on Apple Intelligence or your own Claude or OpenAI account.

How is ModernTex different from TeXShop or Overleaf?

ModernTex is a native macOS app designed specifically for the academic manuscript workflow. It is not a web app and not a general-purpose code editor. It combines multi-file manuscript navigation, synchronized PDF preview, BibTeX autocomplete that searches by author or title, plain-language error diagnostics, and submission-readiness checks. Designed for researchers, not programmers.

Coming from Overleaf: download the project as a zip, or clone it with Overleaf's Git integration, and open the folder. The files stay ordinary .tex, .bib and image files, so you can upload them back to Overleaf or open them in TeXShop at any time. There is no real-time co-editing; for a draft several people type in at once, keep Overleaf. See how the best LaTeX editors for Mac compare, or read what changes when you move from Overleaf to a Mac editor.

Can I move a project from Overleaf?

Yes. Download the project as a zip, or clone it with Overleaf's Git integration, and open the folder in ModernTex. The files stay ordinary .tex, .bib and image files, so you can upload them back to Overleaf at any time. What changes when you write locally

Why not just use a free editor like TeXstudio?

TeXstudio is free, cross-platform, and already parses compile errors into a readable list, so it's a legitimate choice, especially if you also work on Windows or Linux. ModernTex is narrower on purpose: Mac only, built around the manuscript workflow specifically. Three things TeXstudio doesn't do: BibTeX autocomplete that searches your whole .bib by author or title rather than just the keys already cited in the file, submission-readiness checks for what journals actually reject on, and an anonymized export for double-blind review. If none of those matter to you, TeXstudio is a perfectly good free option.

Does ModernTex support multi-file projects?

Yes. ModernTex has built-in multi-file manuscript navigation with root file detection and a structured sidebar for jumping between chapters, sections, and bibliography files without losing context.

Does it work for a dissertation?

Yes. A dissertation is a multi-file project like any other: open the folder and ModernTex finds the root file and lists the chapters in the sidebar. The bibliography can be BibTeX or biblatex with biber (a switch in the compile profile), reading any .bib in the project, including one exported from Zotero. A class file your university supplies goes in the project folder, where the compile picks it up and the submission export includes it. A generic thesis template is bundled.

Will I have to pay again for a new version?

No. Every update to ModernTex is included in the $19.99, forever, including future major versions. There is no upgrade fee.

## Try it on your own manuscript.

Seven days of the full app, no account and nothing to enter. If it earns a place in your workflow, it's $19.99 once, with all updates included, forever.

# Outbound Veil

Outbound Veil checks what you type for personal information before you send it. It runs in the Mac menu bar, the checking happens on your Mac, and the text never leaves it.

Try it free for 7 days

Refunded if you email within 14 days of purchase. Updates are included forever.

The trial is the full app for seven days from first launch, with no account. After that the app asks for a license key. Buying is a single $29.99 payment, and the key goes into the copy you already have. Not useful? Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase (terms). Version 1.1.0 · 38 MB disk image · macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel. First ten minutes: install, Accessibility and your first check.

Also in the Mac Suite: Outbound Veil, ModernTex, Legroom, Keyfeel and Vitae Plus for life, $54.99 once.

Outbound Veil checking a fictional client note typed into a plain text field in Chrome. Every name and number on this page is invented.

## How it works

### It watches the field you are typing in

Outbound Veil reads the text field that has focus, on your Mac, through macOS Accessibility. It does not look at other windows.

### It shows a badge when it finds something

A small badge appears with the number of findings, and the matching text is highlighted where the app allows it.

### You decide

Redact a finding, redact them all, or ignore them. In apps you choose, Outbound Veil can also hold the send key until you have decided.

Watch it work

## Under a minute, from typing to redacted

A client note typed into a text field, personal details marked as they appear, then redacted in one click. Real footage of the app, with invented data.

Play the video on YouTube

## A closer look

### Marked where it is

Each finding is highlighted on the text itself, in a colour, opacity and style you choose, and the highlight follows the text as you edit. The badge shows how many findings the field has. Turn highlighting off from the menu or with Control-Option-H.

### Every finding, in a list

Click the badge to see what was found and what kind of detail it is. Ignore a finding, redact all of them, or switch checking off for that app.

### Redacted, still readable

Redact all rewrites the field in place. Each detail becomes a labelled placeholder, such as [SSN_1] or [EMAIL_1], so the text still reads sensibly when you send it.

## What it finds

People and contactNames, street addresses, phone numbers, email addresses.

Government and taxSocial Security numbers, passport and driver's license numbers, tax identifiers.

MoneyCard numbers, bank identifiers, IBANs.

Health and datesDates of birth, medical record numbers.

## Where it works

Tested on macOS 26 with the apps below. Each one can be read, and Redact all rewrites the field in place.

AppHow findings are shown

TextEditEach finding highlighted word by word.

NotesEach finding highlighted word by word.

Microsoft WordEach finding highlighted word by word.

MessagesBadge and Redact all. Send hold works here, as an example of an app you can choose.

Chrome text areasWord by word in a plain text area. In the ChatGPT and claude.ai prompts the whole field is outlined instead.

Some apps do not expose their text fields to macOS, and Outbound Veil cannot read those. The menu bar says so when it happens. Apple Mail’s compose window is one. Safari, Slack, VS Code and most other apps have not been tested yet. The full table of apps and fields says which are which, and how to check your own app during the free trial.

Comparing it with other ways to keep personal details out of AI chats? See the comparison of redaction tools for ChatGPT and other AI chats, which says plainly where a competitor is the better choice.

## Privacy

### Checked on your Mac

What you type is checked by a model that runs on your Mac. Nothing you type is stored or sent. There are no accounts and no analytics in the app.

### Accessibility permission

macOS asks you to allow Accessibility so Outbound Veil can read the text field you are typing in. Without it the app has nothing to check.

### Input Monitoring, only for send hold

This second permission is requested only if you turn on send hold, so the app can notice the send key. If you never use send hold, you never grant it.

Apart from the download itself, the only network use is the check for a new version. Details are on the privacy page.

## Limits

NamesRecognized in Latin script only.

Public figuresTheir names are flagged too. You can ignore those findings.

AccuracyIt will miss some things, and it can flag things that are not personal information.

ComplianceIt lowers the chance of a mistake. It is not a compliance product, and it does not make any workflow compliant with a regulation.

## Credit

The detection model is Rampart by National Design Studio, released under CC BY 4.0. Purplelink ported Rampart's processing code to Swift and added rules for dates of birth, medical record numbers and IBANs. The model file is unchanged.

## Frequently asked questions

What does it need to run?

macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later, on Apple silicon or Intel.

Which apps does it work in?

Tested and working: TextEdit, Notes, Messages, Microsoft Word, and text areas in Chrome, including the ChatGPT and claude.ai prompt boxes. Not readable: the body of a new message in Apple Mail. Terminal is switched off by default. Safari, Slack, VS Code, Pages, Google Docs and most other apps have not been tested. The table lists each app and field, and you can check your own app during the free trial.

Does it send what I type anywhere?

No. What you type is checked on your Mac. Nothing you type is stored or sent, and the app has no analytics. Apart from the download itself, the only network use is the check for a new version.

Are updates included?

Yes, all of them, forever, including future major versions. Every copy, trial or licensed, checks for a new version and offers to install it in place, or you can choose Check for updates from its menu. Each download is signed by Purplelink LLC.

What happens when the trial ends?

The trial is the complete app for seven days from first launch, with no account. When it ends, Outbound Veil stops checking, shows one notice and asks for a license key. The key arrives in your receipt email and is shown on the success page, and the Find a purchase page sends it again. Choose Enter license key… from the menu-bar menu, or Settings, General, and paste it. It unlocks that copy for good, offline, with no account and no second download.

I already bought Outbound Veil. Do I need a key?

No. If you install this version over a copy you already paid for, it recognizes that copy and never asks for a key.

Can I get a refund?

Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase. See the terms.

How do I get help?

Email ben@purplelink.llc. If you lose your download link or your license key, the Find a purchase page emails them again to the address you paid with.

# Legroom

Legroom shows how much free space your Mac has, warns you before the disk fills, and cleans the folders and developer caches you choose. It runs in the menu bar. Nothing is removed until you have seen a preview and approved it.

Try it free for 7 days

Refunded if you email within 14 days of purchase.

The trial runs for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account. After it ends, the menu-bar readout and the low-space alerts keep working, and the app asks for a license key to unlock the rest. Buying is a single $9.99 payment, and the key goes into the copy you already have. Not useful? Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase (terms). Version 1.1.0 · 6.6 MB disk image · macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel · signed and notarized.

Also in the Mac Suite: ModernTex, Outbound Veil, Legroom, Keyfeel and Vitae Plus for life, $54.99 once.

Sample data: a pretend home folder and invented numbers. The window title comes from the test build.

## What it does

### It shows free space where you can see it

The menu bar shows what is free on your startup disk. The window under it adds the space available now, the space macOS says it can clear, and your other volumes. You set a line, and Legroom warns you when free space drops below it.

### It cleans what you tell it to

You make a rule for a folder or a cache. The rule shows a preview of exactly what it would remove, and you approve it. A rule can then run when you ask, on a schedule, or when free space drops below your line. Each rule either moves items to the Trash or deletes them, and says which.

### It shows what grew

Once a day Legroom measures where your space goes. What Grew compares those measurements over 1, 7 or 30 days, so you can see which folder filled the disk and make a rule for it.

Watch it work

## Under a minute, from free space to what grew

The menu-bar readout, a cleaning rule with its preview, What Grew, the Space Map and Find Files. Every screen uses sample data.

Play the video on YouTube

## A closer look

Every screen below is a capture of the app running on sample data, not on a real Mac.

### You approve every clean

Clean Now lists each rule with the most it would remove and whether that goes to the Trash or is deleted for good. Permanent deletion is shown in red. A rule whose folders changed since you approved it is left out until you preview it again.

Sample data.

### What grew since last week

Each folder that grew is listed with its size and its growth, and a button for the next step: clean it now, add a rule, preview a rule or see a command. Items that come from macOS, such as swap and local Time Machine snapshots, are listed separately with what Legroom can and cannot tell you about them.

Sample data.

### Suggested rules, weekly or monthly

Legroom looks at what grew, at your rules and at its list of known caches, and suggests rules. A suggestion never creates, approves or runs a rule. You see the rule editor and the preview first.

Sample data.

### Space Map: where the space went

A chart of a folder or a whole disk, as rings: the centre is the folder you are in, and each ring outward is the folders inside it. Click a section to select it and double-click to look inside. A selected folder can be revealed in Finder, moved to the Trash or turned into a rule. Folders Legroom could not read are drawn hatched, so a gap is never passed off as empty space.

Sample data. Full Disk Access is off in this capture, so protected folders are skipped.

### Find Files: large, old and duplicate files

Search your home folder, or folders you choose, for large files, files you have not opened in a long time, and duplicates. For duplicates you choose which copy stays, and at least one copy of every group always stays. Find Files only moves files to the Trash, and only the ones you select.

Sample data.

## What is in it

Menu barFree space on the startup disk, the space macOS can clear, your other volumes, and a low-space alert at a line you set.

RulesFolders you choose, with an age limit, a preview and your approval. Run by hand, on a schedule, or when free space drops below your line. A log shows what each run did, and one switch pauses automatic cleaning.

RecommendedCaches Legroom knows, such as Xcode DerivedData, Homebrew downloads and the npm cache, and folders that look like caches, labelled when it is not sure.

Project scanLooks through your code projects for old build folders and offers a rule for them.

What GrewA daily measurement of where your space goes, compared over 1, 7 or 30 days.

SuggestionsRule ideas based on what grew, weekly or monthly.

Space MapA sunburst chart of a folder or disk, with Reveal in Finder, Move to Trash and Add as a Rule.

Find FilesLarge, old and duplicate files. Trash only, and one copy of every duplicate always stays.

## What it does not do

SpeedIt does not make your Mac faster. It frees disk space and does nothing else to performance.

System filesIt does not clean inside system folders and the folders that hold your documents and settings.

CommandsIt does not run commands. Where a fix needs Terminal, such as removing local Time Machine snapshots, it shows the command as text and you decide whether to run it.

Hidden spaceIt does not scan as an administrator, so some space it cannot measure, such as local Time Machine snapshots. It lists those as size not reported rather than guessing.

Unseen deletionsIt does not remove anything you have not previewed and approved, and it does not remove duplicates without leaving one copy.

The cloudThere is no cloud, no account and no sync. Your measurements, rules and log stay on your Mac.

## Privacy

Legroom has no account and no analytics. Your daily measurements, your rules, the log of what was cleaned and the trial clock are stored on your Mac and are not sent anywhere. Apart from two things, Legroom does not use the network. The Buy button opens this page in your browser. And every copy, trial or licensed, asks this site once a day for its update feed: that request carries the app's name and version and an update token that is the same in every copy, plus what any web request carries, such as your IP address. It does not carry your files, your measurements or a profile of your Mac. Legroom asks for Full Disk Access only if you choose to give it, so it can read folders such as Desktop, Documents and Downloads. Details are on the privacy page.

## Frequently asked questions

What does it need to run?

macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later, on Apple silicon or Intel.

Does it delete anything on its own?

Only through a rule you made, after you approved a preview of what the rule would remove. Each rule is set to move items to the Trash or to delete them permanently, and the preview says which. Space Map and Find Files only move items to the Trash, and only the ones you select.

Does it make my Mac faster?

No. Legroom frees disk space. It does not tune or speed up anything else.

Does it need Full Disk Access?

No. It asks only if you choose to give it. Without it, Legroom skips the folders macOS protects, such as Desktop, Documents and Downloads, and says which ones it could not read.

Does it send my files or measurements anywhere?

No. There is no account and no analytics. Apart from the download itself, the daily update check that every copy makes and the Buy link, which opens this page in your browser, Legroom does not use the network.

What happens when the trial ends?

The trial runs for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account. After that the menu-bar readout and the low-space alerts keep working. Cleaning rules, What Grew, Suggestions, Space Map and Find Files stop until you enter a license key. The key arrives in your receipt email and is shown on the success page, and the Find a purchase page sends it again. Choose Enter license key… from the menu-bar dropdown, or Settings, General, and paste it. It unlocks Legroom for good, offline, with no account and no second download.

I already bought Legroom. Do I need a key?

No. If you install this version over a copy you already paid for, it recognizes that copy and never asks for a key.

Are updates included?

Updates to the version you buy are included. Every copy, trial or licensed, checks for a new version once a day and asks before installing it, or you can check by hand from its menu. I have not decided whether a later major version would be a free update.

Can I get a refund?

Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase. See the terms.

Can I see free space without an app, or with a free one?

Yes. Finder's status bar, System Settings and Disk Utility show it on request, and the free app Stats can put it in the menu bar. The guide Show free disk space in the Mac menu bar walks through each and compares the menu-bar apps, including this one.

How do I get help?

Email ben@purplelink.llc. If you lose your download link or your license key, the Find a purchase page emails them again to the address you paid with.

# Keyfeel

Keyfeel plays real recorded keyboard-switch sounds when you press a key on your Mac, and adds mouse-click sounds, scroll ticks and optional trackpad haptics. It runs in the menu bar and works offline.

Try it free for 7 days

The trial is the complete app for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account and nothing to enter. Buying is a single $9.99 payment, for life, with every update included. You get a license key by email and on the page after you pay; paste it into the same app and it stays unlocked, with no second download. Not useful? Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase (terms). Version 1.3.0, released October 7, 2026. 7 MB disk image. Needs macOS 13 or later, Apple silicon and Intel, and the Input Monitoring permission.

Comparing options? See the keyboard sound apps for Mac compared.

Also in the Mac Suite: ModernTex, Outbound Veil, Legroom, Keyfeel and Vitae Plus for life, $54.99 once.

An illustration of the idea, not a screenshot of the app.

Watch it work

## Thirty seconds of real switch sounds

The menu bar, the three recorded profiles, mouse clicks and scroll ticks, trackpad haptics, and silence in the apps you choose. Footage is the running app, and the sounds are the ones it ships with.

Play the video on YouTube

## How it works

### It hears that a key was pressed

Through the macOS Input Monitoring permission, Keyfeel is told when a key goes down and comes back up. It uses the key code, which says which key it was, and never the characters you typed.

### It plays a recording of a real switch

Each press plays a recording from the sound profile you chose, and picks a different recording each time, so a repeated key does not sound like one sample on a loop.

### It stays out of the way

Keyfeel lives in the menu bar. You can silence it in the apps you choose, and it goes quiet by itself while the microphone is in use.

## What it does

Sound profilesRecorded Tactile, Cherry MX Brown and Dome profiles, a Fun set (cat, dog, duck, boing, bubble pop, water drops), a Calm set of soft sounds for all-day use (soft wood, glass and ceramic, marble, kalimba, chimes, clickers, bubble wrap), and synthesized extras. Every recording is licensed for use (CC0), with credits listed in the app.

Your own soundsImport a Mechvibes sound pack (its folder, its zip or its config.json), including packs in .ogg, and each key keeps the sound the pack gave it. Or choose one short sound file of your own.

KeysPress and release sounds, with a different recording on each press. Each key has its own pitch, and the sound moves from left to right in stereo across the keyboard. The space bar and Return have sounds of their own, and you can set the level of the space bar and modifier keys separately. Fast typing gets gently quieter so it does not wear on you.

MousePress and release sounds for mouse clicks, and a ripple on screen where you click.

ScrollingScroll ticks that follow how fast you scroll, in nine styles, including recorded brush, pencil on paper, salt and rice. When a hard flick keeps the page gliding, the ticks keep going and slow down with it. They can stop when the page reaches its end; that one option uses the optional Accessibility permission to read how far the page is scrolled.

ShortcutsEach of eleven shortcuts, such as copy, paste, undo and save, can have its own sound, and so can four trackpad gestures: Mission Control, Application windows, Show Desktop and switching desktops. Copy and cut play a different, softer sound if nothing was copied, so the sound tells you the command took. Switching desktops works as soon as it is on; the other three gestures use the optional Accessibility permission.

TrackpadOptional haptic feedback on scroll and click. Keyfeel produces it only while a finger is on the trackpad.

QuietSilence in the apps you choose, automatic silence on the speakers while the microphone or a camera is in use, and an option to stay silent in full-screen apps. Headphones, wired or Bluetooth, play by default, have their own switch and keep their own volume, which Keyfeel switches to when the output changes; you can also keep sounds off the built-in speakers and play them only on headphones or external audio.

ControlKeyfeel runs from the menu bar and is controlled there, including a volume slider. Keyboard shortcuts turn it on and off and switch sounds, a keyfeel:// link works from Shortcuts and scripts, and you can hide the menu bar icon.

## How it feels

Four parts of the app, drawn rather than photographed. These are illustrations, not screenshots of the app.

### Typing

Every key press plays a recording of a real switch, with its own pitch and a place in the stereo field. Releasing the key can make a sound too.

### Clicking

Mouse clicks have press and release sounds, and a ripple spreads on screen from the point you clicked. Scrolling ticks along at the speed you scroll.

### Trackpad

Optional haptic feedback on scroll and click. Keyfeel produces it only while a finger is on the trackpad.

### Quiet when it should be

Choose apps where Keyfeel stays silent. It also goes quiet by itself while the microphone is in use, so key sounds are not played into a call or a recording.

## Privacy

### Works offline

Keyfeel makes its sounds and haptics on your Mac and needs no network connection. There are no accounts. The only network use is its check for a new version, which carries the app's name and version and nothing you type.

### Key codes, never characters

To choose a sound, Keyfeel needs to know which key was pressed. It reads the key code, not the character the key produced. A key code is still a record of which keys you press, which is why macOS puts it behind a permission you grant.

### Password fields stay silent

When a password field has focus, macOS stops delivering keystrokes to apps like Keyfeel. It hears nothing while you type a password.

Details are on the privacy page.

## The Input Monitoring permission

The first time you open Keyfeel, macOS asks you to allow it under System Settings, Privacy & Security, Input Monitoring. That is the permission an app needs to be told about key presses made in other apps. Without it Keyfeel cannot hear your keyboard and stays silent. You can switch it off again in the same place at any time. Two optional features ask for the Accessibility permission as well: stopping scroll sounds at the end of a page, which reads how far the page under the pointer is scrolled, and sounds for Mission Control, Application windows and Show Desktop, which listen for the Dock announcing them. They read nothing else, and Keyfeel works without them.

## What it is not

A keyloggerIt works from key codes, not the characters you type, and it does not send your typing anywhere.

A keyboard remapperIt listens. It does not change what a key types and does not block any key.

New hardwareSounds play through your Mac's audio output. Haptic feedback is felt only on the trackpad, and only while a finger is on it. Nothing happens inside your keyboard or mouse.

Cross-platformMac only. There is no Windows, iPhone or iPad version.

## Frequently asked questions

What does it need to run?

macOS 13 (Ventura) or later, on Apple silicon or Intel, and the macOS Input Monitoring permission.

Does it read what I type?

No. It reads which key was pressed, as a key code, so it can choose a sound. It does not read the characters. It works offline and does not send your typing anywhere.

Does it hear me type passwords?

No. When a password field has focus, macOS stops delivering keystrokes to apps like Keyfeel, so it hears nothing there.

Can I make it quiet in some apps, or on calls?

Yes. You can silence Keyfeel in the apps you choose, and it goes quiet by itself while the microphone or a camera is in use. An option also keeps it silent in full-screen apps.

Why do the haptics need a finger on the trackpad?

Keyfeel produces trackpad haptics only while a finger is on the trackpad, which is when you can feel them. They are optional.

Is there a delay between pressing a key and hearing it?

A small one, about 8 to 25 milliseconds on a Mac's built-in speakers, depending on the Mac. Settings shows the estimate for your output. Bluetooth headphones add their own delay, often 100 milliseconds or more, which no app can remove; Settings tells you when the current output is Bluetooth.

Can I use sound packs from other apps?

Yes, packs in the Mechvibes format. Choose Import a sound pack in the menu or in Settings, then pick the pack's folder, its zip file or its config.json. Keyfeel converts it once and keeps a copy of its own.

Are updates included?

Yes, all of them. The price is a single payment, for life. Keyfeel checks for a new version and offers to install it in place.

What happens when the trial ends?

The trial is the complete app for seven days from the first time you open it, with no account. To keep using Keyfeel after that, buy it. You get a license key by email and on the page after you pay; choose Enter License Key in Keyfeel and paste it. It works offline and needs no second download.

Can I get a refund?

Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase. See the terms.

How do I get help?

Email ben@purplelink.llc. If you lose your download link, the Find a purchase page emails it again to the address you paid with.

## Everything an academic needs, nothing they don't

### Submission tracking

Log every journal and conference submission with status, dates, each review round, and the decision. Pick target venues with published acceptance rates for about 13,700 journals and conferences, and get a forecast of publication timelines from your own submission history.

## Frequently asked questions

Is Vitae really free?

Yes. Vitae is free to download and use, with all core record-keeping and no limits, and nothing that was free before Plus becomes paid. An optional subscription, Vitae Plus ($2.99 a month or $23.99 a year, with a 7-day free trial), adds newer tools: reports such as an NIH biosketch draft, Word export with your own templates, the revision workspace, Shareables, the collaboration map, batch DOI lookup and ORCID sync, Reminders and calendar sync, and themes. It is also included for life in the Mac Suite. You do not need it to keep your record. A tip via Buy Me a Coffee is also appreciated but never required.

Does Vitae show ads?

Not from anyone else. The sidebar has one small card, labelled "From Purplelink", that suggests another Purplelink tool such as ModernTex, Paper Review or Vitae Plus. If a sponsor ever appears there, the card will say "Sponsor" and the sponsor's name, and this page will say so. There is no ad network, no tracking, and no click reporting, and Vitae sends nothing to sponsors. Vitae reads the card's text from a plain file on purplelink.llc at most once a day, and shows a copy built into the app when you are offline. You can hide the card in Settings, under Support; Vitae then stops fetching it.

How does Vitae update?

Vitae checks purplelink.llc once a day and asks before installing a new version. Updates are signed, and Vitae refuses any that fail the check. You can turn the daily check off, or check by hand, in Settings under About. Version 0.1, the first release, cannot update itself; if you still have it, download the current version (1.0.3) once from this page and it will keep itself up to date after that.

Why isn't it on the Mac App Store?

Distributing outside the App Store lets me ship faster and avoid App Store restrictions. The DMG is Apple-notarized, so macOS Gatekeeper verifies it is safe to run. Just open the DMG, drag Vitae to Applications, and launch it.

What macOS version is required?

Vitae requires macOS 15 Sequoia or later.

Where is my data stored?

All your records are stored locally on your Mac using SwiftData, with no account and no sync. Vitae goes online for lookups you ask for, such as citation counts from Crossref or OpenAlex and Grants.gov funding searches, and reads your email only if you connect a mailbox, read-only. It also makes two small requests to purplelink.llc on its own: the daily update check, and the daily fetch of the sidebar card's text unless you hide the card. Neither sends anything about you or your records. iCloud sync is supported in the schema and can be enabled in future versions.

How do I install it?

Download the DMG, open it, drag Vitae into your Applications folder, and launch it. Because it is notarized by Apple, you will not see a Gatekeeper warning.

How does Vitae compare to Interfolio, ORCID, or a spreadsheet?

Vitae keeps your own record between deadlines; if your university requires Interfolio or Watermark for tenure review, you still submit there, using what Vitae exports. See how to track your academic CV and tenure case for a comparison of sixteen options, or best software for tracking your research record for submission trackers, spreadsheets and profile systems.

## An excerpt from a real report on a machine-learning paper

Every finding quotes the passage it is about.

### Critical blind spots

- 
Hyperparameter search asymmetry favors the proposed method.
Quoted: "We tuned learning rate and batch size on the validation set; baselines used reported defaults."
Surfaced by: Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic (consensus).
Fix: Match the search budget for each baseline and report the protocol in the methods section.

### Data-to-claim contradictions

- Claim: "Our method beats all baselines by a wide margin."
Evidence: Table 2 shows the proposed method tied with Baseline C within reported standard errors on 4 of 7 datasets.

### Rectification checklist

- A Add the hyperparameter search protocol to the methods (page 5, Section 3.2).

- B Reference [17] only weakly matches its CrossRef entry; check the title and DOI.

- C Figure 3's y-axis breaks 0-60 then jumps to 90; redraw on a continuous scale.

### References and citation support

47 of 52 references verified against CrossRef; 3 weak title matches to re-check.

Claim "Method X reduces error by 40%" cites [14], whose abstract reports a 4% reduction. Verdict: contradicted.

## How the review works

- MCMethodology CriticDesign, controls, confounds and what the method can and cannot show.

- SSStatistical SkepticPower, tests, intervals and claims the numbers do not support.

- DIData Integrity OfficerFigures, tables and whether the data shown matches the text.

- ECEditor-in-ChiefNovelty, fit, structure and what a desk editor would send back.

Built by Benjamin Ampel, assistant professor of computer information systems at Georgia State University, with publications in MIS Quarterly and JMIS.

- 
Layer 1: figure-integrity scan.
Every page is rendered and reviewed for digital manipulation
concerns, figure-vs-text contradictions, and presentation issues
(broken y-axes, missing error bars, color-only encoding).
Hedged language; flags concerns to investigate, never accusations.

- 
Layer 2: citation support audit.
Every reference is verified against CrossRef, then we go deeper:
for the most load-bearing claims, we fetch the cited source's
abstract and check whether it actually supports the claim you
attached it to. Each finding shows your claim next to the source's
own words, with a verdict: supported, partially supported, not
supported by the abstract, contradicted, or source unavailable.
Hedged language; verify each against the full text.

- 
Layer 3: a four-reviewer panel.
Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic, Data Integrity Officer,
and Editor-in-Chief each red-team the paper in parallel.
Findings are merged with a cross-persona consensus filter so
issues raised independently by multiple personas surface first.

- 
Layer 4: the report.
A final pass produces the structured report you'll act on:
critical blind spots, data-to-claim contradictions, an A/B/C
rectification checklist, and an honest novelty estimate.

## What you get

- One review of one manuscript (up to 20 MB PDF, ~100 pages). To have supplementary material read too, merge it into the same PDF.

- An anonymity scan for double-blind submission on every tier: author names, institutions, funders, protocol numbers and self-citations left in the text.

- A Markdown report and an annotated PDF with comments on the pages they refer to.

- Standard reviews are usually ready in 4-8 minutes, Deep Review in 10-15, on a status page that updates itself.

Reviewing a grant proposal instead of a paper? Grant Review is an idea for NSF and NIH proposals, and the waitlist measures interest.

## How your manuscript is handled

- Analysis. The PDF is read in memory. To check figures and tables, pages are rendered to images from a private temporary file that is deleted as soon as the rendering finishes.

- Anthropic. The text and page images are sent to Anthropic's Claude API. Anthropic keeps API inputs for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring and does not train on them.

- Delivery and deletion. The report is emailed to you as a PDF when the review finishes. The manuscript and the online copy are deleted 30 minutes after you first open the result, or after 24 hours if you never open it. The email is sent through Resend and carries the report only, never the manuscript or the annotated PDF.

- What we keep. A permanent cost record per job: product, status, price, token counts and model names. It contains no manuscript text.

## Frequently asked questions

What does the review include?

Four layers in sequence: a Claude Vision pass over your figures and tables, a live CrossRef cross-check of every reference, an adversarial four-persona reviewer debate (Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic, Data Integrity Officer, Editor-in-Chief) with consensus filtering, and a synthesis pass producing critical blind spots, data-to-claim contradictions, a prioritised rectification checklist, and a true-novelty estimate.

How long does it take?

Typically 4-8 minutes for a 20-page manuscript. You don't need to keep the tab in the foreground. The status page polls until the review is ready and renders it inline.

What about my privacy? Is the manuscript stored?

Your manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API for analysis. Anthropic retains inputs for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, and does not use them for model training. The report is emailed to you as a PDF when the review finishes. The manuscript and the online copy are deleted 30 minutes after you first open the result, or after 24 hours if you never open it. The email goes through Resend to the address on your Stripe receipt, or to the one you enter at upload. The manuscript is never attached.

Which journals does the Journal Pack check?

25 venues. The pack checks word and abstract limits, required sections and reference-style hints against the one you pick at upload.

- Machine learning: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, TMLR, JMLR

- General science: Nature, Science, Cell, PLOS ONE

- Medicine: Nature Medicine, JAMA, NEJM, The Lancet, The BMJ

- Psychology and management: Psychological Science, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Cognition, Academy of Management Journal

- Chemistry and materials: JACS, Angewandte Chemie, Nature Materials, Nature Chemistry, ACS Nano, Advanced Materials

Not listed? The Standard tier covers everything except this check. Email to ask for a venue.

Is there a referral credit?

Yes. Every report ends with a link carrying your own code. When a colleague opens it and buys a review with a .edu email address, you each receive a single-use $2 code by email. The link counts for 30 days in the browser that opened it.

What domains does it cover?

You pick one of five domain profiles at upload: Machine Learning, Biomedicine, Psychology and Social Science, Chemistry and Materials, or General. Each profile tells the reviewers which failure modes matter most in that field; each link lists them.

How deep is the citation check?

Two levels. First, every reference is checked for existence against CrossRef (dead DOIs, hallucinated or weakly-matched titles). Second, for the most load-bearing claims we fetch the cited source's abstract from OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, or CrossRef and assess whether it supports your claim. This is an abstract-level check: a claim supported only in the full text is marked "not supported by abstract," not wrong. Verify it against the source. When no abstract can be retrieved, the citation is marked "source unavailable" rather than guessed. On citation-heavy papers we audit the most important claims first and tell you how many were not audited.

Am I allowed to use an AI review on my own manuscript?

Yes, under the policies of the major publishers and venues we have checked. Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, IEEE, ACM, ICMJE and NeurIPS let authors use AI tools while preparing a manuscript; the rule against uploading manuscripts to AI is for reviewers, who hold someone else's work. Paper Review writes nothing into your paper, so most disclosure rules, which cover AI-generated text, do not obviously apply; if your venue's policy is strict, a one-line note is enough. The policy guide compares ten publishers and venues.

Is this a replacement for peer review?

No. Treat it as a first-pass red team before you submit: a way to catch the obvious problems a real reviewer will flag before they do. The review is advisory only; you remain responsible for every decision about your manuscript.

What if the review misses something or makes a mistake?

AI reviewers can be wrong. The output flags concerns with hedged language and quotes the manuscript when challenging a claim, so you can verify every finding against your text. Not useful? Email ben@purplelink.llc within 14 days of purchase and it is refunded. One refund per manuscript.

What file format?

PDF up to 20 MB. If you're submitting LaTeX, compile to PDF first (our free LaTeX-to-PDF tool works).

What about clinical or patient data?

Do not upload identifiable patient data, data covered by a data use agreement, or export-controlled material. The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's API, which keeps it for up to 30 days and does not train on it. For papers containing identifiable health information, redact before upload.

Title: Example Paper Review Report: What an AI Pre-Submission Review Finds | Purplelink

← Paper Review

Example report

# What a Paper Review report looks like

This is an example report for a fictional machine-learning manuscript, shown the way you would read it, with a note after each section on what it is for and how to act on it. A real report quotes your own text, and also comes as a Markdown file and an annotated PDF with each comment on the page it refers to.

## Critical Blind Spots

- 

Hyperparameter search asymmetry favors the proposed method.
Quoted: "We tuned learning rate and batch size on the validation
set; baselines used reported defaults."
Surfaced by: Methodology Critic, Statistical Skeptic (consensus).
Fix: Match search budget for each baseline; report the protocol
in the methods section.

- 

Sample-size justification missing for the human evaluation (Experiment 2).
Quoted: "We recruited 24 annotators ... yielding sufficient
statistical power."
Surfaced by: Statistical Skeptic.
Fix: Replace the claim with a sensitivity analysis: the smallest effect 24 annotators can detect at 80% power. Report confidence intervals for the preference rates, not p-values alone.

What this section is for. The problems a reviewer is most likely to raise. Each one quotes the passage it is about, names which of the four reviewers raised it, and says what would fix it. Findings raised by more than one reviewer are marked as consensus and listed first.

## Data-to-Claim Contradictions

- Claim: "Our method beats all baselines by a wide margin."
Evidence: Table 2 shows the proposed method tied with Baseline C
within reported standard errors on 4 of 7 datasets.

What this section is for. Places where the text claims more than the tables and figures show. Reviewers catch these quickly, and they are usually a wording fix rather than new work.

## Rectification Checklist

- A Add hyperparameter search protocol to methods (page 5,
Section 3.2). Match search budget across all baselines.

- A Replace "wide margin" framing in abstract and Section 5
with what the data actually shows.

- B Add per-seed variance to all results tables.

- B Reference [17] only weakly matches its CrossRef entry;
check the title and DOI.

- C Figure 3's y-axis breaks 0-60 then jumps to 90; redraw on
a continuous scale.

What this section is for. The same findings as a to-do list. A items are the ones a reviewer would reject over; B items weaken the paper; C items are polish. Work through the A items first.

## True Novelty Estimate

The core architectural contribution is genuinely novel and not
covered by [11] or [23]. The empirical comparison, as currently
framed, oversells the gap. Marginal advance: the proposed mechanism
is interesting but the published evidence does not yet warrant the
strength of the abstract's claim.

What this section is for. A plain read of what is new in the paper and whether the evidence supports how strongly it is claimed. Useful for the abstract and the cover letter.

## Reference Verification Summary

47 of 52 references verified against CrossRef. 3 had weak title
matches (re-check [12], [17], [31]). 2 had no DOI and could not be
located by title, verify these are correctly cited.

What this section is for. Every reference is looked up in CrossRef. Weak matches and unresolvable entries are listed so you can check them, which catches typos and citations an AI tool invented.

## Citation Support Audit

Verdicts: 18 supported, 4 partially supported, 2 not supported by
abstract, 1 contradicted, 3 source unavailable.

Claim
Cited ref
Verdict
What the source's abstract says

"Method X reduces error by 40%."
[14]
Contradicted
Abstract reports a 4% reduction, not 40%. Verify the figure.

"Prior work proved this is optimal."
[9]
Not supported by abstract
Abstract describes a heuristic; optimality may be in the full text.

5 citations with weaker claims were not audited (per-run cap).

What this section is for. For the claims that lean hardest on a citation, the cited paper's abstract is fetched and compared with what you wrote. "Not supported by abstract" means check the full text, not that the citation is wrong.

A revision review reuses most of the analysis you already paid for, so it costs less to run. The output is also tighter: it's an evaluation against the original review, not a fresh red team.

## Sample report

What does the report look like? View sample

### Response to Reviewers Review

Per-Comment Tracker

#
Reviewer comment
Verdict

R1.2
"Sample size seems small for the claimed effect."
Addressed. Power analysis added to Section 3.2.

R1.4
"Figure 3 axis labels are unreadable."
Partially addressed. Labels enlarged, but the legend still overlaps the plot.

R2.1

Hand-waved. Response says "we are aware of this work" without adding a citation or comparison.

R2.3

Rejected with argument. Response explains X is not applicable to this setting; reasoning is sound.

Missing Responses

has no corresponding response letter entry.

- [B] Fix the overlapping legend in Figure 3.

## What the report includes

- Per-comment tracker. Every reviewer comment, paired with your response, marked as addressed, partially addressed, hand-waved, rejected with argument, or not evaluable.

- Tone concerns. Defensive, dismissive, or argumentative phrasing the reviewer will notice. Suggested rewrites that say the same thing less abrasively.

- Missing responses. Reviewer comments you didn't address at all (it happens, easy to miss one).

- Action checklist. A/B/C-prioritised list of what to fix in the response letter or manuscript before hitting submit.

Same: paste the draft text. We don't accept a PDF for the response.

Does the manuscript have to be the revised version?

Yes. We check whether the response's claimed fixes are actually present in the revision.

# Citation Gap Analysis

The reverse of a citation-verifier: find prior art the manuscript should cite but doesn't. Catches the "you ignored my paper" reviewer complaint before it happens.

- Pay through Stripe

- Upload the manuscript PDF; the link is also emailed, so you can upload from another device

- Read the result on the page, or ask to be emailed when it is ready

Secure checkout via Stripe.

Deleted soon after delivery. The result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do, and if it reads as low-quality we'll refund the $3.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

### Citation Gap Analysis

Result: 5 potential gaps flagged.
Each entry below is a citation a domain reviewer might expect to see. Verify each suggestion against your own knowledge before adding — AI recall can be wrong.

Meta-analytic evidence on sleep deprivation and cognition

- Type: Missing Canonical Paper

- Suggested authors: J. Lim, D. F. Dinges

- Title hint: A meta-analysis of the impact of short-term sleep deprivation on cognitive variables

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1037/a0018883

- What should be cited: The standard meta-analysis of how short-term sleep loss affects attention, working memory, and other cognitive domains.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The introduction claims sleep loss "impairs complex reasoning" using only two small studies. A sleep researcher would expect the meta-analysis behind that claim.

- Section to add it: Introduction

Dose-response effects of partial sleep restriction

- Type: Missing Prior Finding

- Suggested authors: H. P. A. Van Dongen, G. Maislin, J. M. Mullington, D. F. Dinges

- Title hint: The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects on neurobehavioral functions and sleep physiology from chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1093/sleep/26.2.117

- What should be cited: The controlled study showing that deficits from repeated nights of restricted sleep accumulate over time.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The limitations paragraph says chronic restriction "may differ" from one night but does not cite the work that measured exactly that difference.

- Section to add it: Discussion, limitations

Psychomotor Vigilance Task as the manipulation check

- Type: Missing Framework

- Suggested authors: D. F. Dinges, J. W. Powell

- Title hint: Microcomputer analyses of performance on a portable, simple visual RT task during sustained operations

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.3758/BF03200977

- What should be cited: The original description of the reaction-time task the manuscript uses to confirm participants were sleep restricted.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The PVT is used in Section 3.3 without a source for the task or its lapse threshold.

- Section to add it: Methods, Section 3.3

Origins of defect detection in code inspection

- Type: Missing Canonical Paper

- Suggested authors: M. E. Fagan

- Title hint: Design and code inspections to reduce errors in program development

- Verification: Confirmed to exist (CrossRef match) — DOI: 10.1147/sj.153.0182

- What should be cited: The foundational paper on structured code inspection, which introduced defect detection rate as a measure of review effectiveness.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The dependent variable is defect detection rate, and the related work section starts with modern pull-request review without acknowledging where the measure comes from.

- Section to add it: Related work

Prior experiments on sleep loss and developer performance

- Type: Qualitative Gap

- Suggested authors: (unknown)

- Title hint: unknown

- Verification: No searchable title — AI recall only, unverified

- What should be cited: Earlier controlled experiments that measured programming or software-engineering task performance after a night of sleep deprivation.

- Why a reviewer would notice: The manuscript describes itself as the first study of sleep and developer performance. A reviewer familiar with this small literature may question that claim.

- Section to add it: Related work; also soften "first" in the abstract

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What it flags

- Canonical papers in the field that any expert reviewer would expect cited.

- Method or framework foundational references the manuscript builds on without citation.

- Near-identical prior findings the authors should differentiate against.

- Dataset, technique, or theory references missing from the bibliography.

Each suggestion is tagged with the section it belongs in, why a reviewer would notice the omission, and (when known) the candidate authors and title. Always verify suggestions against your own field knowledge. AI recall can be wrong.

## FAQ

How does this differ from the bibliography validator?

The free BibTeX Validator checks the citations you DO have for accuracy and existence. This tool finds the citations you DON'T have but should. Different direction.

What if it suggests papers that aren't actually relevant?

AI recall is imperfect. We mark each suggestion as a candidate to verify, not a definitive call. If a specific scan is low-quality, email ben@purplelink.llc and we'll refund the $3.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The scan result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

Title: Anonymity Check for Blind Submission - $2 | Purplelink

# Anonymity Check

Before you hit submit on a double-blind manuscript, run a leak scan. Flags author names, institution mentions, grant numbers, IRB protocols, self-citation patterns, named software artifacts, and author-owned URLs, anywhere they slipped into the body.

- Pay through Stripe

- Upload the manuscript PDF; the link is also emailed, so you can upload from another device

- Read the result on the page, or ask to be emailed when it is ready

Secure checkout via Stripe. One-time payment.

Deleted soon after delivery. The result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do, and if it reads as low-quality we'll refund the $2.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

### Anonymity Check

Result: 6 potential leaks detected.
Each item below should be removed or generalised before double-blind submission.

Self-citation patterns

- [CRITICAL] Section 2, related work: "In our previous work [14], we found that review accuracy declines after the first hour of a session."

- Fix: Rewrite in the third person ("Prior work [14] found ...") and keep [14] as an ordinary reference.

Institutions

- [MAJOR] methods section: "Participants were recruited from the professional master's program at [University Name]."

- Fix: Replace the name with "a large public university".

IRB and ethics protocol numbers

- [MAJOR] methods section, ethics statement: "The study was approved by the [University Name] IRB under protocol 2024-0917."

- Fix: Write "approved by the authors' institutional review board" and withhold the protocol number until acceptance.

Funding and grants

- [MAJOR] page 14 acknowledgements: "This work was supported by NSF grant #[Grant Number]."

- Fix: Remove the acknowledgements from the review copy and restore them in the camera-ready version.

Emails and URLs

- [CRITICAL] page 6 footnote 3: "Materials and analysis scripts are available at github.com/[username]/sleep-review-study."

- Fix: Link an anonymized copy of the repository for review, with commit history and author names removed.

Named software, datasets and systems

- [MINOR] Section 3.2: "Defects were seeded with ReviewSeed, the tool we released last year."

- Fix: Call it "a defect-seeding tool" and cite it as an anonymized reference.

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What it catches

- Author or co-author names in the body (e.g. "Smith et al." referring to the authors' own prior work).

- Institution names: "at our institution X", lab names, hospital names.

- Funder names and grant numbers ("NSF #1234567", "NIH R01…").

- IRB / IACUC / ethics-board protocol numbers tied to a specific institution.

- Author email addresses, author-owned GitHub repos, lab webpages.

- Named software or datasets that trivially identify the authors.

- "In our previous work [12]" self-citation patterns.

## FAQ

What about acknowledgements?

We scan the body and abstract. Acknowledgement sections often live at the end of the manuscript and we'll catch leaks there too, but always review them manually before submission, especially if your editor strips them automatically.

Is this a replacement for manual blinding?

No. It's a safety net. Manual review of figures, supplementary materials, and metadata is still required.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The scan result is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. The manuscript is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Cover Letter Generator

A draft journal cover letter, calibrated to the journal you're submitting to. No hype, no superlatives. Built from your abstract and the journal name. We never receive your full manuscript.

- Pay through Stripe

- Paste the title, abstract and target journal; the link is also emailed, so you can do it from another device

- Read the result on the page, or ask to be emailed when it is ready

Secure checkout via Stripe. One-time payment.

Deleted soon after delivery. The letter is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do, and if it reads as low-quality we'll refund the $2.

## Sample output

Sample output Show or hide

Dear Editor,

Please consider our manuscript, "One Night Short: Sleep Restriction and Defect Detection in Code Review," for publication in Empirical Software Engineering.

Our central finding is that a single night of restricted sleep was associated with a measurable drop in how many seeded defects experienced developers caught during code review.

We believe the work fits the journal's focus on empirical studies of software engineering practice. Code review is a routine quality gate in most teams, yet the conditions under which reviewers work are rarely measured. The manuscript may interest readers working on reviewer performance, human factors, and the design of review workflows.

In a within-subjects experiment, 42 professional developers reviewed matched pull requests once after a normal night of sleep and once after a night restricted to four hours, in counterbalanced order. Each change contained seeded defects of known type. Mean detection fell from 61% to 48% under restriction, with the largest drop for logic errors, while the number of false-positive comments did not change. The sample came from a single organization, and the effect may differ for chronic sleep loss; we discuss both limitations.

This manuscript has not been published previously and is not under review elsewhere.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

[Corresponding Author Name]
[Signature]

Illustrative example on a fictional manuscript; your result follows the same format.

## What you get

- 200-350 word draft cover letter, calibrated to the journal's scope.

- Methodology and key result summarised in plain prose.

- Originality affirmation included.

- Reviewer suggestions only when the abstract makes the expertise obvious, never invented.

- Plain prose with paragraph breaks; placeholder for your contact name and signature.

## FAQ

Why no PDF upload?

Cover letters are 95% built from the abstract and the target journal's scope. Skipping the full manuscript means we send much less of your unpublished IP to a third-party AI service. The trade-off: the letter cites the manuscript only at the level of detail your abstract supports.

Can you target a specific reviewer or editor?

You can paste an "author note" with that context when you compose. The model will weave it into the letter if it fits naturally.

What model produces the letter?

An Anthropic Claude model at a low temperature, the same model and settings as Paper Review.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The letter is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. Your abstract and journal name are sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Resume Review

Would this resume clear an ATS filter and make a hiring manager read past the first six seconds? A three-persona AI panel (ATS Screener, Hiring Manager Skeptic, Recruiter Red Flags) reads your resume the way the people actually screening it would.

- Pay through Stripe

- Read the result on the page, or ask to be emailed when it is ready

Secure checkout via Stripe.

Deleted soon after delivery. The report is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do, and if it reads as low-quality we'll refund the $5.

## Sample report

What does the report look like? View sample

### Resume Review

ATS Compatibility

- Section header "Experience" is fine, but "Where I've Worked" (used for
the second job block) won't parse: most ATS filters look for a small
set of standard headers. Rename to "Experience" or "Work History."

- Dates in "Jan 2022 - Present" format parse correctly. The single entry
written as "22-24" does not; spell out the years.

Content & Impact

- "Responsible for managing social media accounts" is a duty, not a
result. Rewrite using a number you already have on this resume:
"Grew Instagram following from 4,200 to 11,800 followers in 9 months."

- Three bullets in the 2021 role start with "Helped with...": pick the
one concrete outcome each bullet is actually describing and lead with
that instead.

What a Recruiter Would Flag

- 7-month gap between the Acme and Globex roles isn't explained anywhere
on the resume. Doesn't need a paragraph, just a single line ("Family
leave, 2022") to keep a recruiter from guessing.

- Job title says "Senior Analyst" here but "Analyst II" on LinkedIn per
your notes; pick one and make them match.

Action Checklist

- [A] Rename "Where I've Worked" to "Experience."

- [A] Add the missing number to the social-media bullet.

- [B] Add a one-line explanation for the 7-month gap.

- [C] Reconcile the job title between this resume and LinkedIn.

## What the report includes

- ATS Compatibility. Formatting, section headers, and date-format issues that would break an Applicant Tracking System's parsing, before a human ever sees the resume.

- Content & Impact. Every bullet that reads as generic duty-listing instead of a quantified result, with a suggested rewrite using only the facts you already gave it.

- What a Recruiter Would Flag. Employment gaps, short stints, inconsistent dates, missing basics, framed as what would come up in a first-pass screen, not a judgment.

- Action Checklist. A/B/C-prioritised list of what to fix before you send this resume out.

## FAQ

What file formats do you accept?

PDF or DOCX, up to 20 MB.

Will this rewrite my resume for me?

No. It critiques what you have and suggests specific rewrites for weak bullets, but you decide what to change. It won't invent facts, dates, or metrics you didn't provide.

Does it check for ATS compatibility?

Yes. One of the three personas specifically simulates how an Applicant Tracking System would parse your resume's formatting, section headers, and keywords.

What does Purplelink retain?

Only briefly. The report is deleted from our servers 30 minutes after you first open it, or after 24 hours if you never do. Your resume is sent to Anthropic's Claude API, which retains inputs for 30 days for abuse monitoring, never for training.

# Scholar Utility Belt

Scholar Utility Belt is a Chrome extension that adds journal quality badges, citation velocity, author metrics, lineage trees and retraction alerts to Google Scholar results. The core is free and open source. Since version 0.6.0 a few workflow tools are part of an optional Pro tier. The ranking lists ship inside the extension, so badges need no network request.

Add to Chrome
Source on GitHub

About 1,000 researchers use it. Rated 4.5 out of 5 from 16 ratings on the Chrome Web Store.

The extension on a real, public Google Scholar author profile: journal quality badge counts, authorship breakdown, top collaborators and per-paper rankings. Screenshot, not a mock-up.

Watch the tour

## Rankings and metrics inside Google Scholar

Journal rankings, h-index, citation velocity and retraction alerts, added to the results page.

Play the video on YouTube

What it adds

## Context next to every result

Comparing it with other Scholar extensions? The comparison of Chrome extensions for Google Scholar says plainly where a free alternative or a library tool is the better choice.

### Journal quality badges

ABDC, FT50, UTD24 and SJR rankings shown beside each result, so you can see where a paper appeared without looking the venue up.

### Citation velocity

How quickly each paper is being cited, shown next to its total citation count.

### Author metrics

h-index and g-index for authors, shown on their Google Scholar profiles.

### Academic lineage

Academic lineage trees that place an author among their advisors and students.

### Retraction alerts

A visible warning on results that have been retracted, before you cite them.

### Private by design

No account, no analytics, no remote lookups for rankings. The source is open under the ISC license, so you can read exactly what it does.

Free and Pro

## What is free and what is Pro

Reading and browsing aids stay free: quality badges, the result action grid, citation velocity, the saved-paper library, author summary metrics (h-index, g-index and similar), the query trend tracker, retraction and tortured-phrase warnings, and related works. Pro covers workflow tools that save power users time.

### Pro features

Author compare, citation lineage, extended bibliometrics (p-index, FWCI, Relative Citation Ratio, influential citations), narrative CV, the systematic-review workspace, the citation-graph overlay and the Publish-or-Perish report.

### Prices

$40 once (lifetime), or $3 a month, or $20 a year. Payment goes through ExtensionPay and Stripe.

### If you installed before 0.6.0

Every feature you had stays free, permanently. Updating from an earlier version marks your install as free for good. A fresh install, including reinstalling after removing the extension, counts as new.

Privacy and network calls

## What the extension sends, and to whom

The extension has no Purplelink server and no analytics. It sends no searches, reading history or saved papers to Purplelink. Your library and settings stay in the extension's storage in your browser. It does make these requests from your browser:

- Public scholarly services, for optional enrichment. Depending on the features you enable, it queries OpenAlex, Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenCitations, Semantic Scholar, DBLP, NIH iCite, PubMed, Europe PMC and ROR. These requests carry what the lookup needs, such as a DOI, a title, an author name or a search term, and go straight from your browser to that service.

- ExtensionPay, for the Pro license check. ExtensionPay (extensionpay.com) sells and verifies Pro licenses, with Stripe processing payment. If you never open its payment or sign-in page, the extension makes no request to extensionpay.com. When you click Unlock or "Already purchased", the extension asks ExtensionPay for a random per-install key and stores it in the extension's storage, which Chrome may sync through your Google account. After that, each time the extension checks your Pro status it sends that key to extensionpay.com and receives your plan and paid status, which it keeps locally. On extensionpay.com pages, an ExtensionPay script passes payment confirmation back to the extension. ExtensionPay and Stripe see the key and your IP address like any web request, plus whatever you enter at checkout. Purplelink never sees card details.

- No ExtensionPay calls for early installs. Installs that were updated from a version before 0.6.0 skip the license check entirely.

The full policy is in the Purplelink privacy policy.

From the same studio

ModernTex is a native LaTeX editor for Mac with BibTeX completion that searches by author or title. Paper Review reads your manuscript before a journal does. Both are made by the same one-person studio as this extension.

## Frequently asked questions

Is Scholar Utility Belt free?

The core is free and open source under the ISC license. Since version 0.6.0 there is also an optional Pro tier for people who install for the first time: $40 once, or $3 a month, or $20 a year. Anyone who installed before 0.6.0 keeps every earlier feature free.

Which features are Pro?

Author compare, citation lineage, the extended bibliometrics (p-index, FWCI, Relative Citation Ratio and influential citations), narrative CV, the systematic-review workspace, the citation-graph overlay and the Publish-or-Perish report.

I installed it before Pro existed. Do I have to pay?

No. Installs that were updated to version 0.6.0 or later from an earlier version keep every feature free permanently. A fresh install, including reinstalling after removing the extension, is treated as a new install.

Does it track what I search?

There is no account and no analytics, and nothing about your searches or reading is sent to Purplelink. Ranking badges are looked up locally. Optional lookups go to public scholarly services, and the Pro license check goes to ExtensionPay; both are described under Privacy and network calls above.

Which journal lists does it show?

ABDC, the Financial Times 50 (FT50), the UT Dallas 24 (UTD24) and SCImago Journal Rank (SJR).

Which browsers does it support?

Google Chrome, from the Chrome Web Store.
