## What each one is built around

### TeXShop

TeXShop is a Mac-only front end to TeX, written in Cocoa by Richard Koch with many contributors. It was first released on July 23, 2000, and it is free under the GPL. The MacTeX installer puts it in /Applications/TeX beside TeX Live Utility, BibDesk and LaTeXiT, so if you have installed MacTeX you already have it.

It keeps to the basics of writing LaTeX. Source and PDF preview can share one window or sit in two. SyncTeX takes you from a spot in the source to the matching spot in the PDF and back. For a thesis or book with chapter files, you put a root comment at the top of each chapter, and typesetting a chapter typesets the whole document. It also has a Macros menu, command completion on the Escape or Tab key, a BibTeX item in the Typeset menu, latexmk-based engines, and a manual of about two hundred pages in the Help menu. Its site says the current release runs on macOS 26, Tahoe, and the MacTeX page describes an extra build for Tahoe.

Choose it if you want a free editor made for the Mac, you have MacTeX already, or you have an older Mac: its site lists the current release for macOS 10.13 and later.

### TeXstudio

TeXstudio is free and open source under the GPL, written in C++ with Qt, and runs on Windows, Linux, macOS and BSD. It began in 2009 as a fork of Texmaker. Its site lists a structure view, code folding, a spell checker, grammar checker and reference checker, assistants that generate code for images and tables, more than 1000 math symbols, completion that covers references and bibliography entries, and an integrated PDF viewer with SyncTeX syncing. The build system supports several compilers, latexmk and bibliography tools, and it notices when LaTeX needs another run.

Its manual describes three more things worth knowing. There is a Git panel (the site's news puts it in 4.9.6, July 2026). There is an optional AI chat assistant, which uses your own account with a provider such as Mistral AI or Claude, or a local model. And there is collaborative editing: a second person on another computer opens a shared folder with an access code and sees your cursor and changes as you type. That feature uses a separate program, teamtype, which the manual says is currently available on macOS and Linux.

On a Mac, the download is a zip file. The site notes that the project has no Apple Developer account, so macOS may warn about an unidentified developer, and it gives the workaround of opening the app from its context menu.

Choose it if you also work on Windows or Linux and want the same editor on each, or you want shared editing sessions, a Git panel and an AI assistant without paying for them.

### ModernTex

ModernTex is the native macOS editor we make, built for journal articles, conference papers and dissertation chapters. It handles multi-file manuscripts with root file detection and a sidebar, keeps the PDF in sync in both directions, completes citations by searching your .bib by author, title or key, and explains compile errors in plain language. It adds submission-readiness checks (anonymization, page limits, required sections, packaging), an anonymized export for double-blind review, version snapshots with diffs, and visual editors for TikZ figures and tables that write the LaTeX for you. An optional Fix with AI proposes a repair for a build error and shows it as a diff first; it runs on Apple Intelligence or on your own Claude or OpenAI account.

What it does not do: real-time co-editing. Get Changes and Send Changes sync a project between your Macs or with a co-author, but two people cannot type in the same file at once. It runs only on macOS 14 or later, it is not on Windows, Linux or iPad, and it needs a TeX distribution. It was first released in September 2026, so it has far less of a track record than TeXShop or TeXstudio. Choose it if you write manuscripts on a Mac, mostly alone, and the submission-focused features are the ones you want. The trial is the full app for seven days with no account.

## What each one costs

TeXShop and TeXstudio cost nothing. ModernTex is $19.99 once, with all updates included and no subscription. The trial is the full app for seven days, and if you buy it and it is not useful, email within 14 days of purchase and it is refunded.

All three compile a LaTeX project and show a synced PDF, so the money is not for the basics. It buys the manuscript-specific features described above. If those do not match how you work, you will not get $19.99 of use from them, and a free editor is the better choice.

## Where they differ

- Operating systems and Macs. TeXstudio is the only one of the three on Windows and Linux. On older Macs, TeXShop's site lists its current release for macOS 10.13 and later, TeXstudio's current build needs macOS 13, and ModernTex needs macOS 14.

- Working with co-authors. TeXstudio offers collaborative editing through teamtype, as described above. ModernTex has no real-time co-editing. If several people edit one draft at the same time in a browser, that is Overleaf's job; the Overleaf guide covers how to use it alongside a local editor.

- AI. TeXstudio's assistant and ModernTex's Fix with AI are both optional, and both can use your own provider account. TeXstudio's can also use a local model, and ModernTex's can run on Apple Intelligence on your Mac. Check what each one sends before you use it on unpublished work.

- History and version control. TeXstudio has a Git panel and SVN support. ModernTex takes snapshots you can diff, which is separate from Git.

- Installing. TeXShop arrives with MacTeX. TeXstudio is a zip, with the unidentified-developer note above. ModernTex is a signed and notarized disk image.

## Who should pick which

- You want the Mac default and a price of zero. TeXShop. If MacTeX is installed, it is already there.

- You also use Windows or Linux. TeXstudio. It is the only one of the three that runs on all of them, and it is free.

- You have a Mac older than macOS 14. TeXShop or TeXstudio. ModernTex will not run.

- You want live shared editing without a browser. TeXstudio, within the limits of its teamtype requirement on macOS and Linux. ModernTex does not offer it.

- You write papers alone on a Mac and want submission checks, an anonymized export, snapshots, or visual TikZ and table editors. ModernTex, $19.99 once. Use the free trial on a real manuscript first.

- You are not sure. Start with TeXShop or TeXstudio. They cost nothing, and you can add ModernTex later.

## Trying more than one

A LaTeX project is a folder of ordinary files, so opening it in a second editor costs nothing but time. The setting most likely to differ is the root file. TeXShop and TeXstudio both read a root-file comment at the top of chapter files, and ModernTex detects the root file itself. Compile once in the new editor and compare the page count and reference list with your last PDF. For a longer look at fourteen Mac editors, including Texifier, Octree and VS Code, see the best LaTeX editors for Mac.

## Frequently asked questions

Is there a free TeXShop alternative for Mac?

Yes. TeXstudio is free and open source under the GPL (version 2), and it runs on macOS 13 or later, Windows and Linux. TeXShop itself is also free. Both need a TeX distribution such as MacTeX installed separately; TeXShop comes with the MacTeX installer.

Is ModernTex better than TeXShop or TeXstudio?

Not in general. It is a different kind of editor. ModernTex is a paid, Mac-only app built around writing and submitting a journal manuscript, with submission checks, an anonymized export, version snapshots, and visual editors for TikZ and tables. TeXShop and TeXstudio are free, and TeXstudio also runs on Windows and Linux. If you do not need the manuscript features, a free editor is a reasonable choice.

Do TeXShop, TeXstudio and ModernTex include LaTeX?

No. TeXShop and TeXstudio are editors that call a TeX distribution you install separately; MacTeX installs TeXShop along with TeX Live. ModernTex also needs a TeX distribution, either MacTeX or TinyTeX, and offers a one-click TinyTeX install if it finds none when you compile.

Which of the three runs on Windows or Linux?

Only TeXstudio. TeXShop is macOS only, and ModernTex needs macOS 14 or later.

What does ModernTex cost, and can I try it first?

It is $19.99 once, with all updates included and no subscription. The free trial is the full app for seven days, with no account. If you buy it and it is not useful, email within 14 days of purchase for a refund.

Can I open the same project in all three?

Yes. A LaTeX project is a folder of ordinary .tex, .bib and image files, and each editor reads it in place. Check the root file setting when you switch. TeXShop and TeXstudio both read a root-file comment at the top of chapter files, and ModernTex detects the root file itself.

Title: Overleaf compile timeout: fixes, and when to compile locally | Purplelink

How-to

# Overleaf compile timeout: fixes, and when to compile locally

By Benjamin Ampel · October 5, 2026

Overleaf stops a compile that runs past its limit, which its plan-limits page lists as 10 seconds on the free plan and 240 seconds on premium plans. Most timeouts come from a short list of causes you can fix inside the project. If yours is a heavy project that simply needs more time, a local build has no limit.

Disclosure: Purplelink makes ModernTex, a Mac LaTeX editor, and it is mentioned near the end. The fixes below come from Overleaf's own documentation on compile timeouts, and the limits from its plan limits page. Both can change, so check them if a number matters to you.

## First, check that it is a timeout and not an error

A "Timed out" message does not always mean the project is too big. A fatal error can leave LaTeX waiting for input or looping until the clock runs out, and then Overleaf reports a timeout instead of the error.

Open the Recompile menu and turn on Stop on first error. If the compile now fails quickly with a message, you have an error to fix, not a time limit to beat. Overleaf's documentation lists these as common causes of timeouts that are really errors:

- A blank line inside \author{}, \date{} or \title{}.

- \caption{} placed inside a tabular instead of outside it.

- A missing ; or ] in a tikzpicture command.

- Nested tabular environments.

- \cmidrule{3-3} written without a column range.

- Heavy use of the [H] float option. Overleaf suggests [hbt!] instead.

- Babel shorthands. Overleaf suggests avoiding them or loading babel with shorthands=off.

## Fixes to try, in order

- Stop on first error. As above. It costs nothing and rules out a hidden error.

- Compile in Fast [draft] mode. Draft mode skips rendering images. If the project builds in draft mode and times out otherwise, images are the cost. Save diagrams and plots as PDF, use JPEG only for photographs, and avoid EPS and SVG files.

- Externalize TikZ and pgfplots figures. Without this, LaTeX redraws every figure on every compile. Externalizing makes it draw each one once and reuse the result.

- Replace slow packages. Overleaf names a few: mhchem (use chemformula), version 3 of acro (go back to version 2), tabularray (use ordinary tables), and breqn (use align in place of dmath). With soul or changes, put \protect before \cite and \ref. Remove any leftover \tracingall.

Work down the list and recompile after each step. Changing four things at once tells you nothing about which one mattered.

## If it still times out: time it somewhere without a limit

A local build tells you whether the project is slow or broken. Download the project from the Overleaf menu (Download, then Source), unzip it, and install a TeX distribution: MacTeX on a Mac, or TinyTeX if you want something smaller. In the project folder, run the compiler Overleaf was using:

time latexmk -pdf -interaction=nonstopmode main.tex

Use -xelatex or -lualatex in place of -pdf if the project's compiler setting is XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX. Replace main.tex with the project's main file. The first build on a new install is slower than later ones, because fonts and package files are generated once, so time the second run.

Then read the result:

- It finishes in 30 or 40 seconds. The project is heavy and the free limit was too short. You can build it locally, or stay on Overleaf with a plan that allows more time.

- It finishes in a few seconds locally. Overleaf's shared servers were the bottleneck, or one of the package or image causes above applies there more than here. Fix the project, and the timeout will go away.

- It never finishes. Stop it with Ctrl-C and open main.log. A loop, a missing file prompt or a package conflict shows near the end of the log. No time limit would have rescued this one, so a paid plan would not either.

## Your options when you hit the limit

- Fix the project. Free, and often enough. The checklist above is the whole list.

- Move to a premium plan. Overleaf lists 240 seconds on premium plans, and many universities provide it through a site licence. Check whether yours does before paying.

- Compile locally. No limit and no account. You give up live co-editing for that copy, and you take on a TeX installation.

- Do both. Keep the shared draft on Overleaf for co-authors and build the heavy version on your own machine. The guide to Overleaf alternatives for Mac covers moving a project over and syncing with Git.

## If you are on a Mac

ModernTex is a native Mac editor that compiles on your own machine, so there is no compile limit, and it explains LaTeX errors in plain language instead of leaving you with the raw log. It is a single-user app: two people cannot type in the same document, so keep Overleaf for that. It costs $19.99 once with all updates included, after a free 7-day trial with no account, and it needs macOS 14 or later plus MacTeX or TinyTeX (it offers a one-click TinyTeX install). The free editors in the comparison of Mac LaTeX editors do the same job for no cost if you prefer them.

## Frequently asked questions

What is the Overleaf compile timeout?

Overleaf's plan-limits page lists 10 seconds on the free plan and 240 seconds on its premium plans, as of October 2026. Limits change, so check that page if the numbers matter for your decision.

Why does my project compile in Fast [draft] mode but time out normally?

Draft mode skips rendering images, so a project that compiles in draft mode and times out otherwise is spending its time on images. Convert diagrams and plots to PDF, keep JPEG for photographs, and avoid EPS and SVG, as Overleaf's documentation recommends.

Is there a time limit when I compile LaTeX on my own computer?

No. A local build runs until it finishes. The catch is that a document stuck in a loop never finishes either, so run it once with a timer and stop it with Ctrl-C if it passes a few minutes. The last lines of the .log file usually show where it stalled.

Will upgrading to a paid Overleaf plan fix a timeout?

If the project needs 30 seconds to build and you are on the free plan, yes. If a fatal error or a loop is behind the timeout, a longer limit only makes you wait longer for the same failure. Run Stop on first error before paying.

Can I compile locally and still use Overleaf with co-authors?

Yes. The project is ordinary .tex, .bib and image files. Download the source, build it locally when the compile is too heavy, and keep the shared draft on Overleaf. The Overleaf alternatives guide covers Git sync and the manual route.

From the team behind these tools

ModernTex is a native macOS LaTeX studio: multi-file manuscript navigation, a PDF preview that stays in sync, BibTeX completion that searches by author or title, and compile errors in plain language. $19.99 once, all updates included, forever.

Title: Best LaTeX editor for Mac in 2026: 14 editors compared | Purplelink

Comparison

# Best LaTeX editor for Mac in 2026: 14 editors compared

By Benjamin Ampel · May 31, 2026, updated September 11, 2026

A direct comparison of the LaTeX editors that actually work on Mac in 2026, covering what each one is good at, what it costs, and which workflow it suits. No affiliate links, no rankings padding.

Disclosure up front: I make one of the editors on this list (ModernTex). I've tried to write the comparison honestly. TeXShop is the right call for most academics today, and Texifier is the right call for most people who want a polished modern editor. ModernTex shipped its 1.0 in September 2026; I've kept its entry to what the app actually does today.

## What you actually need to run LaTeX on a Mac

A LaTeX editor is only half of the setup, and this trips up most people
coming to LaTeX on a Mac for the first time. You need two things:

- A TeX distribution. This is the engine that turns your
.tex source into a PDF. On macOS that is almost always MacTeX,
which bundles the TeX Live distribution with a few Mac-specific
applications. It is a large download, around 5 GB, because it ships
every package you might ever cite.

- An editor. This is where you write. It sends your file
to the distribution, shows you the resulting PDF, and tells you what went
wrong when the compile fails. This is the part you get to choose, and it is
what the rest of this page compares.

The distinction matters because a lot of "LaTeX won't work on my Mac"
problems are really "no TeX distribution is installed". If you open a
.tex file and nothing compiles, install MacTeX first and then
pick an editor. The one exception is Overleaf, which runs the distribution on
its own servers, so nothing is installed locally at all.

macOS does not include a TeX distribution, and neither Pages nor TextEdit
will compile LaTeX. There is no built-in option the way there is for Markdown
previewing.

## The shortlist

- TeXShop: free, ships with MacTeX, the default for most academics.

- Texifier (formerly Texpad): paid, polished, modern Mac native.

- Octree: free, AI-assisted, web-based with Mac wrapper.

- VS Code + LaTeX Workshop: free, general-purpose code editor with a strong LaTeX extension.

- Overleaf: web-based, collaborative, runs in any browser.

- ModernTex: $19.99, native macOS, focused on the academic manuscript workflow.

Those six are the ones worth a real look. Eight more that run on a Mac are covered further down, including TeXstudio and Texmaker, with a straight answer on why each is not on the shortlist.

## TeXShop

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS-only. Installed by: almost every academic with a Mac and MacTeX.

TeXShop is the editor that ships with the MacTeX distribution. It's been around for over 20 years, it's actively maintained by Richard Koch at the University of Oregon, and it does one thing well: edit a .tex file and compile it with whatever engine MacTeX provides. Side-by-side editor and PDF preview, SyncTeX click-to-source, basic syntax highlighting, multi-file support via root document declaration.

What it's good at: reliability. Compatible with every TeX distribution macro you'll encounter. No telemetry, no cloud, no subscription. If a tutorial says "open TeXShop and...", that's a feature.

What it lacks: modern UX (the interface looks like 2010), no inline BibTeX autocomplete, no plain-language error messages, no built-in tracked-changes view. Searching across a multi-file project is functional but not great.

Pick TeXShop if you want the closest thing to a default and you don't mind the dated interface. Most senior researchers do, in fact, pick TeXShop.

## Texifier (formerly Texpad)

Cost: $29.99 (occasional discount). Platform: macOS + iOS.

Texifier is the polished Mac-native option that most people who actually shop for a LaTeX editor end up with. It bundles its own TeX distribution (no MacTeX install required), has incremental typesetting (PDF updates as you type with no manual compile), a structure sidebar that maps your manuscript by sections, and the best autocomplete-for-LaTeX experience available.

What it's good at: the "it just works" experience. Outline sidebar makes navigating a long manuscript feel natural. iPad app is genuinely usable. Active development.

What it lacks: deep bibliography tooling. The BibTeX autocomplete is good but not specifically built for academic writing workflows. Tracked-changes via latexdiff requires external tools.

Pick Texifier if you want a polished, modern Mac-native experience and you're willing to pay $30 for it. This is the right answer for most working researchers writing journal-length manuscripts on a Mac today.

## Octree

Cost: Free tier with limits, paid plan ~$10/mo. Platform: Web + Mac wrapper.

The newer entrant. AI-assisted writing (suggestions, grammar, rewrites) on top of a competent LaTeX editor. The cloud-first design is a real distinguishing feature, because your project lives on Octree's servers, accessible from any device.

What it's good at: AI-assisted drafting. If you want copilot-style suggestions while you write, Octree is the only mainstream option that integrates them well.

What it lacks: on-device privacy. Your manuscript is on Octree's servers by default. For sensitive research (medical, military, IP), that's disqualifying.

Pick Octree if AI-assisted writing is core to your workflow and your research isn't sensitive. Avoid if "no cloud" is a requirement.

## VS Code + LaTeX Workshop

Cost: Free. Platform: cross-platform.

If you're a developer who also writes academic papers, VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension is the path of least resistance. Build chains are configurable, snippets are mature, Git integration is the same as your code projects. SyncTeX preview works well.

What it's good at: consistency with the rest of your toolchain if you spend most of your day in VS Code. Free, extensible, version-controllable settings.

What it lacks: a manuscript-first feel. VS Code is a code editor, so the document feels like a code file, not like a paper. Outline navigation works but isn't built for chapters and bibliographies.

Pick VS Code if you already live in VS Code and want one less context switch.

## Overleaf

Cost: Free tier (limited compile time, no Git sync), paid plans $15–$25/mo.

Browser-based, collaborative. Overleaf is the de facto choice for multi-author papers where co-authors aren't all comfortable installing LaTeX. The collaboration model (Google Docs-style) works.

What it's good at: multi-author collaboration. Templates for major journals. No local install required.

What it lacks: offline access on the free tier, Git sync on free, native-Mac feel. The editor itself runs in a browser.

Pick Overleaf if you need real-time collaboration. Many academic teams use Overleaf for collaboration and a native editor for solo writing.

## ModernTex

Cost: $19.99, one-time, all updates included, forever, after a free 7-day trial. Platform: macOS 14+. Status: shipping, shipping since September 2026; current version 1.3.6.

I built ModernTex specifically because the existing options miss a few things that matter for academic manuscript work: plain-language compile error explanations (BibTeX-style cryptic errors are the #1 frustration for new users), BibTeX autocomplete that searches by author or title across your entire .bib, revision snapshots tied to ideas not files, submission-readiness checks that catch journal-specific issues before you upload, and a live TikZ figure editor for building flowcharts and diagrams by dragging boxes instead of writing coordinates by hand.

Why a new editor when Texifier exists: Texifier is excellent but optimizes for general LaTeX users (programmers, technical writers, students). ModernTex narrows the focus to academic manuscript writers, the workflow of writing a journal article or dissertation chapter, from outline to camera-ready. That's a deliberate constraint.

What it lacks: a track record. Version 1.0 shipped in September 2026, so it has none of the twenty years of edge-case coverage TeXShop has, and no iPad app. It needs MacTeX or TinyTeX, and offers a one-click TinyTeX install if neither is found.

Pick ModernTex if you write journal articles or dissertation chapters on a Mac and the manuscript-first features above are what you keep wishing for. The trial is free for seven days; keeping it is $19.99, once.

## Eight more LaTeX editors that run on a Mac

Every one of these works on macOS today. They are not on the shortlist because, for someone choosing an editor on a Mac in 2026, each is beaten by one of the six above at the thing it is best at. The exception is TeXstudio, which is the right answer for a specific person: anyone who also works on Windows or Linux.

### TeXstudio

Cost: Free, open source. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

The most widely installed LaTeX editor that is not tied to one platform. It began as a fork of Texmaker and has grown well past it: an integrated PDF viewer with SyncTeX, a structure panel for long documents, autocomplete for commands and references, wizards for tables and figures, spell-checking as you type. It is a Qt application, so it does not look or behave like a Mac app. Menus, shortcuts and dialogs feel like they were designed elsewhere, because they were.

Pick TeXstudio if you move between a Mac and a Windows or Linux machine and want the identical editor on both. If you only write on a Mac, TeXShop does the same job and feels native.

### Texmaker

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

The editor TeXstudio was forked from, still maintained by its original author, and simpler for it: built-in PDF viewer, SyncTeX, Unicode, spell-check, code folding, and less of everything else. If you opened TeXstudio and found it busy, this is the same idea with fewer panels.

Pick Texmaker if you want a cross-platform editor and TeXstudio felt like too much. Otherwise the same advice applies: on a Mac alone, TeXShop.

### TeXworks

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux. Installed by: you, already, if you installed MacTeX.

TeXworks ships inside MacTeX and TeX Live, and was deliberately modelled on TeXShop's simplicity so that other platforms would have something like it. Source window, PDF window, SyncTeX, a typeset button. That is the whole editor. It is fine for a first document and you will outgrow it by the second chapter.

Pick TeXworks if it is already on your machine and you need to compile something today. Then pick something else.

### LyX

Cost: Free, open source. Platform: macOS, Windows, Linux.

LyX is not a LaTeX editor in the sense of the rest of this page. It is a document processor that generates LaTeX for you: you work in a structured, roughly formatted view and rarely see a backslash. For a thesis written alone, where you never need to hand a .tex file to anyone, that can be pleasant. The moment a journal template, a co-author, or a fussy figure needs raw LaTeX, you are fighting the tool. It still needs a TeX distribution installed.

Pick LyX if you want LaTeX output without writing LaTeX and will never share source. Most academics eventually need to share source.

### Archimedes

Cost: Paid, one-time. Platform: macOS, with an iOS version.

A native Mac editor for Markdown with LaTeX math, with live preview and a math-focused toolbar. It is built for writing notes, problem sets and math-heavy documents, not for compiling a full journal manuscript with a bibliography and a class file. Good at what it is for, which is not what most of this page's readers are doing.

Pick Archimedes if your LaTeX is mostly equations inside otherwise plain documents. For a paper, use one of the six above.

### TeX64

Cost: Paid. Platform: macOS.

A newer native macOS editor that compiles locally through the MacTeX or TeX Live installation you already have, rather than bundling its own distribution the way Texifier does. It is recent enough that I would not yet rely on it for a deadline, for the same reason I say that about ModernTex: no track record. Worth watching if native-Mac matters to you and you already have MacTeX installed.

Pick TeX64 if you want a native app, do not want a second TeX distribution on disk, and are comfortable being an early adopter.

### Emacs with AUCTeX

Cost: Free. Platform: anything.

AUCTeX plus RefTeX is, feature for feature, one of the most capable LaTeX environments that exists: inline previews of equations, cross-reference and citation lookup that understands your whole project, folding, and a compile loop you can bend to any shape. The learning curve is the entire Emacs learning curve. If you already live in Emacs you know this and did not need this page. If you do not, this is not the week to start.

Pick AUCTeX if you are already an Emacs user. Nobody else.

### Neovim or Vim with VimTeX

Cost: Free. Platform: anything.

VimTeX is excellent: compilation, syntax, text objects for environments and commands, folding, and forward and inverse search when paired with a PDF viewer such as Skim on the Mac. The same caveat as Emacs applies. It rewards people who already think in Vim and punishes everyone else.

Pick VimTeX if Vim is already how you write everything. Otherwise VS Code with LaTeX Workshop gives you most of the benefit with none of the modal editing.

Sublime Text with the LaTeXTools package and BBEdit with its TeX syntax highlighting also exist. Neither adds anything the eight above do not, so they are not covered separately.

## Decision matrix

- Want the default? TeXShop.

- Want polished and modern, willing to pay? Texifier.

- Want AI-assisted drafting? Octree.

- Already in VS Code? VS Code + LaTeX Workshop.

- Need real-time collaboration? Overleaf.

- Academic manuscripts on macOS as your dominant use case? ModernTex, $19.99.

- Also work on Windows or Linux? TeXstudio.

- Already live in Emacs or Vim? AUCTeX or VimTeX. You knew that.

For a closer look at three of these side by side, see ModernTex, TeXShop and TeXstudio compared.

## Installing LaTeX on a Mac: MacTeX, BasicTeX, or Overleaf

Whichever editor you land on, the install order is the same: distribution
first, editor second. And "MacTeX vs Overleaf" is not really an either-or.
One is a distribution you install, the other is a website that installs
nothing. The question is whether you want LaTeX on your own machine.
If you are weighing that move, Overleaf
alternatives for Mac covers what you give up and how to move a project.

MacTeX is the standard choice. Download the package from
the TeX Users Group, run the installer, and you have TeX Live plus TeXShop,
BibDesk and LaTeXiT. It is about 5 GB installed. Nearly every tutorial
you will read assumes this is what you have, which is a real advantage when
something breaks at 11pm before a deadline.

BasicTeX is the same distribution trimmed to roughly
100 MB. It omits most packages, so you install them individually with
tlmgr as documents demand them. Worth it if disk space is tight,
painful if you are new, because a missing package surfaces as a compile error
rather than a prompt.

Homebrew works too, via brew install --cask
mactex or mactex-no-gui. Same distribution, managed
alongside your other packages.

Installing nothing is also an option. Overleaf runs entirely in the browser.
For a single co-authored paper on a borrowed machine that is often the right
answer, and you can move to a local setup later without changing your source
files. Our LaTeX to PDF compiler will also
build a document without any local install if you just need one PDF.

Apple Silicon no longer needs any special handling. MacTeX has shipped native
arm64 binaries for years, and every editor on this page runs natively on M
series hardware.

### Which LaTeX compiler to use on a Mac

People search for the best LaTeX compiler for Mac, and the honest answer is
that it is not a Mac question. MacTeX ships all three engines you would ever
choose between, and every editor above lets you pick. pdfLaTeX
is the default, the fastest, and what nearly every journal template assumes;
start there. XeLaTeX adds system fonts and proper Unicode,
which matters for non-Latin scripts or a document that must use a specific
typeface. LuaLaTeX does what XeLaTeX does and is where newer
packages are heading. Switch engines only when a package or a font forces
you to, not because one is "best".

## Frequently asked

### Is there a free LaTeX editor for Mac?

Yes, several. TeXShop is free and arrives with MacTeX, so most people
already have it. VS Code with the LaTeX Workshop extension is free. Overleaf
has a free tier with limits on compile time and no Git sync. Of the paid
options, Texifier is a one-time $29.99 rather than a subscription.

### Does macOS come with LaTeX?

No. macOS ships no TeX distribution and no LaTeX editor. You need to
install MacTeX, or use a browser-based option like Overleaf.

### What is the difference between a LaTeX editor and a TeX distribution?

The distribution compiles your document. The editor is where you write it
and read the errors. MacTeX is a distribution, TeXShop and Texifier are
editors. You need one of each, except with Overleaf, which provides both.

### Which LaTeX editor is best for academic writing on a Mac?

For most researchers today, Texifier if you will pay for polish, TeXShop if
you want the default that every tutorial assumes. Choose Overleaf instead when
co-authors need to edit the same file at the same time.

### Is TeXstudio available for Mac?

Yes. TeXstudio runs on macOS, Windows and Linux and is free. It is the best
choice if you also work on another platform. On a Mac alone, TeXShop does the
same job and feels like a Mac app, which TeXstudio does not.

### MacTeX or Overleaf?

MacTeX if you want LaTeX on your own machine: it works offline, compiles
faster on any recent Mac, and every native editor on this page needs it.
Overleaf if co-authors need to edit the same document live, or you are on a
machine you cannot install 5 GB on. Many people use both.

### Which LaTeX compiler should I use on a Mac?

pdfLaTeX, unless something forces a change. It is the default in every
editor here and what journal templates assume. Use XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX when
you need system fonts or full Unicode. All three ship with MacTeX.

## Tools that work alongside any of these

Whichever editor you pick, these free in-browser utilities pair well:

- LaTeX to PDF: compile when you're on a machine without a TeX install.

- LaTeX to Word: convert your manuscript for journals that require .docx.

- LaTeX Diff: generate a tracked-changes PDF between two versions.

- BibTeX Validator: catch citation errors before compile.

Once the writing is done and submission is next, Paper Review red-teams the manuscript before a referee does: four reviewer personas argue over it, citations are checked against the live record, and figures are scanned for integrity problems. That one is paid, from $9 per review.

For more on the academic LaTeX workflow generally, see the LaTeX hub and the BibTeX and citations hub.

From the team behind these tools

Title: Best PII redaction tools for ChatGPT and AI chats (2026) | Purplelink

Comparison

# Best tools to redact personal information before you use ChatGPT and other AI chats (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 4, 2026, updated October 4, 2026

What each option does, what it costs, where the checking happens and what it misses, for anyone who keeps pasting client, patient, student or personal details into an AI chat. Three of the options are not software you install: provider settings, a local model and find-and-replace.

Disclosure up front: I make one of the tools on this list (Outbound Veil, a Mac menu-bar app). I have tried to write the comparison honestly, and in several cases a competitor is the better choice. Predact is free and handles files, which Outbound Veil does not. PrivacyScrubber works on Windows and Linux, which Outbound Veil does not. If your data cannot leave your machine at all, a local model beats every redaction tool here. Prices and platforms were read on each vendor's own page on October 4, 2026, and they change. Where a vendor says its software runs on your device, I write "says": I have not audited that.

## What you actually need to stop leaking data into AI chats

Redaction means replacing specific details in your text, such as a name, a date of birth or a card number, with a placeholder before the text goes to the AI. The model still answers, because it sees "[PERSON_1] was seen on [DATE_1]" and can work with that. You put the real details back yourself, or a tool does it from a saved mapping.

There are four places to intervene, and the tools here sit in different ones:

- As you type or paste. A menu-bar app or browser extension watches the text box and flags or replaces details before you press send. This is where the mistake usually happens.

- Before you paste. An app or web page where you drop in text or a file and paste the clean copy. It works on the days you remember it.

- At the account. The provider's settings and plan decide whether what you send is used for training. This removes nothing from their servers.

- Off the cloud. A model that runs on your own computer, so nothing is sent.

All of them share two limits, covered in what redaction cannot do: detection misses things, and a redacted note can still describe a situation someone could recognize.

## The shortlist

- Outbound Veil: $29.99 once, a Mac menu-bar app that checks the text field you are typing in.

- Predact: free, Mac and Windows, drop in documents, images or text.

- PrivacyScrubber: browser-based, free tier, extension for 12 chat and work sites.

- Microsoft Presidio: free open-source library for developers.

- The provider's own controls: ChatGPT settings, Temporary Chat, business plans and the API.

- A local model: Ollama or LM Studio, so nothing leaves your machine.

- Find and replace by hand: free, slow, and still useful.

Those seven cover most situations. Seven more tools and seven narrower ones follow.

## Outbound Veil

Cost: $29.99, one-time, updates included, after a free 7-day trial with no account. Platform: macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel. Mac only. Status: version 1.0.1.

Outbound Veil lives in the menu bar and reads the text field that has focus, through macOS Accessibility. When it finds something it shows a badge with the number of findings and highlights the matching text where the app allows it. You can ignore a finding, or press Redact all, which rewrites the field in place with labelled placeholders such as [SSN_1] or [EMAIL_1]. In apps you choose, it can also hold the send key until you have decided. It looks for names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, government, tax, bank and card numbers, dates of birth, medical record numbers and IBANs.

A model that runs on your Mac does the checking. Nothing you type is stored or sent, and the app has no analytics. The model is Rampart by National Design Studio, released under CC BY 4.0, and I did not train it. Purplelink ported Rampart's processing code to Swift and added rules for dates of birth, medical record numbers and IBANs. The model file is unchanged.

What it's good at: sitting where the mistake happens, in any Mac app it can read rather than one website. I tested TextEdit, Notes, Microsoft Word, Messages and text areas in Chrome. In the ChatGPT and claude.ai prompt boxes in Chrome, Redact all works, but the whole box is outlined instead of each word highlighted.

What it lacks: Mac only, and names in Latin script only. It flags the names of public figures too, which you can ignore, and it will miss some things and flag some things that are not personal information. It checks text in fields, not files, so a PDF or an image needs another tool from this list. Some apps do not expose their text fields to macOS: in my testing the Apple Mail compose window could not be read, and Safari, Slack, VS Code and the ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps are not on the tested list (the full table). It needs the Accessibility permission, plus Input Monitoring if you turn on send hold. After Redact all it does not put the original values back into the AI's answer; you swap them back yourself. By default it does not report a bare city, state or ZIP code. It is new, with no track record, and it is not a compliance product.

Pick Outbound Veil if you write or paste client, patient or student details into chat boxes on a Mac and want a check as you send. Pick something else if you are on Windows, mostly share files or screenshots, or your data has names in non-Latin scripts. The trial is free for seven days; keeping it is $29.99, once.

## Predact

Cost: Free, no card; you enter an email address to get the download link. Platform: Mac (macOS 14 recommended, Apple silicon supported) and Windows.

Predact is a desktop app where you drop in PDFs, Word files, text files, images and email clippings, or paste text and screenshots. It shows what it found, lets you select more words to redact, and you copy the result out or open a built-in browser linked to ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Perplexity. Its page says processing is local, with a Safe Mode that goes online only when you export to an AI service and a Fully Offline Mode that blocks all network use. "Persona filtering" swaps in consistent made-up details instead of tags.

What it's good at: being free, handling files and images, and running on Mac and Windows. What it lacks: it does not check what you type in other apps, so using it is a step you have to remember. The local-processing statement is the vendor's claim.

Pick Predact if your risk is documents, scans or screenshots, you are on Windows, or the budget is zero. Outbound Veil's case is that the check happens while you type, whether or not you remembered.

## PrivacyScrubber

Cost: Free up to 15,000 characters per scrub; Pro is $15 a month or $110 once; Teams is $99 a month; a developer SDK is $299 a month. Platform: a web app, a Chrome extension, an MCP server and a Node.js SDK.

The Chrome extension adds a shield button to chat boxes on 12 listed sites, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity. Click it, or press Alt+Shift+X, and the text becomes placeholders such as [NAME_1]. After the answer arrives, "Reveal Original Data" restores the real values inside the page. Its page says all of this runs in the browser tab with no server contact.

What it's good at: the full loop of redact, ask, restore, on many sites, on any system that runs Chrome. What it lacks: it lives in the browser, so it does not help in a desktop app. You press the button, so a rushed send can skip it. Larger inputs, PDF OCR and custom rules need a paid plan. I have not tested the local-processing claim.

Pick PrivacyScrubber if you use several AI sites in a browser, want the original values restored in the reply, and are on Windows or Linux or do not want an app.

## Microsoft Presidio

Cost: Free, MIT license. Platform: a Python library, with Docker and Kubernetes options.

Presidio is an open-source framework for finding and anonymizing personal data in text, images and structured data, using named-entity recognition, regular expressions, rules and checksums. You can write your own recognizers, and it runs wherever you run it with no external service. The project warns there is no guarantee it finds everything. It has moved from Microsoft's GitHub organization to a community-owned one, and its documentation says that transition is under way.

What it's good at: control. You can run it over a folder of interview transcripts and keep the pipeline in your own infrastructure. What it lacks: an interface. It will not watch a chat box, and nothing happens until you write the code that calls it. How well it works on your data is yours to measure.

Pick Presidio if you write code and need to scrub a dataset or a set of transcripts before sending it to an AI service. Everyone else should pick an app.

## The provider's own controls

Cost: The settings are free; business plans are priced by OpenAI. Platform: any.

This is not redaction, and it is the first thing to fix. OpenAI's help pages describe three things worth knowing. Under Settings, Data Controls, "Improve the model for everyone" decides whether chats on a personal account can be used to train its models. Temporary Chat is documented as not appearing in your history, not creating or updating memories and not being used to improve models while it stays temporary, though OpenAI may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety. And for ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and Edu and for the API platform, OpenAI says business data is not used for training by default unless the customer opts in. For regulated health data there is a further contract, the Business Associate Agreement; the addendum OpenAI publishes names parts of its API as eligible, and which ChatGPT plans qualify is a question for OpenAI and your counsel. Claude, Gemini and the others have their own settings.

What it's good at: it covers everything you type, costs nothing at the free end and settles the training question. What it lacks: your text still reaches the provider's servers and is kept for some period. A setting is a promise, not a physical barrier: in 2025 a US court order in a newspaper lawsuit reportedly required OpenAI to preserve chats that users had deleted, for a period that reportedly ended in September 2025, with some of what was preserved still held. And a business plan does not change what you are allowed to share. Your duties to a client, patient or student are the same either way.

Fix this layer first. For a team, a business plan with a signed agreement matters more than any redaction tool.

## A local model

Cost: Free to download. Platform: macOS, Windows and Linux for both Ollama and LM Studio.

Ollama and LM Studio run open models on your own computer. LM Studio's documentation says it can operate entirely offline once a model is downloaded, and its privacy policy says messages, chat histories and documents are not transmitted from your system when you run models locally; update checks and model downloads do use the network. Ollama has a catch: it also offers cloud models, whose names end in :cloud, that run on Ollama's servers. Its documentation says prompts to those are processed there, and that cloud features can be turned off. Choose a local model if the point is that nothing leaves the machine.

What it's good at: it is the only option here where redaction is not needed, because there is no recipient. You can paste the whole note. What it lacks: setup time, memory and capability. Open models that fit on a laptop are generally less capable than the largest hosted ones, which matters for hard reasoning and less for summarizing or drafting. That is my judgment, not a benchmark.

Pick a local model if the material must stay on your machine and a smaller model is good enough for the job.

## Find and replace by hand

Cost: Free. Platform: any text editor.

Copy the text into a plain-text editor, replace each name with "Person A", "Person B" and each date with "Date 1", and keep a small key in a separate note. Ask your question, then reverse the replacements in the answer. It works with any AI service, no vendor sees anything, and it forces you to read every line, which a tool does not. The cost is reliability on long text: a misspelled surname, a nickname or an employer slips through. Use it for short, occasional documents, or as the read-through after a detector's first pass.

## Seven more tools

Each is real and useful to someone. None is on the shortlist because one of the seven above covers the same ground for most people, or the tool addresses a different problem.

### Caviard

Cost: Free for up to 10 protected values per document; a lifetime plan at $9, which the page lists as an early discount from $15.30. Platform: Chrome extension for ChatGPT and DeepSeek.

It masks details in the browser before a prompt is sent, and Alt+R toggles original and redacted text. Its page describes detection as pattern-based, which suits emails and card numbers and tends to be weaker for names; I have not tested it on names. Pick Caviard if you use only ChatGPT or DeepSeek in Chrome and want a low-priced lifetime plan.

### ClipScrub

Cost: $29 once, 14-day free trial. Platform: macOS 15 or later; the AI-enhanced detection needs Apple silicon.

The closest Mac peer on price. ClipScrub redacts PDFs, Word files, screenshots, screen recordings, JSON, CSV, XML and clipboard text, on the Mac and with no internet needed, according to its page. A keyboard shortcut starts it. It does not watch your typing, and it says it is not a compliance service and does not guarantee complete de-identification. Pick ClipScrub over Outbound Veil if your material is files, screenshots or recordings rather than text typed into boxes.

### Clipmask

Cost: Free to download, with no subscription and no time limit. Its page also mentions a 500-copy trial limit, after which you may decide to continue, and gives no price for that. Platform: Apple silicon Macs only, macOS 14 or later.

The clipboard-only sibling of Predact, made by QCG. You copy text as usual, and a shortcut (Option+Space) offers a redacted version to paste. Its page says detection runs on the Mac, and that the only server contact is a check that the app is a licensed current version. Pick Clipmask if you want a free Mac tool that works on whatever you copy.

### RedactDesk

Cost: Free, open source (MIT). Platform: macOS 14 or later.

A Mac app for redacting PDFs, scanned ones included, with OpenAI's open-source privacy-filter model running locally. It deletes the text from the PDF rather than covering it. PDFs only. Pick RedactDesk if your whole job is PDFs.

### BlurData

Cost: $79 a year or $149 once for one person; team plans are listed. No free tier is shown. Platform: macOS 13 or later, with an iOS version.

It finds and blacks out personal details in JPG and PNG screenshots and in PDFs, on the device, in batches. Pick BlurData if your leaks are screenshots.

### Nightfall

Cost: By quote, per user per year, in two editions. Directories quote conflicting figures, so I give none. Platform: browser, endpoint, SaaS and AI-app coverage, run by an administrator.

Data loss prevention for organizations: a security team sets policies, and the software blocks or flags sensitive data going into AI apps, email and other services. Pick Nightfall if you have to enforce a policy across many employees.

### Microsoft Purview

Cost: Depends on your Microsoft licensing, which I did not confirm. Platform: managed devices, Edge and other browsers.

Microsoft's documentation describes Endpoint DLP policies that block pasting and uploading sensitive information to AI app websites on managed devices, and Edge policies that inspect prompts typed or pasted into consumer AI apps including ChatGPT, Copilot, DeepSeek and Gemini. Pick Purview if your organization already runs Microsoft 365 security and IT can turn it on.

Seven narrower options, most of them young, with a handful of installs or stars as of this writing. ChatGPT Privacy Shield is a free Chrome extension for ChatGPT only, with Pro ($9 a month) and Team ($49 a month) plans listed as a waitlist. Rescriber is a free, open-source ChatGPT extension from Northeastern University researchers. PII Scrubber (ChatGPT, free for 5 uses a day, Pro $7 a month) and Paste Redactor (four browsers, free for 100 redactions a month, then $1 a month) are small extensions with paid tiers. PIIGuardAI is an open-source Mac menu-bar proxy that blocks AI requests containing patterns such as emails and card numbers but uses regular expressions only. Maskbase is an open-source Mac app for documents. Veil (helloveil.com, $8 a month) is a different company's meeting recorder with a privacy engine; its changelog lists nothing that checks what you type in other apps.

## What redaction cannot do

Some vendors above say this plainly, and everyone should assume it. Rampart, the model behind Outbound Veil, calls itself harm reduction, not perfect protection, and Presidio says there is no guarantee it finds everything.

- It lowers the chance of a mistake. It is not compliance. No tool here makes a workflow compliant with a regulation or a contract.

- It misses things. Nicknames, initials, a case number in a format the detector has not seen. Read the text yourself before you send it.

- It flags the wrong things too. A detector cannot tell your client from a famous person, so public figures get flagged. You ignore those.

- Non-Latin scripts are a gap. Rampart's documentation reports about 98% recall for names in seven Latin-script languages but about 14% across non-Latin scripts in aggregate, from 2% for Russian to 46% for Japanese. Any tool built on it, Outbound Veil included, inherits that. Other tools use other models; test each on your languages.

- Context can identify a person with no name in sight. A rare diagnosis, a job title at a small employer, a town and a date. Detectors are built around identifiers such as names and numbers, and Rampart's documentation lists indirect identifiers as unaddressed.

- Text tools do not touch files. Attachments, screenshots and metadata need a file tool, or should not be uploaded. Nor is redaction retroactive.

## HIPAA, FERPA and client confidentiality

This is not legal advice, and the answer depends on who you are and what you hold.

HIPAA. The rule that defines de-identified health information (45 CFR 164.514) offers two routes: an expert's documented determination that the risk of identifying a person is very small, or removal of a listed set of about 18 identifier types, including names, geographic detail, dates tied to a person, contact numbers and record and account numbers, with no actual knowledge that what is left could identify someone. A detector that catches names and numbers is neither route, so text it has cleaned can still be protected health information. Whether you may send data to an AI service at all usually turns on a Business Associate Agreement and your organization's policy, so ask your compliance officer.

FERPA. The law gives parents, and students once they are 18 or in postsecondary school, rights over personally identifiable information in education records. If you grade, advise or write recommendations, check your institution's AI policy before pasting anything that names a student. Removing the name is a habit, not a rule.

Client and participant confidentiality. Lawyers, therapists, consultants and researchers have duties in codes of conduct and contracts. The American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512 (July 2024) is reported to say that a lawyer's confidentiality duty applies to generative AI tools, and that tools which train on inputs call for the client's informed consent. For research, your IRB protocol and data management plan probably already say who may see participant data, and an AI service is a new recipient. For manuscripts, see what publishers allow when you run your own manuscript through AI.

## Decision matrix

- Mac user typing or pasting client or patient text into chat boxes? Outbound Veil, $29.99.

- Documents, scans or screenshots, or on Windows, or want it free? Predact. On a Mac, ClipScrub too.

- Several AI sites in a browser, values restored in the reply? PrivacyScrubber.

- Only ChatGPT in Chrome? Caviard, Privacy Shield or Rescriber.

- Only PDFs? RedactDesk. Mostly screenshots? BlurData or ClipScrub. Whatever you copy? Clipmask.

- A developer scrubbing a dataset or transcripts? Presidio.

- A team with a policy to enforce? A business plan first, then Nightfall or Purview.

- The data must not leave the machine? A local model.

- Occasional short text, no new software? Find and replace.

## A routine that holds up

- Write down what must never go in, then fix the account: turn off the model-improvement setting or use a business plan, and use Temporary Chat for one-off questions.

- Put a detector where you type. A menu-bar app or an extension, or a scrubber page you open every time.

- Test it with fake data first. Paste a made-up record with a name, a number, an address and a date, and see what it catches. This applies to every tool here, including mine, and takes two minutes.

- Read what you are about to send. Look for what a detector would not know: a nickname, an employer.

- Ask with placeholders and restore by hand. Keep any key in a separate local note. For the most sensitive material, use a local model or skip AI.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best way to remove personal information before using ChatGPT?

Use layers. Set the account so chats are not used for training, or use a business plan. Put a detector where you type. Read what you are about to send. For material you cannot send at all, use a local model.

### Does ChatGPT Temporary Chat keep my data private?

Only partly. OpenAI says a temporary chat stays out of your history, creates no memories and is not used to improve its models while it remains temporary, but that it may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety. The text still reaches OpenAI's servers.

### Is a redaction tool enough for HIPAA?

No. HIPAA defines de-identified data by an expert determination or by removing a listed set of identifiers with no actual knowledge that the rest could identify the person. A tool that catches names and numbers is neither. This is not legal advice; ask your compliance officer or counsel.

### Do these tools send my text to a server?

Most say detection runs on your device or in your browser. That is the vendor's claim, not something I tested. Enterprise DLP and the provider's own plans involve servers by design. A local model keeps text on your machine.

### Is there a free tool to redact personal information for AI chats?

Yes. Predact (Mac and Windows) is free, and Clipmask (Apple silicon Macs) is free to download, with a 500-copy trial limit mentioned on its page. RedactDesk is a free, open-source Mac app for PDFs. Rescriber is a free, open-source Chrome extension for ChatGPT. PrivacyScrubber and Caviard have free tiers with limits.

### Is there a Mac app that checks for personal information as I type?

Outbound Veil, which Purplelink makes, checks the text field you are typing in, in the apps it can read. It costs $29.99 once with a 7-day trial. Other Mac tools work on what you copy or drop in: Clipmask, ClipScrub and Predact. I found no other that watches the typing itself, but I may have missed one. Outbound Veil is Mac only, recognizes names in Latin script only, and will miss some things.

### Should I run a local model instead of redacting?

If the material must not leave your machine, yes. Ollama and LM Studio run open models on your computer. The cost is setup time and usually a less capable model. Ollama also offers cloud models that run on its servers, so choose a local one.
