Title: Best software for tracking your research record: submissions, grants and CV (2026) | Purplelink

← All guides

Comparison

# Best software for tracking your research record: submissions, grants and your CV (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 4, 2026, updated October 4, 2026

What each option costs, what it tracks, where your data lives and what it leaves out, for anyone who wants to know where a paper is in review, which grants are pending and what goes in the CV, without rebuilding it from old emails. Several options are not apps: a spreadsheet, profiles you already have, and your university's own system.

Disclosure up front: Purplelink, the studio I run, makes one tool on this list, Vitae, a free Mac app, and sells the tracker spreadsheets described under spreadsheets. I have tried to write the comparison honestly, and in several cases something else is the better choice. Manuscripts is a more focused submission tracker for the Mac. Papertrek runs in a browser, which Vitae does not. A spreadsheet you build yourself costs nothing and does much of the job. If your university runs Interfolio or Watermark, you will submit your tenure case there whatever else you use. Prices and platforms were read on each vendor's own page on October 4, 2026, and they change. I did not test the other tools; the entries describe what each vendor's page says. Some vendor sites refused automated reading; where I relied on a search excerpt, or could not read a page, I say so. Enterprise systems publish no price, so I give none.

## What you are tracking, and two kinds of record

A research record has four layers, and tools differ mostly in how many they cover:

- Published work. Papers, books, talks. Every tool here handles it.

- Work in motion. A manuscript under review at a particular journal, each revision round, the reviewer comments, a grant proposal pending, the effort you have committed. A CV shows none of it, and a tenure case or a grant renewal leans on it.

- Teaching, service, mentoring and reviewing. Easy to forget and hard to evidence years later.

- Documents made from the above. The annual report, the CV, the NIH biosketch, the promotion dossier. Each cuts the same facts a different way for a different period.

There are also two kinds of record. An institutional faculty-activity or dossier system (Interfolio, Watermark Faculty Success, Elsevier Pure, Symplectic Elements) is bought by the university, built for reporting and review, and usually mandatory. You do not choose it. A personal record is one you choose, hold in a form you control and take with you when you change employers. It can also hold what no one asks to see: the rejections, the timing, the grant you dropped. The sensible arrangement is both: keep your own record, and copy from it into the institutional system at each deadline. This page compares software for the personal record. For how to assemble a tenure case itself, see how to track your academic CV and tenure case.

## The shortlist

- Vitae: free Mac app that keeps submissions, grants, projects and teaching in one local record and builds the CV from it.

- A spreadsheet: your own, or one of Purplelink's trackers ($9 to $14 each, $39 for the bundle).

- Notion or Airtable: a database you shape yourself.

- A dedicated submission tracker: Manuscripts for Mac, or Papertrek, Paperpin and Subthesis in a browser.

- ORCID and Google Scholar: free profiles for published work.

- Your university's system: Interfolio, Watermark and others.

- Zotero and plain notes: your papers next to your reading.

- A LaTeX or Word CV: the document is the record.

Those eight cover most situations. More tools follow, then what to log whichever you pick.

## Vitae

Cost: Free, no account, no limits on the record. Vitae Plus, an optional add-on, is $2.99 a month or $23.99 a year with a 7-day trial, and is included for life in the $54.99 Mac Suite. Platform: macOS 15 Sequoia or later, Mac only. Status: version 1.0.1, which its page labels beta.

Vitae is a Mac app with structured records for submissions, grants, projects, collaborators, teaching, service and mentoring. A submission keeps its venue, dates, each review round, the decision, manuscript versions and a cover letter. When you pick a target venue it shows published acceptance rates for about 13,700 journals and conferences, and it forecasts publication timelines from your own history. A grant runs from planning to award with requested and awarded amounts, your share and reporting dates, and the app can search Grants.gov and fill an NSF or NIH award from its number. You can connect a mailbox read-only, and Vitae proposes updates from journal-system messages; you review each one. A tenure view counts your record against expectations you enter, such as articles, funding, h-index, talks and service.

The CV is built from the record. You can import the CV you have, from Word, PDF, RTF, ODT or a web page, and check every parsed entry before it saves. Pick a format, a length and a date range and it fills itself in. Export goes to PDF, LaTeX or rich text that opens in Word; Word (.docx) export with your own templates is a Plus feature. There is also RIS export, aimed at Interfolio, Watermark and reference managers, and one-click send to Zotero.

What it's good at: covering the work in motion and the finished record in one place that lives on your machine. Everything is stored on your Mac with a daily backup and undo, and the free tier is the whole record.

What it lacks: it runs on a Mac only, with no Windows, Linux, iPhone, iPad or web version. Records are not synced between machines; the page says iCloud sync is supported in the data model and may be enabled in a future version. It is a one-person, one-computer record: I found nothing on its page describing shared editing, so coauthors are people you record, not people who log in. It does not submit anything to Interfolio or Watermark; you export and upload. The revision workspace (which splits a decision letter into reviewer points and exports a response letter), the NIH biosketch and Current and Pending drafts, Word templates and ORCID sync are Plus features. It is a new app with a beta label, and the forecasts and counts are only as good as what you enter.

Pick Vitae if you work on a Mac and want the pipeline, the record and the CV in one place you own. Pick something else if you are on Windows or Linux, need to work from a phone, or want one record that several people edit. Vitae is a free download.

## A spreadsheet

Cost: Your own: whatever you already pay for Excel, Numbers or Google Sheets. Purplelink's trackers: $12 each for the submission, tenure and grant trackers, $9 for the job-market tracker, $14 for the screening matrix, $39 for all six with the Grant Budget Builder. Platform: Purplelink's are .xlsx files that open in Excel and import into Google Sheets.

A spreadsheet with one row per submission attempt is the most common personal tracker, and it works. Record the journal, the date submitted, the manuscript number, each decision and its date. The failure is the rest: reviewer comments, grants, teaching and service end up in other files, and nothing makes a CV from the rows.

The Purplelink trackers, which I make, skip the building. The Journal Submission and R&R Tracker keeps one row per round and counts days in review, flags a revision that is overdue or due soon and an editor worth nudging, and has a matrix for reviewer comments. It holds 150 rounds and 400 comments. The Tenure and Promotion Dossier Tracker has five logs (publications, grants, teaching, service, mentoring) measured against targets you set. No institution's standards are built in, and it tracks progress, not the likelihood of a decision. The Grant Pipeline and PI Effort Tracker follows up to 100 proposals through stages and adds up each person's committed effort. It does not know your sponsor's effort rules and does not connect to a grants system.

What a spreadsheet is good at: any platform, no account, a file you own, and Google Sheets lets a coauthor see it. What it lacks: everything is typed by hand, nothing produces a formatted CV or a dossier, and the Purplelink files have row limits and one worksheet per job rather than one connected record.

Pick a spreadsheet if you want something plain, you are on Windows, or you want to share it with a coauthor. Build your own if you like that, buy ours to start from a finished design, or choose Vitae if you want the CV generated.

## Notion or Airtable

Cost: Notion: free; Plus is $10 per member per month, and students and educators with a school email get Plus free for one member. Airtable: a free plan for individuals and small teams; Team is $20 per user per month billed annually. Platform: web, with apps.

Both are databases you design. Notion's template gallery lists several academic trackers, including "Submission Tracker - Scientific Manuscripts", "Manuscript Submissions Tracker", "Paper Tracker" and "Research Project Tracker". I did not find an academic submission tracker among Airtable's templates, though it has a grant tracker template aimed at nonprofits. Either can hold submissions, grants and teaching in linked tables.

What it's good at: linked records, views by deadline or status, phone access and sharing. What it lacks: the structure is yours to design and keep tidy, nothing turns the rows into a CV, and the record lives on the vendor's servers, so test the export before you rely on it.

Pick Notion or Airtable if you already run your work in one of them and enjoy building.

## A dedicated submission tracker

Manuscripts (manuscripts-app.com). Cost: $49 once, 14-day free trial; all 1.x updates are included. Platform: macOS 14.6 or later, Apple silicon and Intel.

Manuscripts is a Mac app for the submission lifecycle: drafting, review rounds, revisions, authors, journal submissions, deadlines and decision letters. Its page says there is no server and that data stays on your Mac with automatic backups on launch; one license covers up to three Macs, and lab licenses exist for five or more people. Its page mentions nothing about grants, teaching or a CV.

What it's good at: being focused. If papers are the whole job, it is a simpler tool than Vitae. What it lacks: everything outside submissions, and it is Mac only. Pick Manuscripts if you only track papers on a Mac and prefer to pay once. Pick Vitae if you also want grants, teaching and the CV. Papertrek, Paperpin and the Subthesis tracker, covered below, are the ones to look at if you are not on a Mac.

## ORCID and Google Scholar

Cost: Both free. Platform: web.

ORCID is a not-for-profit registry that gives you a persistent identifier. Its record has eleven activity sections, including works, funding, employment, education, service and peer review. You can add works yourself or let connected systems add them. One limit worth knowing: peer review items can only be added through its API, not typed in. Many systems read from ORCID, and for NIH applications due on or after January 25, 2026, the biosketch and Current and Pending forms must be completed in SciENcv with your ORCID iD linked to your eRA Commons account, according to NIH notice NOT-OD-26-018. Any biosketch draft from another tool, Vitae's included, is something to copy into SciENcv. ORCID has no place for a manuscript under review or a decision, and it does not make a CV.

A Google Scholar profile needs a Google account. It computes total citations, h-index and i10-index, both overall and for recent years, and updates them as it finds new citations. You can add articles by search, enter them by hand, or let it add new ones automatically, and automatic additions are worth an occasional check for papers that are not yours. It tracks published work only.

Pick both if you publish. They are the cheapest, lowest-effort part of the record, other people look at them, and keeping them current takes minutes. They are not a system of record for anything unpublished.

## Your university's system

Cost: Paid by the institution; no public price for any of these. Platform: web.

Interfolio, which is part of Elsevier, sells Faculty Activity Reporting and Review, Promotion and Tenure to universities. Its pages describe the first as a place to collect teaching, research and service activity and export it to CVs, promotion files and annual reviews, and the second as where candidates assemble their case, pulling from the first or from institutional systems. Both say to request a consultation for pricing. Watermark Faculty Success, formerly Digital Measures, covers teaching and mentoring, publications, presentations and grants, service and administrative data such as appointments and tenure timelines, and produces CVs, biographical sketches and annual reports; its page directs institutions to contact sales.

What they're good at: they are the official record. Deans and committees read from them, and they pull in course data, grants and HR data so you do not retype it. What they lack: they hold what your institution asks for, in its categories, for as long as you are employed there, and they are built around reporting more than around your own planning. Ask what you can export before you change jobs.

If your university has one, use it for what it requires, and keep a personal record in the same categories so each deadline is copying, not reconstruction. Elsevier Pure and Symplectic Elements, below, are the same kind of system.

## Zotero and plain notes

Cost: Zotero is free with 300 MB of file storage; 2 GB is $20 a year, 6 GB $60, unlimited $120. Platform: Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS and Android.

Zotero is a reference manager, not a record of submissions or grants. It does one thing well for this job: its My Publications collection builds a bibliography of your own work and can share it on your zotero.org profile, with copyright options. Keep your papers there if you keep your reading there. A plain folder of dated notes, one file per paper with the decision letters pasted in, is the low-tech option: it survives any software, and a text search finds what you need.

Pick Zotero as a complement, not a replacement. It has no concept of a grant, a review round or a course.

## A LaTeX or Word CV

Cost: LaTeX is free; Overleaf's free plan allows one collaborator per project, the student plan is $8.25 a month billed annually, Standard is $199 a year. Word templates come with Word or from your department. Platform: anywhere.

The oldest method makes the CV the record. In LaTeX, moderncv offers five ready-made styles, its current version is 2.6.1 (June 2026), and it ships with TeX Live and MiKTeX. In Word, the template your department circulates is usually the right one. If you write LaTeX on a Mac, see the Mac LaTeX editors comparison, and for browser editing the Overleaf alternatives guide.

What it's good at: total control of the output, in exactly the format a committee wants. What it lacks: memory. Papers under review, rejected attempts and grant resubmissions live in your inbox, and each differently cut document is another file to keep in sync. Generators fill the gap: Vitae builds from your own records and exports LaTeX, and SigmaCV is free, open source and builds a CV from ORCID, OpenAlex and Crossref into PDF, DOCX, LaTeX or Markdown. Pick a hand-made CV if the document is all you are ever asked for.

## More tools

Each is real and useful to someone. None is on the shortlist because one of the eight above covers the same ground for most people, or the tool solves a narrower problem.

### Papertrek

Cost: Free while in beta; paid plans arrive in 2027 at the earliest, with a free tier planned. Platform: web, hosted in the EU.

Tracks a paper from idea to published: submissions, revisions, reviewer notes and decisions. You connect ORCID or drop in a BibTeX file to import, and its page says you can export or delete everything at any time. Grants, teaching and the CV are not on its page. Pick Papertrek if you want a submission tracker in a browser, on any computer, and accept an early-stage product.

### Paperpin

Cost: Free, no card. Platform: web.

Its page lists deadlines for more than 600 conferences and 75 journals, manuscript status, rebuttal windows and decision dates; I have not checked those counts. Pick Paperpin if conference deadlines drive your year and you want a free web tracker.

### Auctorium

Cost: $4.99 on the App Store; I could not confirm whether further unlocks are sold in the app, because its website did not load. Platform: iPhone, iPad and Mac, on OS version 26.2 or later.

Tracks papers with venues, coauthors, attachments, several deadlines per submission and reminders. Pick Auctorium if you want deadlines on your phone and are on a recent Apple OS. It does not cover grants or a CV.

### Subthesis journal submission tracker

Cost: Free, no login. Platform: web.

A form-style log with the fields a submission record needs: title, journal, date, manuscript ID, editor, status, decision dates and revision deadlines. Its page says the data is kept in your browser's local storage, with export available, so switching machines loses the log unless you exported. Pick it if you want a free log without an account.

### VitaMine

Cost: Free tier; VitaMine+ is 25 euros a year. Platform: web, with invitation codes for early testers.

A CV manager built on a structured database: import an existing CV or biosketch, sync from ORCID, OpenAlex and Zotero, download the whole thing as an SQLite database, and export to Word templates. Its page says selected CV text goes to OpenAI if you use AI-assisted import. I found no submission or deadline tracking on its page. Pick VitaMine if you can get an invitation and want a browser-based CV record.

### Interfolio Dossier

Cost: Free tier; Dossier Deliver is $59.99 for 50 deliveries. Platform: web.

A personal account for career materials and confidential letters of recommendation, with free applications to Interfolio-hosted positions. It is the place for letters on the job market. It stores documents, not records. Pick Dossier if you are applying for positions.

### Elsevier Pure

Cost: Institutional; its page says contact sales. Platform: web.

A research information management system used, per its page, by more than 500 institutions. It brings together publications, funding, people and projects, syncs with Scopus, ORCID and HR and finance systems, and powers researcher profiles. It is built for research administration. If your university has it, expect it to know your published work and your funding; your pipeline still needs a home.

### Symplectic Elements

Cost: Institutional; its page says book a demo or contact the company. Platform: web.

From Digital Science. It harvests publications from PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Crossref and arXiv for you to claim, picks up grants through its Dimensions integration, and records teaching and professional activities, with faculty activity reporting on top. The harvesting means less typing, if the matches are right. If your university has it, check what it matched, then let it fill in the rest.

### Web of Science Reviewer Recognition

Cost: Free to reviewers, according to Clarivate. Platform: web.

Formerly Publons. You opt in, and reviews for participating journals (Clarivate's page counts more than 9,500) are added to your Web of Science Researcher Profile as verified, without exposing the review, and the profile can produce a CV that includes them. It records reviews you do, not manuscripts you submit. Clarivate's page refused automated reading, so this entry rests on a search excerpt. Use it if you review a lot and want evidence for a promotion file.

### Journal systems: ScholarOne and Editorial Manager

Cost: Not sold to authors; the journal's publisher licenses it. Platform: web.

The system a journal uses is itself a tracker. ScholarOne's Author Center, per Clarivate, shows your submitted manuscripts, recent correspondence and status, with prompts for a revision. Editorial Manager lets authors track manuscript status. Each journal picks its own system, so your history is spread across logins. It is the authority on one submission and a poor place to keep the whole record.

### ResearchGate, Academia.edu and Semantic Scholar

Three profile sites. ResearchGate calls itself a professional network, is free to join, lets you claim publications and shows reads for work you upload. Academia.edu is built around uploading and sharing papers; its site refused automated reading, so I give no price. Semantic Scholar creates an author page automatically from public papers, and you can claim and correct it. All three are about visibility of published work. None tracks submissions, grants or tenure.

## What to log, whatever tool you pick

The tool matters less than the habit. The aim is that the dossier, the annual report or a grant renewal is an afternoon of copying. The existing tenure case guide covers the dossier side; this is the record underneath it.

For each submission attempt:

- Venue, manuscript number, date submitted and the version you sent.

- Each decision, its date and its verdict, and the editor's letter saved whole.

- For each round: the reviewer comments, your response and the date you resubmitted.

- The outcome, and when it is a rejection, where the paper went next. "Rejected twice, 14 months to acceptance" can only be written from dates.

For each grant: sponsor, mechanism, your role, date submitted, requested and awarded amounts, your share, the effort you committed, reporting dates, the outcome and the reviewer feedback. Keep the unfunded ones; resubmissions start there.

For teaching, service, mentoring and reviewing: course, term and enrollment with the evaluation score and its response rate; committees with the dates; advisees and where they went; the journals you reviewed for and the year. Log a review by journal and year, not by manuscript title, and check the journal's confidentiality terms.

Once a year: write a paragraph on what the research, teaching and service added up to while you remember. Update ORCID when a paper is accepted. Tag each item with its year so a review period is one filter.

## Decision matrix

- Mac user who wants submissions, grants and the CV in one place? Vitae, free.

- Only papers, on a Mac, and you prefer to pay once? Manuscripts, $49.

- Papers in a browser, on Windows or Linux? Papertrek or Paperpin. For a free log with no account, the Subthesis tracker.

- Deadlines on a phone? Auctorium, or a spreadsheet in Google Sheets.

- Want a plain file you control? A spreadsheet, or the Purplelink trackers at $9 to $14.

- Already live in Notion or Airtable? Build it there.

- Publishing at all? ORCID and a Google Scholar profile, both free.

- University runs Interfolio, Watermark, Pure or Elements? Use it for what it requires, and keep your own record.

- Reviewing a lot? Web of Science Reviewer Recognition.

## How to choose

- Find out what your university requires. Ask your department which system the tenure case and annual review go into, and what you can export.

- Decide what has to be on a phone. If you need a record on a phone or on two computers, rule out any tool that is local to one Mac, Vitae and Manuscripts included.

- Count how many things you track. Only papers: a tracker or a spreadsheet. Papers, grants and teaching: Vitae, a database or several sheets.

- Check the exit. Before you enter five years of history, find the export. A file you can open elsewhere is worth more than a feature. Then test the tool on one real paper and one real grant.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best software for tracking journal submissions?

On a Mac, Manuscripts ($49 once) or Vitae (free) track each attempt, round and decision; Vitae also covers grants and the CV. In a browser, Papertrek and Paperpin are free for now. A spreadsheet with one row per attempt also works.

### Is there free software that tracks submissions, grants and a CV together?

Vitae does, on macOS 15 or later. Its record-keeping is free with no limits; an optional paid add-on covers reports and Word templates. Elsewhere, a spreadsheet or Notion setup can hold all three if you build it, but nothing formats the CV for you.

### Do I still need my own record if my university uses Interfolio or Watermark?

Yes. The university's system holds what the institution asks for, in its categories, while you work there. A personal record keeps the rest, such as rejections and timings, and moves with you. At each deadline you copy from it into the required system.

### Do ORCID or Google Scholar track papers under review?

No. ORCID is a registry of works, funding, employment and similar items, and Google Scholar counts citations to published work. Neither has a place for a manuscript's status or decisions, and neither makes a CV.

### Does Vitae work on Windows or iPhone, and does it sync?

No. Vitae runs on macOS 15 or later only, and records live on your Mac with no sync between machines. Its page says iCloud sync is supported in the data model and may be enabled in a future version. For a phone or a second computer, use a web tool or Google Sheets.

### Is a spreadsheet good enough?

For submissions, usually yes, with one row per attempt and every decision date. It struggles once you add reviewer comments, grants and teaching, because the pieces end up in different files and nothing builds a CV from them. Purplelink sells ready-made trackers, so weigh that disclosure.

### What should I log for each submission?

The venue, manuscript number, date submitted, the version sent, each decision with its date and verdict, the reviewer comments and your responses, the resubmission date and the outcome. Save each decision letter whole. Then a paper's history and a venue's turnaround come from fact.

Title: Best Chrome extensions for Google Scholar (2026) | Purplelink

← All guides

Comparison

# Best Chrome extensions for Google Scholar (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 4, 2026, updated October 4, 2026

What each extension does on or around Google Scholar, what it costs, what the store says it collects and what it cannot do, for anyone who searches Scholar daily and wants journal context, metrics, retraction warnings, full text and a way to save what they find.

Disclosure up front: I make one of the extensions on this list (Scholar Utility Belt). I have tried to write this honestly, and in several places another tool is the better choice. Two free extensions, Rapid Journal Quality Check and ExCITATION, each list about 200,000 users to my 1,000, and they show journal rankings as well as mine does or better. For full text, Google's own Scholar Button and your library's tool do something mine does not. I did not install or test any of the other extensions. What I say about them comes from their Chrome Web Store listings and the vendors' own pages, read on October 4, 2026; user counts, ratings and versions are as shown that day, and privacy labels are what each developer declares, not something I audited. Some tools fetch papers from unauthorized copies. I do not cover or recommend them.

## What you want an extension to do

Google Scholar is good at finding papers and thin on everything around them. A result shows a title, authors, a venue string, a citation count and maybe a PDF link. It does not say whether the venue is any good, whether the paper was retracted, whether you can read it through your library, or what later papers said about it. Extensions fill six gaps: venue context (a badge or quartile beside each result), citation and author metrics, full text (a legal copy or a library link), saving and exporting to a reference manager, trust signals (retractions, how later papers cite it, public comments) and finding more (related papers, alerts).

Scholar already does some of this. Its help page describes email alerts from any search (the envelope icon, no Google account needed), a private library with your own labels, and Cite export to BibTeX, EndNote, RefMan and RefWorks. Try those first, then add extensions for what is still missing.

## The shortlist

- Scholar Utility Belt: rankings, citation and author metrics, retraction warnings and a saved list. Free core.

- Rapid Journal Quality Check: free, the longest list of rankings.

- ExCITATION: free, SJR quartiles plus ABS and ABDC.

- Scholar H-Index Calculator: free, indices with custom formulas.

- Google Scholar Button: Google's popup for finding, citing and saving from any page.

- Zotero Connector: free, saves references and PDFs; Zotero warns about retractions.

- Paperpile extension: the capture tool for a paid reference manager.

- Unpaywall: free, finds legal free copies.

- LibKey Nomad and Lean Library: free, links to full text your library subscribes to.

- EndNote Click: free, one-click PDF access from Clarivate.

- scite: shows whether later papers support or dispute a paper.

- Publish or Perish: a free desktop program for citation analysis, not an extension.

Those twelve cover most situations. Seven more extensions follow, then what I left out and why.

## Scholar Utility Belt

Cost: Free core, open source under the ISC license. Optional Pro is $40 once, $3 a month or $20 a year. Platform: Chrome only. Store listing: version 0.6.2, about 1,000 users, 4.5 out of 5 from 16 ratings.

It adds badges beside each Scholar result. The store listing names ABDC, FT50, UTD24 and CORE, and the project's README names more, including VHB, CCF, SCImago quartiles and ERA. The lists ship inside the extension, so badges need no network request. Beside them are citations per year, an "Emerging" signal for recent papers, a retraction warning and a tortured-phrase warning, which checks each result's title and snippet against the Problematic Paper Screener's list of odd paraphrases that can point to paper-mill text. The retraction warning looks up the DOI in a Retraction Watch-derived list that ships with the extension, and can ask Crossref if that list is not loaded. Author profiles get h-, m-, L-, g- and h5-index and the share of open access papers. There is also a local saved-paper library with notes and tags, BibTeX export, a query trend panel and related works.

Pro adds author compare, citation lineage, extended bibliometrics (p-index, field-weighted citation impact, Relative Citation Ratio, influential citations), a narrative CV, a systematic-review workspace, a citation-graph overlay and a Publish-or-Perish-style report. Anyone who installed before version 0.6.0 keeps the features that existed then, free.

Privacy, exactly: no account, no analytics, no Purplelink server; your library and settings stay in the extension's storage in your browser. Depending on the features you turn on, it sends lookups from your browser to public services (OpenAlex, Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenCitations, Semantic Scholar, DBLP, NIH iCite, PubMed, Europe PMC and ROR), carrying what the lookup needs, such as a DOI, title, author name or search term. Pro licensing goes through ExtensionPay and Stripe: no request to ExtensionPay unless you open the payment or sign-in page, and after that a random per-install key is sent to check your plan. An optional setting in Options asks Chrome for access to all sites and does nothing unless you press its button. The product page lists each call, and the source is on GitHub.

What it's good at: several jobs in one free extension, with rankings that need no lookup. What it lacks: it works in Chrome only. Its lists are strongest for business, information systems and computing venues. Elsewhere you get the broader lists the README names (SCImago quartiles, ERA, the Norwegian register), which are coarser than a field's own list, so I expect it to be less useful for medicine, law or the humanities, though I have not tested it there. It does not know your library's subscriptions: its PDF button opens the best link it can find (a publisher link, an arXiv or SSRN copy, or an open access copy flagged through Unpaywall), which is not the same as a full-text finder. It is not a reference manager: the saved list exports BibTeX, but you cannot cite from it in Word or Google Docs. The README says OpenAlex asks for a free API key, and without one some lookups may be rate-limited or fail. With 16 ratings, it has little track record.

Pick Scholar Utility Belt if you search Scholar in business, information systems or computer science and want badges, retraction warnings, author metrics and a saved list in one place. Pick something else if you only want badges (the next two), need full text, or need a reference manager.

## Rapid Journal Quality Check

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 4.1.4, about 200,000 users, 4.3 from 66 ratings.

It shows rankings next to Scholar results, on author profile pages and on related subpages. The listing names SJR, ABDC, ABS, VHB, FT50, CORE, CCF, BFI, CNRS, FNEGE, HCERES and the SCImago journal and country rank. You choose which to display, a plus button reveals others, hovering shows the journal name and h-index, and the toolbar icon opens a search box for looking up a journal by name. The listing says it is open source and that the developer will not collect or use your data.

What it's good at: the widest list of rankings here, including European ones. What it lacks: going by the listing, badges and nothing else: no citation velocity, retraction warning, author metrics or saved list.

Pick it if you want only journal rankings and need a list that I do not carry, for example CNRS or HCERES.

## ExCITATION

Cost: Free; the listing says "No registration, no account, no premium tier required for any feature." Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 1.4.1, about 200,000 users, 4.5 from 108 ratings.

It adds SCImago (SJR) quartiles and impact scores to every result, covering more than 32,000 journals in all disciplines, plus ABS Academic Journal Guide 2024 and ABDC 2025 classes. It can also sort results by citation count, flag predatory journals and preview abstracts without leaving the page. Its privacy label lists personally identifiable information, user activity and website content.

What it's good at: SJR across all fields, and sorting. What it lacks: only three ranking sources, so no FT50, UTD24 or CORE, and, going by the listing, no retraction warning or author metrics.

Pick it if you work outside business and computing and want quartiles and a predatory-journal flag with nothing else on the page.

## Scholar H-Index Calculator

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 4.4.1, about 10,000 users, 4.3 from 54 ratings, developer listed as Agelin Bee.

It computes bibliometric indices over Scholar pages as you browse, lets you write your own formulas, can remove self-citations and ghost citations from the totals, completes author lists that Scholar truncates, and clusters authors who share a name. The listing says it runs in the browser with no backend.

What it's good at: custom formulas and self-citation cleaning, which my extension does not do. What it lacks: no journal rankings or retraction warnings, and the listing does not name which indices it ships, so check before relying on a specific one.

Pick it if you evaluate authors or journals and want self-citations out of the numbers. For a formal citation analysis, see Publish or Perish below.

## Google Scholar Button

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 3.6, last updated May 16, 2024, about 3,000,000 users, 4.6 from 1.4K ratings, made by Google.

It is a popup, not a change to the Scholar page. Select a paper title on any web page and click the button to find the full text on the web or in your university library. Send a web search to Scholar and see the top three results. Press the quote button for a formatted reference, or the star to save the paper to your Scholar library. Off-campus library links need a proxy set in Scholar Settings.

What it's good at: reaching Scholar from a publisher, news or blog page in one click, from the company that runs Scholar. What it lacks: it adds nothing to the Scholar results page itself, and the listing was last updated in May 2024.

Pick it if you read papers cited on other sites and want a quick route to the Scholar record, a citation or the library copy.

## Zotero Connector

Cost: The connector and the Zotero software are free; Zotero's storage page lists 300 MB of free file storage, then plans from $20 a year for 2 GB. Platform: Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari, plus the Zotero desktop app. Store listing: version 5.0.217, updated October 1, 2026, about 8,000,000 users, 4.0 from 2.5K ratings.

It detects a paper on the page and saves the reference to your library in one click, with the PDF if one is available. Zotero's documentation lists Google Scholar among supported sites and describes a two-step route for several papers: star them in Scholar, then select and export them from My Library. The store label says the developer will not collect or use your data.

Zotero also checks for retractions. Under a 2019 partnership with Retraction Watch it flags retracted items in your library and warns when you cite one. At that announcement it covered items with a DOI or PubMed ID, about three quarters of the database. Crossref made the database open in September 2023.

What it's good at: capture for a mature, free reference manager that also writes your citations. What it lacks: it adds nothing to the Scholar page and needs the desktop app. Pick it if you want a reference manager and have none. For BibTeX, see converting between BibTeX, RIS and EndNote.

## Paperpile extension

Cost: The extension is free but needs a Paperpile account. Paperpile's pricing page lists annual billing only, a 30-day trial and a 50% academic discount; I could not reconcile the figures I read there, so check the price yourself. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 1.5.1188, updated September 28, 2026, about 300,000 users, 4.6 from 194 ratings.

It collects references and PDFs from publisher sites and names Google Scholar, PubMed, arXiv, Scopus and Web of Science among the sites it integrates with. It also has a PDF viewer with annotation, citations in Google Docs, and a way to send PDFs to AI chat tools. The store label lists personally identifiable information, web history, user activity and website content.

What it's good at: the best rated of the three reference-manager connectors here, with Google Docs citing. What it lacks: it is paid, and adds nothing to the results page.

Pick it if you write in Google Docs and would rather pay than set up Zotero.

## Unpaywall

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 3.99, last updated January 8, 2025, 1,000,000+ users, 4.0 from 283 ratings.

When you land on a paywalled article, Unpaywall looks for a legal free copy and shows a tab if it finds one. Its listing says it draws on an index of about 20 million free, legal PDFs, mostly author-posted manuscripts on university and government servers, which publishers permit. The store label lists location and website content. My extension uses Unpaywall's data only to flag open access results; Unpaywall itself opens the copy.

What it's good at: being free, legal and independent of your institution. What it lacks: it only finds copies that already exist outside the paywall, and as far as the listing says it acts on the article page you reach, not on the Scholar list. The listing was last updated in January 2025.

Pick it if your library has no tool of its own, or you are off campus.

## LibKey Nomad

Cost: Free to install, but it links through your library, so your library must be a LibKey customer. Platform: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Brave, Vivaldi and Safari, per Third Iron. Store listing: version 1.60.0, updated September 22, 2026, 1,000,000+ users, 4.5 from 17 ratings.

After you choose your institution, it shows links to the full text your library subscribes to, or an open access copy, on article pages and when you search sites such as Google and PubMed. The listing says more than 2,000 libraries in over 35 countries support it, and library guides report that it works in Google Scholar. Library guides report that it flags retracted articles using Retraction Watch data, which fits Third Iron's 2022 announcement about its LibKey services. The store label lists location data.

What it's good at: getting you to the PDF your institution already pays for, in one click. What it lacks: it is no use without a participating library, and it is not a reference manager.

Pick it if your university library lists LibKey Nomad on its website. Ask your librarian.

## Lean Library

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: updated October 1, 2026, about 200,000 users, 3.4 from 142 ratings.

Another library-access extension. You select your institution to reach its resources, and the listing says it also lets you save references, highlight and annotate pages, get journal alerts, and see article retraction alerts and trust ratings. A "Lean Library Open" mode redirects to open access copies if you have no institution. The store label says the developer will not collect or use your data.

What it's good at: the same access job as LibKey Nomad, with retraction alerts named in the listing. What it lacks: the lowest store rating of the access tools, and, like LibKey Nomad, it only helps if your library uses it. The listing does not name Google Scholar.

Pick it if your library points you to it instead of LibKey.

## EndNote Click

Cost: Free. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 3.5.0, last updated May 28, 2025, about 6,000,000 users, 4.0 from 379 ratings, made by Clarivate.

One-click access to PDFs on Web of Science, PubMed, arXiv, Scopus and other sites, through your library's subscriptions and open access copies. It integrates with Mendeley, EndNote, Dropbox and Zotero. The store label is the broadest of the tools here: personally identifiable information, authentication information, location, web history, user activity and website content.

What it's good at: one click from the supported sites to a PDF, and a hand-off to Mendeley, EndNote or Zotero. What it lacks: the listing does not say what your institution must set up for the library part to work, the data label is broad, and there has been no update since May 2025 as of this writing.

Pick it if you want one-click PDFs and a hand-off to your reference manager, and your library has not chosen LibKey Nomad or Lean Library.

## scite

Cost: The store lists the extension as free. scite's pricing page lists a 7-day trial and paid plans from $20 a month for "full platform access" including Smart Citation reports, and does not say what the extension shows without a plan, so check what its badge opens before you rely on it. Platform: Chrome. Store listing: version 1.40.0, updated July 1, 2026, about 100,000 users, 4.1 from 40 ratings.

It shows how many citations support, contrast or only mention a paper's claims, on Google Scholar, PubMed and journal sites, instead of a bare citation count. The store label says the developer will not collect or use your data.

What it's good at: the one tool here that tells you how a paper was cited, not just how often. What it lacks: clarity about what is free, and as I understand it the labels are assigned by software, so read the cited statements yourself.

Pick it if you are judging whether a finding holds up before you build on it.

## Publish or Perish

Cost: Free; the page invites voluntary donations. Platform: Windows and macOS, and Linux through an emulator. A desktop program, not an extension.

Anne-Wil Harzing's program retrieves publications and computes citation metrics, including the h-index, for an author, journal or topic. Its data-sources page lists Crossref, Google Scholar (profiles have needed a Google login since April 2025), OpenAlex and PubMed as free, Scopus and Semantic Scholar with a free API key, and Web of Science with a paid subscription, and says it cannot guarantee any source stays available. The version the page names, 8, is dated November 2021, so check the download page for the current build.

What it's good at: an established tool for a citation analysis you can describe in a tenure file, with a choice of data source. What it lacks: it adds nothing to the results page. My Pro tier has a Publish-or-Perish-style report; for a formal analysis, use the original. Pick it if you need metrics for a tenure case, grant or bibliometric study; see tracking your academic CV and tenure case.

## Seven more extensions

Each is real and useful to someone. None is on the shortlist because one above covers the same ground for most people.

### Mendeley Web Importer

Free, from Elsevier. Version 3.3.49, updated March 31, 2026, about 3,000,000 users, 2.3 from 3.1K ratings, the lowest rating on this page. It imports papers and PDFs into Mendeley Reference Manager; Mendeley's page does not say whether it works from Scholar results. The store label lists authentication information, location, web history, user activity and website content. Pick it if your library is already in Mendeley.

### Google Scholar PDF Reader

Free, from Google. Version 0.5.2, updated June 5, 2026, about 2,000,000 users, 4.1 from 713 ratings. A PDF reader with reference previews, a generated outline, figure jumps, highlighting, and cite and save buttons. Pick it if you read many PDFs in the browser and follow their references.

### PubPeer

Free, from The PubPeer Foundation. Version 1.7.1, updated November 29, 2024, about 40,000 users, 3.7 from 37 ratings. It shows a link when the paper has comments on PubPeer and stays silent otherwise. A comment is not a verdict, but a thread of methodological concerns is worth reading before you cite. The store label says the developer will not collect or use your data. Pick it if you review or replicate work.

### Scholarcy

Free extension, with premium features through a Scholarcy Library subscription; I could not read the price because its pricing page returned an access error. Version 5.4.0, updated March 14, 2026, about 80,000 users, 4.0 from 39 ratings. It turns an article into a summary flashcard with key points and links to open access versions of the references. Pick it if you screen many papers, and read the paper before you cite it.

### Elicit extension

Free extension; Elicit has a free Basic plan and a Pro plan listed at $49 a month or $588 a year. Version 1.5, updated September 4, 2026, about 30,000 users, 4.5 from 11 ratings. It is narrower than the name suggests: it fetches full-text papers for Elicit's systematic reviews through your institutional access, and Elicit says your login stays on your device. It does not annotate Scholar. Pick it if you already run systematic reviews in Elicit.

### LitRank and Journal List

Two very small free badge extensions. LitRank (version 1.6.0, 128 users) shows SJR quartiles and h-index with filters by quartile, document type and citations, and its developer says no paid tier is planned. Journal List (version 1.3.0, 184 users, from a PhD candidate at the University of Manchester) shows ABS, ABDC, FT50, UTD24, the FMS list, the CCF list and JCR quartile. Pick Journal List if you need the FMS list, which I did not find on the larger extensions.

Four web apps help with finding more but are not Chrome extensions that I could confirm. ResearchRabbit says on its homepage that it is free to sign up. Scholar Inbox describes itself as a free paper recommender that indexes arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, ChemRxiv and open access computer science proceedings. I could not read the pricing pages of Connected Papers or Consensus, so I give no price.

## What I left out and why

I dropped anything I could not confirm on October 4, 2026. The CORE Discovery listing did not resolve on the Chrome Web Store, and CORE's own page returned an access error. Semantic Scholar's FAQ links to an extension listing that does not resolve either. RetractOMatic, a retraction-highlighting extension that library guides mention, is gone from the store. The Open Access Button was discontinued by its operator, OA.Works, in November 2025, and its page points people to Unpaywall; a listing called Open Research Button, from a different publisher (PaperPanda), is still on the store, and I did not establish how the two relate. Check the listings yourself if any is back.

## What a badge does not tell you

- A venue is not a verdict on the paper. Top-ranked journals publish weak papers and obscure venues publish strong ones. Rankings help you decide what to read first.

- Lists disagree. ABDC, ABS, FT50, CORE and SJR rank by different rules and cover different fields, so a paper can be A* on one and unlisted on another. Pick a list your field uses.

- Retraction data is incomplete. Tools built on the Retraction Watch database share its gaps, and a very recent retraction may not be in a bundled copy. Check the publisher's page before you cite anything important.

- Extensions read the pages they run on. One limited to Scholar sees less than one that runs on every site. My extension's manifest limits it to Google Scholar pages, the public lookup services and extensionpay.com. Open each listing's privacy tab and compare.

- Several extensions can crowd one page. I have not tested combinations. Start with two or three and remove what you do not use.

## Decision matrix

- Journal rankings only, in a business or computing field? Rapid Journal Quality Check, or Scholar Utility Belt if you want more on the page.

- Rankings in any field, quartiles? ExCITATION.

- Rankings plus citation velocity, author metrics, retraction warnings and a saved list? Scholar Utility Belt.

- Author metrics with self-citations removed or custom formulas? Scholar H-Index Calculator. For a formal analysis, Publish or Perish.

- Full text through your library? LibKey Nomad or Lean Library, whichever your library uses; EndNote Click if neither.

- Free copies, no library? Unpaywall.

- Saving references? Zotero Connector (free), Paperpile (paid), Mendeley Web Importer (if you use Mendeley).

- Retraction warnings? Zotero for your library, Lean Library or LibKey Nomad, and Scholar Utility Belt on results.

- How later papers cite it? scite. Public critique? PubPeer.

- Reaching Scholar from other sites? Google Scholar Button.

- Not on Chrome? Scholar Utility Belt does not run elsewhere. Zotero Connector and LibKey Nomad list Firefox, Edge or Safari versions.

## A setup that holds up

- Set up access first. Ask your library which tool it supports. If it has none, install Unpaywall.

- Install one reference-manager connector. Zotero if you have no preference.

- Add one badge extension. Pick the one whose list matches your field. Check that the badge you care about appears on a few papers you already know.

- Add one trust check. Zotero's retraction notices, scite or PubPeer, and look at the paper itself before you cite it.

- Use Scholar's own alerts and library for what is new and what you saved.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best Chrome extension for Google Scholar?

There is no single best one, because they do different jobs. For full text, use your library's tool (LibKey Nomad or Lean Library) or Unpaywall. For saving references, use your reference manager's connector, such as Zotero Connector. For journal rankings, Rapid Journal Quality Check and ExCITATION are free and widely installed. Scholar Utility Belt, which Purplelink makes, combines rankings, citation and author metrics, retraction warnings and a saved list.

### Is there a free Chrome extension that shows journal rankings in Google Scholar?

Yes. Rapid Journal Quality Check and ExCITATION are free and each lists about 200,000 users on the Chrome Web Store. Scholar Utility Belt has a free core with rankings, and LitRank and Journal List are free and much smaller. They draw on different lists, so check that your field's list is among them.

### How do I find the full text of a paper I found on Google Scholar?

Start with the link beside the result. If there is none, an extension that knows your library's subscriptions (LibKey Nomad, Lean Library or EndNote Click) or one that looks for legal free copies (Unpaywall) will usually find it. Library tools need your institution's support. Scholar Utility Belt opens the best PDF link it can find but does not know your subscriptions.

### Can a Chrome extension warn me about retracted papers?

Some can. Scholar Utility Belt marks results whose DOI is on a Retraction Watch-derived list. Lean Library lists retraction alerts among its features, and Third Iron's library tools are reported to flag retractions using Retraction Watch data. Zotero checks the references in your library. Coverage is never complete, so check the publisher's page before you cite anything important.

### Do these extensions track what I search?

Each developer declares its own practices on the Chrome Web Store, and I have not audited them. Zotero Connector, Lean Library, scite, PubPeer and Rapid Journal Quality Check declare that they do not collect or use your data. Others declare collecting location, browsing activity or website content. Scholar Utility Belt has no account, no analytics and no Purplelink server, and sends optional lookups to public scholarly services.

### Which extension should I use to save papers from Google Scholar to a reference manager?

Use the connector for the manager you already have: Zotero Connector, the Paperpile extension or Mendeley Web Importer. Zotero's documentation describes a two-step route for several papers at once: star them in Scholar, then export from My Library. Scholar Utility Belt keeps a local saved list and exports BibTeX, but it is not a reference manager.

### What does Scholar Utility Belt cost, and where does it fall short?

The core is free and open source under the ISC license. Optional Pro is $40 once, $3 a month or $20 a year, and anyone who installed before version 0.6.0 keeps the earlier features free. It works in Chrome only, its lists are strongest for business, information systems and computing venues, it does not know your library subscriptions, and it does not manage references.

- How to track your academic CV and tenure case.

- Catch AI-hallucinated citations before you submit.

- Best LaTeX editor for Mac, for writing the paper once you have found the sources.

- Scholar Utility Belt and all guides.

Title: Best travel map and country-tracking apps for iPhone (2026) | Purplelink

Comparison

# Best travel map and country-tracking apps for iPhone (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 4, 2026, updated October 4, 2026

What each app records, what it costs, whether it needs an account and where your data lives, for anyone who wants a map of the countries, cities and flights they have been to. Some of the options are not travel apps at all: Apple Maps, Google Maps Timeline, a spreadsheet and a wall poster.

Disclosure up front: I make one of the apps on this list (GlobePin, free on the App Store, with a paid option). I have tried to write the comparison honestly, and in several cases another app is the better choice. Flighty is far better for flight alerts. Polarsteps records your route for you, which GlobePin does not. Visited and been are quicker for ticking off countries. Wanderlog is the one to use for planning. I did not install or test any of the other apps. Prices, platforms, in-app purchases and privacy labels were read from each app's App Store listing and, where one exists, the vendor's own page on October 4, 2026, and they change. Where a page would not load for me, I say so and write "reported as".

## What a travel map app can do, and which job you want

These apps look alike in the App Store but do different jobs. Decide which of these you want before you compare prices:

- A country checklist. Tap the countries you have visited, see a percentage of the world. Visited, been and Skratch live here.

- A map of places. Pins for cities, landmarks and restaurants, with photos, notes, stats and goals. GlobePin and Pin Traveler.

- A flight log. Every flight you have taken, with distance and airports. Flighty, YourFlights, OpenFlights.

- A trip journal with a recorded route. The phone logs where you go and you add photos. Polarsteps and FindPenguins.

- A trip planner. Itineraries for trips you have not taken. Wanderlog, Stippl, TripIt.

Two more questions matter as much as features. How does a place get on the map? By your tap, by a boarding pass, or by the phone watching your location. Where does the data live? On your device and your own iCloud, or on the developer's servers behind an account. Each App Store listing carries a privacy label of what the developer declares it collects, under Apple's headings "Data Used to Track You", "Data Linked to You" and "Data Not Linked to You". I quote them below. They are declarations, and I did not audit them.

## The shortlist

- GlobePin: places, flights and a 3D globe, kept in your iCloud. Free; Pro $14.99 once.

- Visited: the big country checklist, with lists and goals. Free with add-ons.

- been: countries and US states, a 3D globe. Free with paid options.

- Pin Traveler: city pins, trips and an optional social layer.

- Polarsteps: records your route automatically. Free, with a Plus subscription.

- Flighty: the best flight tracker, with a lifetime Passport.

- YourFlights: a flight log on a 3D globe.

- Apple Maps and Apple Photos: built in, free, automatic once turned on.

Those eight cover most needs. Six more options and seven shorter entries follow, then a decision matrix.
