## GlobePin

Cost: Free to download. GlobePin Pro is a $14.99 one-time purchase, listed as a lifetime purchase and not a subscription, that removes the ads and the watermark. Platform: iPhone and iPad, iOS or iPadOS 17 or later; the listing's compatibility section also shows Macs with Apple silicon and Apple Vision. Status: version 1.2, first released September 3, 2026.

GlobePin is a record you keep by hand. You pin places on a 3D globe or a flat world map, log flights by scanning a boarding pass or entering airports, and log road trips, cruises and train journeys with animated routes. The stats cover countries, continents, nights abroad, furthest point and total miles. Each place can hold photo postcards and a private journal. Travel Goals cover every continent, every country or a list of your own. A trip planner handles destinations you have not visited, and "I Went!" turns a plan into a pin. It also makes Travel Reel videos, a Year in Review, share cards and widgets, and it imports and exports CSV.

The listing says everything stays on your device and in your own private iCloud, with no accounts. Sync is iCloud through CloudKit, not a Purplelink server.

The ads. The free version shows ads, and the listing says so. There is a small banner on some screens, a short ad before Year in Review and Map Collage and when you export a Travel Reel, and a small "Made with GlobePin" mark on shared cards and reels. Pro removes all of it. The privacy label lists Identifiers and Usage Data under "Data Used to Track You", and Diagnostics, Identifiers and Usage Data under "Data Not Linked to You". Our privacy page says the free tier uses Google AdMob, which collects device identifiers, usage data and diagnostics, and that your travel content itself never goes to Purplelink or Google. The listing's own text also says "no tracking", which sits badly beside that label. Go by the label: the free version has an advertising SDK, and your places and photos stay on the phone and in iCloud.

What it's good at: a lifetime record of places, flights and goals in one app, with no account and no social feed. What it lacks: it is new. Version 1.0 shipped in September 2026 and the listing has two ratings, so it has none of the track record that Polarsteps, Visited or Flighty have. Nothing in the listing describes recording your route in the background, so you add places yourself. Our privacy page says location is used on the device to set a home point and calculate distances. It has no social network and no Android version. It does not send delay alerts, so Flighty is better for the flight itself, and it has no deep checklist of 150 world lists like Visited.

Pick GlobePin if you want one private record of places and flights, are fine with banner and short ads or $14.99 once, and will add the entries yourself. Pick something else if you want the route recorded for you (Polarsteps), flight alerts (Flighty), a fast country tick-list (Visited or been), or an Android app. What GlobePin does; there is also a three-way comparison with Polarsteps and Visited.

## Visited

Cost: Free. The listing shows in-app purchases for city ($9.99) and region ($3.99) add-ons, itineraries ($7.99), ad removal ($3.99) and a Pro tier ($59.99), plus monthly ($9.99) and yearly ($34.99) options. Platform: iPhone (iOS 17.6 or later), and Android.

Visited is the long-running country checklist, by Arriving In High Heels, first released in 2014. You mark countries, and on paid maps states, regions and cities, and a dashboard shows what share of the world you have covered. It adds more than 150 travel lists (UNESCO sites, national parks, beaches and so on), goals, journal notes by country, itineraries, and a printed poster of your map. The vendor's page says the free tier has country maps, travel lists, stats and friend comparisons.

From a summary of its page, the vendor says it does not track your location or read photo coordinates, and that signing up saves your data on its servers so any of your devices can reach it. Its label lists contact info, identifiers and usage data as linked to you.

What it's good at: the quickest way to get a complete country map, with a large catalog of lists. What it lacks: neither the listing nor the vendor page describes flights, and cities and regions cost extra. Sync needs an account on its servers. Pick Visited if the goal is a country map and lists to work through.

## been

Cost: Free. The listing shows a purchase named Premium Features at $2.29 beside a yearly plan at $19.99 and a weekly plan at $4.99. I cannot tell from the listing which one includes which feature. Platform: iPhone, iOS 16.6 or later. Developer: VINCI APPS LTD.

been has been in the store since 2013. It records the countries and US states you have visited, optionally with dates, and shows them as a list with a ratio per continent, a world map and a 3D globe. You can compare maps with friends who have the app. The listing says Premium adds regions in 25 or more countries, cities and airports, more globe filters, a chronological map, separate local profiles for several maps, and a video of your timeline. I could not load the vendor's own site, so everything here is from the App Store listing. Its label lists usage data as used to track you.

What it's good at: a quick, light country and state tracker with a globe. What it lacks: cities and regions sit behind Premium, and no flight log is described. A warning on the name: a search for "been" returns several apps from different developers. The long-running one is from VINCI APPS LTD. Pick been if you want a lighter alternative to Visited.

## Pin Traveler

Cost: Free for unlimited pins and trips. Premium, which the listing says adds unlimited photo uploads, custom pins and colors and unlimited saved places, is sold as weekly, monthly, yearly and lifetime plans at many listed prices, from $2.49 to $44.99. I give no single price because I cannot tell which one you will be offered. Platform: iPhone (iOS 17.6 or later) and Android, with a shareable web map.

Pin Traveler is a pin map: search and pin any city, country or US state, color pins by trip or wish list, and see a color-filled map with stats such as most visited place and farthest pin. Trips hold dates, favorite spots, restaurants and photos. It adds an optional social layer: follow friends, share trips and view their maps, or share a link to an interactive web map, and you can go private at any time. The vendor's page says you sign up to create your map, and the listing says data syncs across your devices. Its label lists usage data as used to track you and a long list as linked to you. The same developer makes a simpler app, Travel Pins, free with an ad-removal purchase at $4.99.

What it's good at: city-level pins with trips, and sharing, without paying. What it lacks: flights are not described, an account is needed, and the label is long. Pick Pin Traveler if you want pins and trips with friends who also use it.

## Polarsteps

Cost: Free. Polarsteps Plus is $9.99 a month or $34.99 a year in the US App Store listing, and EUR 8.99 or EUR 29.99 on the vendor's page, which says prices vary by region. Platform: iPhone, iOS 17 or later.

Polarsteps is the automatic one. You start a trip and the app records your route in the background. The vendor says it works offline and typically uses less than 4% of battery a day while tracking. You add photos, videos and stories to each step, invite travel buddies, and share a trip with everyone, followers only or only yourself. Afterwards you can make a Trip Reel video or order a printed Travel Book. The listing also describes an AI itinerary planner and travel stats with countries visited and distance covered. The vendor says 22 million or more travelers use it. Plus adds 3D maps, more map styles, a play mode and up to 10 travel buddies instead of 5, and the vendor says planning, tracking, sharing and reliving trips stay free.

Support pages that I could not load (they returned a 403) are reported as saying you can add a past trip by hand, with the steps joined by straight lines, so it can serve as an after-the-fact record. Its privacy label lists location, contacts, purchases and several other types as linked to you.

What it's good at: a trip diary that writes itself, and the printed book. What it lacks: it is built around trips, not a whole-life map. It needs background location for tracking, its label lists contact info as linked to you, which suggests an account that I did not confirm on the vendor's pages, and its flights are limited to a transport mode on a step. Pick Polarsteps if you want the route recorded while you travel and a story to share. The GlobePin vs Polarsteps vs Visited guide goes into the difference at more length.

## Flighty

Cost: Free to use, including a personal flight log, map and stats, with no ads. Pro is free on your first flight; the vendor's pricing page shows it at $59.99 a year, and the App Store lists monthly, annual and lifetime options, the lifetime one at $299. Platform: iPhone (iOS 18 or later), iPad, Mac and Apple Watch. The vendor does not mention Android.

Flighty is a flight tracker first: delay alerts that its listing claims arrive 2 to 90 minutes before airline apps' alerts, plus gate and aircraft information and live tracking. For this guide the interesting part is Passport, which builds your personal flight map and lifetime stats: total mileage, where you went, and comparison with friends. The free tier keeps unlimited flights, the flight log and map, annual and all-time stats, and iCloud backup and sync. Adding or importing historical flights is capped to the past 365 days unless you pay. It imports from several older flight logs, and from calendar, TripIt and email. The listing says no account is required. Its label lists contact info, identifiers and usage data as linked to you.

What it's good at: in my judgment the best flight tracker on this list. What it lacks: flights only, no places or countries other than the ones your flights reach, and years of back-history costs money. Pick Flighty if you fly often and want alerts, or want a flight history that imports from older logs. Pair it with a map app for places that are not airports.

## YourFlights

Cost: Free, with in-app purchases listed that include Premium at $3.99 a month or $24.99 a year and flight packs of a fixed size up to an unlimited one at $29.99. Platform: iPhone, iOS 16.6 or later.

YourFlights is a personal flight log. You add flights by flight number, route or boarding pass scan, and see them on an interactive 3D globe with statistics for distance, time in the air, countries, airports, airlines and aircraft. You can add ratings, notes and photos, earn badges, and, if you choose, follow friends and see their flights in a feed. It is a small app, with 48 ratings when I looked.

What it's good at: a flight-only log with a globe and boarding pass entry, plus an optional social side. What it lacks: places that are not flights, and the paid flight-pack structure needs reading before you rely on it for a long history. Pick YourFlights if your whole interest is flying and you want friends to see it.

## Apple Maps and Apple Photos

Cost: Free, built into iPhone. Platform: iPhone, per Apple's iPhone guide.

Two built-in tools work as a passive record. Apple's guide describes Visited Places in Maps: you turn it on, then open Places and Visited Places to search by name, category, address or notes and filter by date, category or city. Apple says Visited Places are end-to-end encrypted, cannot be read by Apple and appear on all your synced devices, and that you choose how long they are kept. It is not available in all countries or regions. Photos adds a map of your library (Library, then Show Map), but only pictures with embedded location data appear.

What it's good at: it costs nothing, needs no new app and records without you doing anything. What it lacks: it has no country count, stats, goals or flight log, and it only knows about places the phone saw. Pick them if you want a free memory aid, or a source to look things up in when you fill in a proper map afterward.

## Six more worth knowing

Each is useful to someone. None made the shortlist because it does a different job or overlaps with one that did.

### Wanderlog

Cost: Free, with an optional Pro subscription. Platform: iPhone, Android and the web; an account is needed, according to the vendor's page.

A trip planner: itineraries, a map of planned places, reservations imported by email or Gmail, budgets, offline access and shared editing. Its listing does not describe a map of where you have already been. Pick Wanderlog if the trip is the thing you are mapping, not the lifetime record.

### Stippl

Cost: Free, with Stippl Pro listed at $3.99, $24.99 and $34.99. Platform: iPhone, Android and the web; an account is needed to save itineraries.

A planner that also has a scratch map: the listing says you can pin every country you have visited and see statistics, and that the country maps for the USA, Germany, Japan, Canada, Australia and the UK are Pro. It also has a day planner, budget tracker, journal, reels and an eSIM store. Pick Stippl if you want the planner and a simple country map in one app.

### Journi

Cost: Free, with Premium at several price points; photo books are priced separately, starting at EUR 22.99 in the listing text. Platform: iPhone and Android.

Journi is a journal that ends in a printed book. The App Store app is "Journi Blog - Travel tracker". It builds timelines from photos, notes and maps, with four privacy levels per journal, offline use and backup to Dropbox and Google Drive. The vendor's current home page leads with photo books and does not describe the app as a tracker. Pick Journi if the end product is a book.

### Google Maps Timeline

Cost: Free. Platform: the Google Maps app, on iPhone and elsewhere.

Timeline is a location history, and Google's help page says it is off by default. Turning it on in the iPhone app needs Location Services set to Always. You can export it from the phone as location-history.json, back it up as an encrypted copy on Google's servers, and set it to auto-delete after 3, 18 or 36 months. It is a source, not a map of countries: it counts nothing and draws no globe, and the JSON needs converting before another app can use it, as far as I can tell. Use it if you already have years of it and want to reconstruct a trip history. Turning it on only for this is a bigger privacy trade than the manual apps.

### A spreadsheet or Notion

Cost: Free. Platform: anything.

One row per trip: country, city, dates, who with, a note. It is the most portable record there is, it is yours, and it will outlive any app. It will not draw you a globe. GlobePin's listing says it imports and exports CSV, so a sheet can act as a backup of a tracker or a starting point for one, though I have not tested which columns it expects. Pick this if you care most about owning the data and are happy with a table.

### A scratch-off map

Cost: Reported as roughly $12 for a small poster to about $25 for a large one, depending on the retailer. Platform: a wall.

Luckies' Scratch Map, which its seller says was conceived in 2009, is a poster with a foil layer you scratch off country by country. It has no data, no sync and no privacy question, and it only knows countries. Visited sells a printed poster of your digital map. Pick a scratch-off map if you want an object on the wall.

## More tools

Live in October 2026. One short entry each, because they overlap with the ones above.

### TripIt

An itinerary organizer: forward booking emails to plans@tripit.com and it builds the schedule. TripIt Pro is $48.99 a year in the App Store and $49 on the vendor's page. Its listing does not describe a lifetime map or stats. News reports say App in the Air's shutdown notice recommended TripIt Pro and Flighty to its users. Pick TripIt if you want bookings in one place.

### FindPenguins

Automatic route tracking that the listing calls battery-friendly and offline, with 3D flyover videos and a printed travel book. The vendor says the core app is free and that an account is needed, and the listing shows no in-app purchases. iPhone and Android.

### Skratch

A scratch map of countries, cities and regions, with a bucket list and an eSIM store. Free, with add-ons such as Cities and Regions at $9.99. Its label lists identifiers and usage data as used to track you.

### Places Been

Tag cities, UNESCO sites, national parks and 8,000 or more airports, and it fills in countries and regions from the cities you tag. Free, with many paid add-ons listed from $1.99 to $19.99.

### Mark O'Travel

Countries and regions, Travelers' Century Club and World Heritage lists, and sync through iCloud and Dropbox. Free, with a $9.99 Traveler Pro and $0.99 map packs listed. Its label lists diagnostics only, not linked to you.

### myFlights

A flight diary that stores data locally on the device, imports .pkpass and PDF boarding passes and, per its listing, bulk imports from Flightradar24 and App in the Air. Optional account for cloud backup. Pro is $1.99 a month, $17.99 a year or $39.99 for life. It has 13 ratings.

### OpenFlights and myFlightradar24

OpenFlights is a free, open-source website for logging flights, mapping them and generating statistics, with import and export. It needs an account and JavaScript, is not an iPhone app, and posted a news line dated September 2026. FlightDiary.net now redirects to my.flightradar24.com, which describes a flight diary. That page returned a 403 to my fetches, so I cannot say what it costs, and I give no price. Flighty's listing names it as an import source.

Narrower: Tripsy (an itinerary planner), Stampie (a passport-style country tracker, released in late 2025) and Swarm (Foursquare's check-in app and location history, which declares location as linked to you). App in the Air is gone: news reports say it left the stores on September 19, 2024 and ended support on October 19, 2024, so ignore articles that still recommend it. Several newer look-alike apps by solo developers exist and I did not review them.

## What an app can know about where you have been

A travel map records where you are not, as well as where you are. Three things are worth checking:

- Automatic tracking costs location permission. Polarsteps and FindPenguins record your route in the background, and both declare location data as linked to you. Manual apps such as Visited, been and GlobePin avoid that, at the price of typing the places in.

- An account usually means a server. Visited, Pin Traveler, Wanderlog and Stippl use accounts, and Visited says plainly that signing up saves your data on its servers. GlobePin says its data stays in your own iCloud.

- Check that you can get the data out. I did not test export in each app. GlobePin's listing mentions CSV, Flighty imports from several flight logs, and Google Timeline exports JSON. Look before you invest years of entries.

## Decision matrix

- One private record of places and flights, no account? GlobePin.

- Just tick off countries quickly, with lists and goals? Visited, or been for a lighter app.

- City pins, trips and friends? Pin Traveler.

- Route recorded for you, and a story or a book at the end? Polarsteps, or FindPenguins.

- You fly a lot and want alerts and a lifetime flight log? Flighty. A flight log on a globe, with friends: YourFlights.

- Planning the next trip? Wanderlog, Stippl or TripIt.

- A printed photo book? Journi or Polarsteps.

- Nothing new to install? Apple Maps Visited Places and the Photos map.

- Own the data above all? A spreadsheet.

- A thing on the wall? A scratch-off map.

## How to choose

- Decide how much typing you will accept. If none, choose Polarsteps or FindPenguins and accept the location permission. If a minute per trip is fine, the manual apps are simpler and more private.

- Decide what the unit is. Country, city, place or flight. A country checklist cannot show a restaurant, and a place map takes longer to fill.

- Decide where the data lives, in your iCloud or on the developer's servers, and read the privacy label.

- Enter ten places in the free tier. Several of these put cities, regions or long flight histories behind a purchase. If you fly a lot, Flighty for flights plus a separate map app is a reasonable split.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best travel map app for iPhone?

It depends on the job. For a country checklist, Visited or been. For a private record of places and flights with no account, GlobePin, which Purplelink makes. For a route recorded automatically, Polarsteps. For flight alerts and a flight log, Flighty. For planning, Wanderlog. I tested none of the others, so this is a reading of listings, not a ranking by use.

### Is there a free app to track the countries I have visited?

Yes. Visited, been, Pin Traveler, GlobePin, Skratch and Stippl are free to download, and each puts some features behind a purchase or subscription. Visited's free tier covers country maps and stats, with cities and regions as paid add-ons. GlobePin's free version shows ads, and a $14.99 one-time Pro removes them. A spreadsheet is free with no catch.

### Which app logs flights on a map?

Flighty has a free personal flight log and map, though history and import beyond 365 days need Pro. YourFlights and myFlights are flight diaries, and OpenFlights is a free website. GlobePin logs flights by boarding pass scan or by airports, alongside places, but sends no delay alerts.

### Do travel map apps need an account?

Many do. Pin Traveler, Wanderlog and Stippl use accounts, and Visited needs one to sync across devices. Polarsteps' privacy label lists contact info as linked to you, and I did not confirm its account rules. Flighty's listing says no account is required. GlobePin says it has no accounts and syncs through your own iCloud. Check each app's privacy label.

### Can an app track my travels automatically?

Polarsteps and FindPenguins record your route in the background, which needs location permission. Apple Maps Visited Places and Google Maps Timeline are off until you turn them on. GlobePin's listing does not describe automatic tracking, so you add places yourself.

### Does GlobePin have ads or a paid version?

Yes to both. The free version shows a small banner on some screens, a short ad before Year in Review and Map Collage and when you export a Travel Reel, and a small watermark on shared cards. GlobePin Pro costs $14.99 once, is not a subscription, and removes them. Its privacy label lists Identifiers and Usage Data under data used to track you. It is also new, with two App Store ratings so far.

### Can I move my travel data between apps?

Sometimes. GlobePin's listing mentions CSV import and export. Flighty imports from myFlightradar24, App in the Air, OpenFlights, FlightMemory, Logmyflight and JetLovers. Google Maps Timeline exports a JSON file. I did not test export in the others, so check before you invest years of entries.

- Best on-device health apps for iPhone: the same privacy question, for health data.

GlobePin is an iPhone and iPad app for pinning places, logging flights and setting travel goals on a 3D globe, with stats, photo postcards and Travel Reels. It has no accounts and syncs through your iCloud. Free, with an optional $14.99 one-time Pro that removes the ads.

Download on the App Store
See what it does

Requires iOS 17 or later. The free version shows ads and its privacy label lists tracking data. New app, no social network, no Android version, and you add places yourself.

Title: Best disk space analyzer and cleaner for Mac (2026) | Purplelink

← All guides

Comparison

# Best disk space analyzer and cleaner for Mac (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 4, 2026

What is using your Mac's disk, what is safe to remove, and which tool to trust with the deleting. Short version: Apple's own settings plus a free or $10 disk map cover most full disks, and the tools differ most in whether a delete goes to the Trash or is final.

Disclosure up front: Purplelink, which publishes this site, makes one app on this list, Legroom, a menu-bar app sold as a 7-day trial and a $9.99 one-time purchase. It is new and unproven, and where another tool is the better choice I say so. I did not install or test any of the other tools either. Everything below is read from vendor pages, Mac App Store listings, privacy labels, project repositories, Apple support pages and the built-in Terminal help on my own Mac, all on October 4, 2026. Prices and versions change. Where a page did not say something, I write "not stated" rather than guess.

## Three jobs, and which tools do which

"Disk space tool" covers three different jobs.

- See what is big. Analyzers draw a map or list the biggest items: DaisyDisk, GrandPerspective, OmniDiskSweeper, the Terminal tools.

- Remove what regrows. Cleaners go after caches, logs, build output and app leftovers: CleanMyMac, Mole, DevCleaner, AppCleaner.

- Stop it filling again. Rules and alerts on a schedule or threshold: Hazel, Optimize Storage, a few free menu-bar apps.

One number trips people up. Apple's Disk Utility help says available space can include free space plus "purgeable space", space that macOS can free up when needed. Finder counts it as available and some tools do not, so two apps can show different free space for the same disk. Neither is wrong.

Deletion is where tools differ most, so each entry says how the tool deletes: to the Trash, for good, or "not stated" on the pages I read. Before deleting anything, read what is safe to delete, and what is not.

## The shortlist

- macOS Storage settings: free, built in, start here.

- DaisyDisk: $9.99 once, the visual map, deletes for good.

- GrandPerspective: free, a maintained treemap.

- OmniDiskSweeper: free, a plain largest-first list, Trash.

- Hazel: $42, rules that delete by age.

- Mole: free command-line cleaner with a dry-run mode, and a $19 app.

- DevCleaner for Xcode: free, Xcode's caches only.

- du, ncdu or gdu: free, in Terminal.

Legroom is not on the shortlist because it is new; it has its own section below. Eight more entries follow the full reviews, then a decision matrix, how to choose and the section on what is safe to delete.

## macOS Storage settings and Optimize Storage

Cost: Free, built in. Platform: macOS. In macOS Ventura 13 or later it is System Settings, General, Storage, per Apple's page on freeing up storage.

The bar shows categories, and a More Info button next to some of them (Applications, Documents, Messages, Trash and others) opens options for that category. System Data is, in Apple's words, a general category covering all Apple and third-party files that do not belong to a more specific one. It is not a single thing you can delete. Apple's Optimize Storage page lists three recommendations: Store in iCloud, Optimize Storage (removes Apple TV movies you have watched and keeps only recent mail attachments), and Empty Trash automatically, which erases items that have been in the Trash more than 30 days. The same page says that when space is needed, macOS also clears caches and logs that are safe to delete, including interrupted downloads, staged updates and Safari website data.

What it lacks: a map of your own folders, and any view inside System Data. Pick it if you want the free first step with no new software to trust. Turn on Empty Trash automatically only if you never keep things in the Trash on purpose.

## iCloud Drive and Optimize Mac Storage

Cost: Uses your iCloud plan; Apple's page says storage starts at 50 GB for $0.99 a month in the US. Platform: macOS.

With Optimize Mac Storage on (Apple Account, iCloud, Drive), Apple says older documents are kept in iCloud when space is needed. Control-click an item and choose Remove Download to drop the local copy, or Keep Downloaded to pin one. Read this twice: Apple's iCloud Drive deletion page says deleting a file on one device removes it from every device on the same Apple Account, recoverable for 30 days. Remove Download keeps the file in iCloud. Delete removes it.

What it lacks: it moves space around and does not show what is big. Pick it if you already pay for iCloud and most of your disk is documents and photos.

## DaisyDisk

Cost: $9.99, one-time, on the vendor site and the Mac App Store. The site says minor updates are included, covers up to 5 personal Macs, offers a 30-day money-back guarantee and a free trial. Platform: macOS 10.13 or newer, Apple silicon supported; version 4.34.

A ring-shaped disk map. The vendor says it scans in seconds. You tear items off the map into a Collector area at the bottom, where they wait until you delete. It shows hidden space, which includes purgeable space and local snapshots, and can scan as administrator to reach restricted folders. The deletion model is stated plainly in its guide: files stay put until you click Delete, you then get 5 seconds to cancel, and DaisyDisk "permanently removes files and folders instead of moving them to the system Trash". It will not accept /System, /Library or your home folder into the Collector, and the site says it "doesn't collect or transmit anything".

The Mac App Store edition is partly limited, according to the guide's snapshots page: no snapshot size estimates, and deleting snapshots means using Terminal. The guide does not describe the direct edition as limited.

What it's good at: the clearest picture of where space went, including the hidden part. What it lacks: any automation or rules, and a Trash step. Pick it if you want to look at a map and delete by hand, and you accept that deletes are final.

## GrandPerspective

Cost: Free from the developer's site, or $2.99 on the Mac App Store, which the developer says is the same app. Platform: macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel; version 3.8.1; open source under the GNU GPL.

A treemap: every file is a rectangle sized by its size, grouped by folder, and you can color by type, folder, or creation, modification or access time. It has filters, saved and exported scans, Quick Look, and hard-link support for looking inside Time Machine backups. It can delete files and folders from the view. The page and help files I read do not say whether that goes to the Trash or is permanent, so check on a throwaway file first.

What it lacks: it is a map, not a cleaner. Nothing I read says it explains purgeable space or snapshots. Pick it if you want a treemap and would rather not pay, or you want the open-source one.

## OmniDiskSweeper

Cost: Free, from the Omni Group. Platform: macOS. The current download is version 1.16, in a folder labeled macOS 11, but the page states no macOS requirement or release date.

The simplest tool here. The vendor describes it as showing "the files on your drive, largest to smallest", with a way to Trash or open them. That is the whole description, and sometimes it is all you want.

What it lacks: a map, rules, and any explanation of what you are looking at. Pick it if you want the least software that answers "which folder is huge".

## Disk Inventory X

Cost: Free, GPL. Platform: The page lists version 1.3, copyright 2019, for macOS 10.13 to 10.15.

A treemap app. I found no newer build, and the page does not describe deletion. On a current Mac I would use GrandPerspective, which draws the same kind of map and is updated. Pick it if it is already on an older Mac you are not upgrading.

## Nektony Disk Space Analyzer

Cost: Free to download. Pro Mode is an in-app purchase: $4.99 monthly, $9.99 annual or $19.99 lifetime. Platform: macOS 11 or later; version 6.0.2, updated June 2026. App Store listing, "Disk Space Analyzer: Inspector".

A sunburst diagram with real-time scan results, Quick Look, Show in Finder and a purgeable-space readout. Pro adds removing big files, a full sorted list, and moving or copying items to another drive. The listing's privacy label is "Data Not Collected", which is self-reported. The listing does not say how Pro removes files.

What it lacks: removal in the free tier, which lists only the 8 biggest items. Pick it if you want a sunburst map and will pay for Pro.

## CleanMyMac

Cost: Free to download from the vendor or App Store, with a 7-day trial, after which the listing says you are charged automatically. The App Store in-app list shows a Basic yearly plan at $39.99, Plus yearly at $65.99 and a monthly plan at $9.99. The vendor page says "from $3.33/month" and mentions a one-time option; I give no lifetime figure because the sources disagree. Platform: macOS 11 or later; version 5.6.

An all-in-one cleaner; the listing claims over 29 million downloads. It describes junk and cache cleaning, a malware scan, an uninstaller, duplicates, large and old files, and performance tools. For disk space the relevant part is Space Lens, a storage map. MacPaw's help page describes a Review and Remove list where you can deselect items, then says CleanMyMac "deletes the items from your Mac". It does not say Trash or permanent. The app is notarized by Apple per the listing, and its label is "Data Not Linked to You", covering contact info, identifiers, usage data and diagnostics.

What it lacks: a clear statement of Trash versus permanent deletion on the page I read, and a price that is easy to state. Pick it if you want the extras, especially the uninstaller and malware scan, in one app. For disk space alone, in my reading, a map and Apple's own settings cover most of the same ground for less.

## Hazel

Cost: Hazel 6 is $42, a family pack for up to 5 household members is $65, and an upgrade from an earlier version is $20, per the Noodlesoft store. There is a free trial. Platform: macOS; I did not find the requirement on the pages I read.

Hazel is not a disk tool. It watches the folders you name and applies rules: by name, date, type or source, move, rename, tag, or delete files that are too old. Its manual describes selectively deleting items from the Trash so the space is recovered, and App Sweep, which notices when you trash an app and offers to remove its support files. For keeping a disk from filling, a typical rule is deleting items in Downloads older than 30 days. What I did not find is a built-in free-space condition. The manual's scripting page lists "the amount of free space on my disk is less than 10 GB" as the kind of thing a script can check, so a threshold trigger means writing one.

The manual's Preview a Rule shows live match indicators for a selected item, plus a rule status view for a folder. That checks a rule; it is not a list of everything the rule would delete.

What it lacks: a free-space trigger, an analyzer, and a dry-run list. Pick it if you want general file rules on any folder. This is the right tool for that, today.

## Mole

Cost: The command-line tool is free, GPL-3.0, and installs with brew install mole; it needs macOS 12 or newer. A separate app, Mole for Mac, is $19 once for 2 Macs, with a 14-day refund and macOS 14 or later, per mole.fit. The CLI is at version 1.58.

The README describes cleaning caches, logs and leftovers, uninstalling apps, cleaning project build artifacts (mo purge), and a disk explorer (mo analyze). Its safety section is specific: --dry-run previews clean, uninstall, optimize, purge and installer runs; mo analyze "moves selected items to Trash after confirmation"; clean commands can delete, so preview first; activity is logged to ~/Library/Logs/mole/operations.log; and protected caches can be whitelisted. The app page says scans and cleanup stay on your Mac and that moving anything to Trash asks for confirmation.

What it lacks: a Trash step in its clean commands, which can delete; the dry run is the safeguard. Pick it if you are comfortable in Terminal and want a cleaner that tells you what it will do before it does it.

## AppCleaner and Pearcleaner

Cost: Both free. Platform: AppCleaner 3.7 needs macOS 15 or later, with 3.6.8 for 10.14 up to 15.6. Pearcleaner is a source-available app.

AppCleaner does one job: drop an app on its window and it finds related files, which you remove with the delete button. The page does not say Trash or permanent. Pearcleaner adds orphaned file search, but its README marks the project "On Hold", last release 5.4.3 in November 2025, and warns that pearcleaner.com is a fake site and itsalin.com the only real one. That applies to any cleaner: download from the vendor, the App Store or the project's own repository.

Pick AppCleaner if you only want leftovers removed with an app. Hazel's App Sweep, Mole and CleanMyMac do this inside bigger tools.

## DevCleaner for Xcode, and Xcode's simulators

Cost: Free, with optional tips of $1.99, $3.99 and $9.99 in the app; GPL-3.0 source. Platform: macOS 14 or later; version 2.8.0, November 2025.

It inspects and cleans Xcode's generated files: device support, archives, DerivedData, documentation caches and old simulator and device logs, with a command-line tool for scripts. The README is honest about risk: it relies on "internal folder structures and undocumented features", may stop working with newer Xcode versions, and tells you to make a backup first. Its label is "Data Not Collected".

Simulators can be handled without a third-party app. On my Mac, the built-in help for xcrun simctl delete says unavailable deletes devices not supported by the current Xcode SDK, and xcrun simctl runtime delete takes a runtime identifier or --notUsedSinceDays with a --dry-run option. Use the dry run.

Pick it if Xcode is where your space went. Keep Archives you may need for crash symbolication.

## du, ncdu, gdu and dua

Cost: Free. Platform: macOS, installed with Homebrew (brew install ncdu, gdu or dua-cli); du is already there.

The built-in answer is du -hxd 1 ~ | sort -h: the size of each folder one level below your home folder, smallest last, staying on one file system. The interactive versions are friendlier. ncdu (MIT) has a built-in delete that asks for confirmation by default and a -r flag that makes it read-only. gdu (MIT) uses d to delete and D to move to the Trash, with --no-delete to turn deleting off. dua (MIT) has an interactive mode with multi-stage deletion, a config option to disable permanent deletion, and a dua clean command that says nothing is deleted automatically.

Pick one if you work over SSH, on a server, or simply like Terminal. Use read-only mode until you trust your own typing.

## Time Machine local snapshots and tmutil

Cost: Free, built in. Platform: macOS.

This is the usual reason deleting files does not free space. Apple says Time Machine saves a snapshot about every hour and keeps it for 24 hours, keeps an extra snapshot of your last successful backup until space is needed, and saves one before a macOS update. Your Mac counts the space as available, and Time Machine deletes snapshots as they age or as space is needed. Apple's documented way to remove them by hand is to set Time Machine backups to manual for a few minutes, then turn them back on. The tmutil man page on my Mac also lists listlocalsnapshots, deletelocalsnapshots and thinlocalsnapshots, and says several verbs need root and Full Disk Access. I ran only the listing (none on this Mac), not a deletion verb.

Pick this if you deleted a lot and the free number did not move. Most of the time, waiting or leaving it alone is right.

## Legroom (Purplelink's)

Cost: A free 7-day trial, then $9.99 once, with no subscription; also part of the $54.99 Mac Suite. Platform: macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel, direct download from its page, no Mac App Store build. Status: version 1.0.0, signed and notarized, which makes it the newest and least proven tool in this guide. I make it, and I have not compared it with the others on a test Mac.

I designed it after my own disk emergency, which came from system-level items such as staged updates and swap that no folder sweeper can touch. It lives in the menu bar and shows free space on the startup disk, the space macOS says it can clear, and your other volumes, and it warns you when free space drops below a line you set. You make rules for folders and caches; each rule shows a preview of what it would remove, you approve it, and then it can run by hand, on a schedule, or when free space drops below your line. Each rule either moves items to the Trash or deletes them for good, and the preview says which. A daily "what grew" comparison over 1, 7 or 30 days names the folders that filled the disk, and Suggestions proposes rules without creating or running any. Space Map draws a folder or disk as rings, with folders it could not read shown hatched. Find Files looks for large, old and duplicate files and only moves the ones you select to the Trash, always leaving one copy of every duplicate.

What it lacks: it does not scan as an administrator, so space such as local Time Machine snapshots is listed as "size not reported" rather than measured, and where a fix needs Terminal it shows the command as text and does not run it. It does not clean inside system folders and it does not make your Mac faster. Its page lists no uninstaller, widget or command-line tool. After the trial ends, the menu-bar readout and low-space alerts keep working, while rules, What Grew, Suggestions, Space Map and Find Files need a license key, which unlocks the same download. Its page says there is no account and no analytics; every copy checks for updates once a day. Full Disk Access is optional. Legroom's own page says it does not run commands or remove anything you have not previewed and approved, but that is the vendor describing itself, and this is the first release.

Where others are better today: DaisyDisk for a visual map, and for hidden space and snapshots, because it can scan as administrator, which Legroom does not. GrandPerspective if you want free. OmniDiskSweeper if you want simple. Hazel for general rules on any folder. For cleaning developer caches when space is low, free open-source apps such as Harbofly and Dustpan exist, listed below. The gap Legroom is aimed at is folder rules with a free-space trigger, a readout and a "what grew" explanation in one app. Pick Legroom if you want rules that clean on a free-space trigger with a preview you approve each time, and you accept a first release from a one-person studio. Pick another tool if you want a visual map of everything including system space.

## Eight more worth knowing

Each is useful to someone. I searched for PrunePanda, SpaceSift and Funter and found no live product page or store listing for a disk tool by those names, so they are not covered.

### Disk Diag

A scanner-style cleaner for macOS 12 or later, last updated October 2025. Free to download, but removing scan results is capped at 1 GB a month; Unlimited Cleaning is $16.99 yearly or $44.99 once. The listing does not say how removal works, and its label lists email address and product interaction, with developer advertising or marketing among the purposes.

### Gemini 2

MacPaw's duplicate finder. Free to download, with Yearly Access and Smart Cleanup each listed at $19.99, for macOS 10.13 or later. It finds duplicate and similar files and photos. Check which copy it keeps before accepting an auto-selection.

### Stats and iStat Menus

System monitors for the menu bar. Stats is free and MIT-licensed, for macOS 12 or later, and lists disk utilization among its modules. iStat Menus 7 is $11.99 on the App Store for macOS 14 or later. Both are monitors, not cleaners.

### OnyX

A free utility from Titanium Software, supported by donations, for maintenance and settings that would otherwise need Terminal commands. There is a separate build for each macOS version, and the page says to use the right one. For disk space alone, I would start elsewhere.

### Lemon Cleaner

Tencent's open-source Mac cleaner, with duplicate detection and disk space analysis. Its repository has about 6,300 stars, a last release in October 2025 and a Chinese-language description. I read only the repository.

### Harbofly, Dustpan and ClearDisk

Free, open-source menu-bar apps for developer caches. Harbofly says it uses the Trash by default and offers opt-in auto-clean, including when the disk runs low, with opt-in anonymous analytics. Dustpan offers opt-in auto-clean daily, weekly or when space is low, and says it deletes project artifacts permanently after confirmation; it is at version 0.1.3. ClearDisk, for macOS 14 or later, says Trash first and no data collection. They overlap with what Legroom plans for caches.

### Rulewright

A Hazel-style folder rules app on the App Store: $14.99, macOS 14 or later. Its listing describes previewing what each rule will do, a Trash action, and working only inside folders you grant, with no Full Disk Access needed.

### Spacie, mac-cleaner-cli and cleanmymac-cli

Spacie is a native Apple-silicon disk analyzer with sunburst and treemap views and a duplicate finder (about 86 stars on its repository). mac-cleaner-cli is a free MIT command-line cleaner, not MacPaw's. MacPaw's own cleanmymac-cli, released July 2026, targets developer caches, and its README says analytics can be disabled.

## Decision matrix

"Deletes" is how each tool removes things, as stated on the pages I read; "not stated" means they did not say. US prices, October 4, 2026.

- Want free? GrandPerspective, OmniDiskSweeper, or du with ncdu.

- Want deletes you can undo? OmniDiskSweeper, or Mole's analyze mode, which use the Trash.

- Want it to stay empty? Hazel for age rules; Harbofly or Dustpan for developer caches.

- Xcode ate the disk? DevCleaner and the simctl commands.

## How to choose

- Find out what is big before anything else. A map costs nothing or about $10, and DaisyDisk's FAQ says it is typically your own files that take the most space, not system files.

- Check how a tool deletes. Trash is undoable until you empty it. A permanent delete is not. If a tool does not say, assume it is permanent and test on a throwaway file.

- Prefer preview before action. Mole's dry run and a rule you can inspect beat a button that says Clean.

- Be wary of automation until you have seen it work. I would not leave any tool deleting by itself until I had read its first list, and I have audited none of these.

- Keep Time Machine running. DaisyDisk's own FAQ says to, so a mistake can be rolled back.

- Download from the source. Vendor site, App Store, or the project's own repository, not a search ad.

## What is safe to delete, and what is not

No tool can tell you what is safe on your Mac, and I have not tested any of them. This is what Apple and the tools' own pages say, kept cautious on purpose.

- The Trash. Apple says a file's space is not available until you empty the Trash. Emptying is permanent, so look first.

- Your own files. DaisyDisk's FAQ says to delete only files you recognize by location, name and preview as ones you created or downloaded, such as videos, games, music and downloaded programs.

- System Data. A catch-all, not a folder. Apple says macOS clears safe caches and logs itself when space is needed. Do not delete inside /System, /usr, /bin, /sbin or /var; Apple's System Integrity Protection page says those are protected, and /Library and /Applications are where installers write. Anything that tells you to remove files there by hand is a reason to stop and check.

- Caches. Apple says macOS clears the caches and logs that are safe to delete when space is needed, and DevCleaner's README says DerivedData can be regenerated, with a slower next build. Delete a named cache folder, not a whole hidden directory, because some tools keep credentials next to their caches. Quit the app first.

- APFS snapshots and purgeable space. Apple counts them as available and removes them as they age or as space is needed. Leave them unless you need space for a task right now, and then use Apple's documented route above.

- iCloud-evicted files. Remove Download keeps the file in iCloud. Deleting it from iCloud Drive removes it from every device on the account, recoverable for 30 days, per Apple.

- Photos, Mail, Messages, device backups and Time Machine backups. Use each app's own storage controls, not Finder; DaisyDisk's FAQ says the same for Photos, iTunes and Time Machine. Apple's page lists deleting old iPhone and iPad backups as one way to free space.

- Xcode simulators and archives. Unavailable simulators and unused runtimes can go through simctl, with --dry-run for runtimes. Keep Archives you may need to symbolicate crashes.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best disk space analyzer for Mac?

For a visual map, DaisyDisk at $9.99 once. For free, GrandPerspective, or OmniDiskSweeper if you want a plain list. Start with macOS Storage settings either way. I tested none of them, so this is a reading of vendor pages and listings, not a ranking by use.

### Is it safe to delete System Data on a Mac?

System Data is not one folder. Apple describes it as a general category for all Apple and third-party files that do not belong to a more specific category, and says macOS clears safe caches and logs itself when space is needed. Do not delete inside protected system folders. Use a map to find large items by location instead.

### Why did deleting files not free up space?

Files in the Trash keep using space until you empty it. Time Machine local snapshots can hold copies for up to 24 hours or until space is needed, and macOS counts that space as available. Tools also count purgeable space differently, so the free number can differ.

### Should I delete Time Machine local snapshots?

Usually not. Apple says Time Machine keeps one about every hour for 24 hours and removes snapshots as they age or as space is needed. If you need the space for a task now, Apple's documented route is to set backups to manual for a few minutes. The tmutil command can also list and delete them; I did not run its deletion commands.

### Do I need a paid Mac cleaner app?

Often not for disk space. Apple's settings, a free map such as GrandPerspective and, for developers, Mole or DevCleaner cover most of it. Paid cleaners add one-click removal, uninstallers, scheduling or malware scans. Before paying, check how the tool deletes, whether it uses the Trash, and what its privacy label says.

### Can anything clean my Mac automatically when space runs low?

For some things, yes. Hazel runs rules on folders, though a free-space trigger needs a script. Harbofly and Dustpan, both free and open source, offer opt-in auto-clean for developer caches, including when space is low. None of them is a reason to skip reading what a rule will remove first, and I have audited none of them.

### Is Legroom available, and what does it cost?

Yes. Legroom is Purplelink's Mac menu-bar app: a free 7-day trial, then $9.99 once with no subscription, for macOS 14 or later on Apple silicon and Intel. I make it, it is a first release, and this guide describes it from its own product page rather than from a test against the other tools.

## Related guides

- Best LaTeX editor for Mac: MacTeX is about 5 GB and BasicTeX about 100 MB, a real choice if your disk is tight.

- Show free disk space in the Mac menu bar: the built-in views and the menu-bar apps that keep a free-space number in view.

- Legroom: the Purplelink Mac menu-bar app described above.

- Outbound Veil: another Purplelink Mac menu-bar app, direct download.

- Purplelink's privacy page, all products and all guides.

Title: Best keyboard sound apps for Mac (2026) | Purplelink

Comparison

# Best keyboard sound apps for Mac (2026)

By Benjamin Ampel · October 7, 2026

Apps that make your Mac's keyboard, mouse and trackpad sound or feel like something else. Short version: Klack is the simple paid one, KeyOpera is the cheapest, Thock and Mechvibes are free, Snick and HapticPad do one narrow job, and the real differences are how much each plays beyond key presses and which macOS permission it asks for.

Disclosure up front: Purplelink, which publishes this site, makes one app on this list, Keyfeel, sold as a free 7-day trial and then $9.99 once. It is new, and where another app is the better choice I say so. I did not install or test any of the other apps. Everything below is read from vendor pages, Mac App Store listings, project repositories and launch pages, all on October 7, 2026. Prices and versions change, and where two sources disagreed I say so instead of choosing one.

## What these apps do, and what they do not

A keyboard sound app plays a recorded sound when you press a key, so a quiet laptop keyboard or a membrane keyboard sounds like a mechanical one. They differ in four ways that matter more than the length of the sound list.

- What plays. Key presses only, or also key releases, mouse clicks, scrolling and shortcuts.

- Where the sounds come from. Recordings of real switches, community packs you can add, or your own files.

- Feel beyond sound. Whether it can tap the trackpad's haptic motor. That works only on a Mac with a Force Touch trackpad, and only while a finger is on it.

- What it needs from macOS. To be told which key was pressed, an app needs a permission, usually Input Monitoring. It needs the key, not the character you typed. Most of these say so on their pages, and you can check it in System Settings, Privacy & Security.

One thing no app fixes: Bluetooth audio adds its own delay, often 100 milliseconds or more, so on Bluetooth headphones every one of these sounds late. Built-in speakers, wired headphones or a USB audio device keep the sound in step with your fingers.

## The shortlist

- Klack: $4.99, the polished, simple one. Keys and mouse clicks, and since version 2.2 (July 2026) scroll sounds with haptic ticks.

- KeyOpera: $3, sound packs you can add, and spoken key names.

- Thock: free, open source, with a command line and a Raycast extension.

- Mechvibes: free, open source, community sound packs.

- Klakk: about $3 to $5, with a 3-day trial.

- Snick: $7, scrolling sounds and haptics only.

- HapticPad: web-page haptics, no sound.

Keyfeel is not on the shortlist because I make it; it has its own section below. A decision matrix, how to choose and a short FAQ follow.

## Klack

Cost: $4.99 on the Mac App Store, which is the price on that listing. The Klack site sells it too, but I could not read a price there. Platform: the listing says macOS 15.0 or later; by Henrik Ruscon.

Klack is the one most people mean when they say "that Mac keyboard sound app". It lives in the menu bar and plays recorded switch sounds. The listing names Japanese Black, Cream, Oreo, Cardboard, Milky Yellow and Super Red, and the site lists switches from CherryMX, Gateron, Keychron, NovelKeys and Everglide. It randomizes pitch a little on each press, plays separate up and down sounds, supports spatial audio on AirPods, has a tone control, and has sleep automation. The listing's privacy label says no data is collected. The site says it is a native app.

Mouse and scroll: its changelog lists mouse click sounds since version 1.7 (January 2025) and, in version 2.2 (21 July 2026), scroll sounds with haptic ticks and support for macOS 27. What I did not find: any mention of adding your own sounds on the pages I read. Pick it if you want a polished, simple app with the most established name, and macOS 15 is not a problem.

## KeyOpera

Cost: $3, on the Mac App Store and on Gumroad, per the developer's page. Platform: the developer's site says Apple silicon and Intel on macOS 13 or later.

A small menu-bar app. Version 2.0, which the developer's launch post puts around August 2026, added .keypak sound packs you can install with a click, a Homebrew command for creating and controlling packs, and Key Announcement, which speaks the name of each key you press, with better VoiceOver support. The page lists six packs: Cherry MX Black in PBT and ABS, EG Oreo, EG Crystal Purple, MX Black and a synthetic pack. The launch post describes keyboard and mouse sounds with separate volume controls; the product page I read did not mention mouse sounds, so check before you rely on them.

What it lacks: a free trial, as far as I could see. Pick it if you want the lowest price, custom packs, or spoken key names for accessibility.

## Thock

Cost: Free, MIT-licensed, from its GitHub repository, also installable with brew install --cask kamillobinski/thock/thock. Platform: macOS 13.5 or later.

A native menu-bar app with its own audio engine. The README lists switch profiles you can extend with JSON files, automatic muting while Spotify, Apple Music or VLC is playing, a command-line tool and a Raycast extension, and interface text in nine languages. It had about 955 stars when I read it. The README did not give a profile count or spell out the permission it needs; like the others, it has to be told when a key is pressed.

What it lacks: mouse and scroll sounds and haptics, on the page I read. Pick it if you want free, open source and scriptable.

## Mechvibes

Cost: Free, MIT-licensed. The site says it is available on Windows, macOS and Linux, and that the sound packs are community made and free.

The long-running original: it plays a sound pack when you type, with an editor for making and sharing packs. Its big strength is the pack library; installing one is described as two clicks. Its README says the original repository is transitioning to legacy status and that development has moved to MechvibesDX, a rewrite whose documentation lists keyboard and mouse button sounds. Because the same pack format is used by other apps, importing a Mechvibes pack is a feature in its own right, covered below under Keyfeel.

What it lacks: a native Mac app feel, and a clear future for the original on the page I read. Pick it if the community packs are the point, or you also use Windows or Linux.

## Klakk

Cost: One-time, with a 3-day free trial. The Mac App Store listing shows $4.99 and also lists $2.99, so I cannot give you a single figure. Platform: macOS 14.0 or later; version 1.3.8, 28 MB; by Ting Dong.

Not the same app as Klack, and the similar spelling is confusing. The listing claims 14 or more sound packs of switches such as Cherry MX and Gateron, response under 10 milliseconds, switching packs from the menu bar, and no data collection. One review says it did nothing at first, and the developer's reply is the useful part: turn on Input Monitoring in System Settings. That is true of every app here, and the first thing to check if any of them stays silent.

Pick it if you want a trial before paying and the price is about right to you.

## Snick

Cost: One-time purchase, $7 per its AlternativeTo listing; the vendor page I read says one-time but gives no amount, and mentions no trial. Platform: macOS 14 or later; version 1.6.

Snick does one thing: it makes scrolling click. Seven voices modeled on mechanical wheel detents, trackpad haptics in step with each click, and spacing that follows how fast you scroll, so a slow scroll is fine and a fling is smooth. Haptics need a Force Touch trackpad; the sounds work on any Mac. It asks for the Accessibility permission, and says it reads no content and sends nothing off the Mac. It updates itself through Sparkle.

What it lacks: keyboard and click sounds. It is the only one here that is only about scrolling. Pick it if scrolling is what bores you and you already have a keyboard sound app.

## HapticPad

Cost: The sources disagree. The hapticpad.app page I read says free, with no trial and no in-app purchase. Other listings and write-ups say a 7-day trial and then $4.99 once on the Mac App Store. Check the listing you are buying from. Platform: macOS 13 or later and a Force Touch trackpad.

Not a sound app at all. It uses the trackpad's haptic motor to tap when the pointer crosses a link, button or text field in the browser, with different patterns for different elements, through a Mac app plus Chrome, Firefox and Safari extensions. The page says it never reads page content or URLs. It plays no sound, and it is built as an accessibility aid.

Pick it if you want something you can feel on web pages. It is a companion to the others, not a substitute.

## Keyfeel (Purplelink's)

Cost: Free for 7 days, then $9.99 once with a license key, no subscription; also part of the $54 Mac Suite. Platform: macOS 13 or later, Apple silicon and Intel, direct download from its page, no Mac App Store build. Status: version 1.1.0, signed and notarized, released October 7, 2026, which makes it the newest and least proven app in this guide. I make it, and I have not compared it with the others on a test Mac.

I built it because I wanted the keyboard sounds, the click sounds and the scroll feel from one place. It plays recorded switch sounds with a different recording on each press, per-key pitch and left-to-right stereo, separate press and release sounds, and sounds for the space bar and Return. It adds mouse click sounds, scroll ticks that follow how fast you scroll and keep going while a hard flick glides, optional trackpad haptics on scroll and click, and an optional ripple on screen where you click. Beyond keyboards it has a Fun set (cat, dog, duck and others) and a Calm set of soft sounds for all-day use, all recordings licensed for use and credited in the app. It can play its own sound for shortcuts such as copy and paste, with a different sound if a copy did not take. It imports Mechvibes packs, including .ogg ones, and keeps the different sound each pack gives each key.

It goes quiet in the apps you choose, while the microphone or a camera is in use, and, if you want, in full-screen apps. It reads which key was pressed and not the character, works offline, and its only network use is checking for updates. Settings shows an estimate of the delay from key press to sound for your output, and warns when that output is Bluetooth.

What it lacks: it is Mac only, it is new, and it has no Mac App Store build. It does not have the spoken key names KeyOpera offers or the command line Thock has. It does not claim the community pack library Mechvibes has; it imports those packs instead. Where others are better today: Klack for a keyboard-only app with years of polish, KeyOpera for the lowest price, Thock and Mechvibes for free, Snick if scrolling is all you want. Pick Keyfeel if you want keys, clicks, scrolling and haptics in one app and would rather pay once than collect several.

## Also worth knowing

I read only the AlternativeTo and launch-page descriptions of these, and nothing else about them.

- Keeby says it uses sounds recorded from real switches, with 11 profiles including Gateron Red, Holy Panda, Alps Blue and Box Navy.

- Haptyk says it uses the MacBook's hidden accelerometer to play sounds that match how hard you type, and is listed as free.

- TypeLouder is listed as a paid app for mechanical click sounds with low latency and offline use.

## Decision matrix

US prices, October 7, 2026, as listed. "Not stated" means the pages I read did not say.

Correction, October 8, 2026: an earlier version said Klack had no mouse or scroll sounds. Its changelog lists mouse click sounds since version 1.7 and scroll sounds with haptic ticks since version 2.2, so this page now says so.

- Want free? Thock, or Mechvibes for the pack library.

- Want the simplest keyboard app? Klack.

- Want scrolling to feel like something? Snick, or Keyfeel if you also want key and click sounds.

- Want to feel the web? HapticPad.

## How to choose

- Decide what should make a sound. If it is only keys, most of this list works and the price gap is a few dollars. If you want clicks, scrolling or shortcuts too, the list shortens quickly.

- Check your macOS version. The requirements run from macOS 13 to macOS 15, and Klack's is the highest.

- Look at the permission. Input Monitoring lets an app see which key was pressed. Accessibility is a broader permission. Either way, the app should say what it reads and sends, and a repository you can read is a real advantage for a tool that watches every key.

- Try before you buy where you can. Thock and Mechvibes are free, Klakk offers 3 days and Keyfeel 7. Keystroke sounds are a taste thing, and a bad pick is annoying within a day.

- Use real headphones. If the sound feels late on Bluetooth, the app is not the cause.

- Download from the source. The vendor site, the Mac App Store or the project's own repository, not a search ad.

## Frequently asked

### What is the best keyboard sound app for Mac?

For the simplest paid option, Klack at $4.99 on the Mac App Store. For the cheapest, KeyOpera at $3, or Thock and Mechvibes for free. For sounds on scrolling and clicks as well as keys, Klack (since version 2.2), Keyfeel (which I make), or Snick for scrolling only. I tested none of the others, so this is a reading of vendor pages and listings, not a ranking by use.

### Do keyboard sound apps record what I type?

They all need a macOS permission to be told which key was pressed, usually Input Monitoring, and one of them (Snick) asks for Accessibility. A sound app needs the key, not the character. Keyfeel reads the key code and not the character, and the vendors of Klack, Klakk and KeyOpera state on their listings that they collect no data. I did not audit any of them, so read each privacy statement and check the permission yourself.

### Is there a free keyboard sound app for Mac?

Yes. Thock is free and MIT-licensed, and Mechvibes is free and open source with community sound packs. Mechvibes' original repository says it is moving to legacy status, with development continuing in MechvibesDX.

### Can a keyboard sound app also make scrolling and clicks feel better?

Some can. Snick plays click sounds and trackpad haptics as you scroll. Keyfeel plays key, mouse click and scroll sounds, with optional trackpad haptics. HapticPad gives haptics for links and buttons in the browser and plays no sound. Most of the others play keyboard sounds only.

### Will Bluetooth headphones make the sound late?

Yes, on any app. Bluetooth audio adds its own delay, often 100 milliseconds or more, which no keyboard sound app can remove. Built-in speakers, a wired headset or a USB audio device keep the sound in step with your keys.

### Is Keyfeel available, and what does it cost?

Yes. Keyfeel is Purplelink's Mac menu-bar app: free for 7 days, then $9.99 once with a license key, for macOS 13 or later on Apple silicon and Intel. I make it, it is new, and this guide describes it from its own product page rather than from a test against the others.

# Show free disk space in the Mac menu bar

By Benjamin Ampel · October 8, 2026

macOS has no setting that puts free disk space in the menu bar. Finder, Storage settings, Disk Utility and Terminal each show it on request. For a number that stays in view, you need a small app, and several are free.

Disclosure up front: I make Legroom, a menu-bar app for free disk space, and it is in the table below. It is $9.99 once after a 7-day trial. I did not install or test any of the other apps. Their rows come from vendor pages, Mac App Store listings, project source code and Apple support pages that I read on October 8, 2026. Prices and versions change. Where a page did not say something, the table says "not stated" instead of guessing.

## The short answer

Open a Finder window and turn on the status bar (View, then Show Status Bar). It shows the available space for the disk you are looking at. That is the fastest built-in check, and it costs a window. To see free space without opening anything, install a menu-bar app. Stats and Activity Bar are free and can show the number. Mister Plimsoll is free and only warns you. Legroom shows the number and warns you, and both stay free after its trial.

## See free space without an app

Four built-in views, from quickest to most detailed. All four are in Apple's documentation, linked below.

- Show the Finder status bar. Open a Finder window and choose View, then Show Status Bar, or press Command-Slash. Per Apple's page on file, folder and disk information, it shows the number of items and the available disk space. The path bar (Option-Command-P) shows the folder path, not space.

- Open Storage settings. In macOS Ventura 13 or later, choose System Settings from the Apple menu, click General, then Storage. Apple describes what the categories mean, including System Data, which is a catch-all rather than a folder.

- Check the volume in Disk Utility. Select the volume in the sidebar. Apple says the panel shows total capacity and the space available, which can include purgeable space that macOS frees when needed.

- Ask Terminal with df. Run df -h /System/Volumes/Data and read the Avail column. On my Mac, running macOS 27.2, that printed 22Gi, and diskutil info / printed 23.1 GB of container free space: about the same space in binary and decimal units. Use df -H for decimal units.

The numbers can differ between these views. Purgeable space is one reason: Finder counts it as available and some tools do not. Units are the other, as in the Terminal example. Apple's note on how capacity is measured explains the decimal and binary difference. Neither number is wrong.

## Menu-bar apps that show free space

US prices and requirements, October 8, 2026. "Not stated" means the page I read did not say. Apps on this list that are monitors only (Stats, iStat Menus, Activity Bar, System Monitor) show free space as one item among CPU, memory and network readings.

AppPriceFree space in the menu barLow-space alertCleaningmacOS

Legroom (mine)$9.99 once; 7-day trialYes: startup disk, space macOS can clear, other volumes. Stays free after the trialYes, at a line you set. Stays free after the trialYes: rules with a preview you approve. Needs a license key after the trial14+

StatsFree, MIT licenseYes: the Disk module has a text widget that can show free spacePercent-used threshold, off until you turn it on. Not a free-GB lineNo12+

iStat Menus 7$11.99 on the App Store; 14-day trial from the vendor; vendor price not readableYes: vendor says used and free space in the menu barVendor says rules can notify you if disk space is lowNo13+ per vendor; 14.0 per App Store

Mole (app)$19 once, 2 Macs, 14-day refundNot stated: menu bar shows "your chosen metrics"; disk is among the live metricsNot statedYes: caches, app leftovers, disk analysis14+

Mister PlimsollFree; optional tips $0.99 to $4.99Not stated in the listingYes: percent-used threshold per volume; notification, floating window, email, Pushover or webhookNo; shows how much Time Machine snapshots hold when a volume passes its line14.0

Activity BarFree; Pro $1.99 a year or $8.99 onceYes: used, free or total space on diskNot statedNo13.0

Free Disk Space Monitor$1.99Yes: current free space, refreshed at an interval you setNot statedNo10.10; last updated September 20, 2020

Sources, all read October 8, 2026. Legroom: its product page. Stats: the GitHub repository (version 3.0.20, released October 4, 2026), including the Disk module's settings and notification source files. iStat Menus: Bjango's page, which shows version 7.5 and a price field that did not load for me, and the App Store listing for iStat Menus 7 (version 7.30). Mole: mole.fit. Mister Plimsoll, Activity Bar, System Monitor and Free Disk Space Monitor: their Mac App Store listings, through Apple's public lookup service.

Two things I could not settle. Mole's page lists disk among its live metrics and says the menu bar shows chosen metrics, but I found no statement that free space is one of them. And Mister Plimsoll's listing says it lives in the menu bar and warns you, without saying whether it shows a number there. Free Disk Space Monitor has not been updated since 2020, so check that it runs on your version of macOS before paying.

Not menu-bar readouts. DaisyDisk draws a map of your disk and its home page does not mention the menu bar. Hazel runs rules on folders and has no free-space readout; its manual shows a free-space check only as a script example. DiskFox and StorageRadar, two newer disk apps, show free space inside their windows, and I found no menu-bar readout on their home pages. The disk space analyzer guide covers these in more detail.

## What Legroom does here, and what it does not

Legroom shows free space on the startup disk in the menu bar. The window under it adds the space available now, the space macOS says it can clear, and your other volumes. You set a line, and it warns you when free space drops below it. After the 7-day trial, those two parts keep working with no license key. Cleaning rules, What Grew, Suggestions, Space Map and Find Files need a key, which unlocks the same download. There is no account and no analytics. Every copy checks for updates once a day.

It does not make your Mac faster. It does not clean inside system folders. It does not run commands, and it does not scan as an administrator, so some space, such as local Time Machine snapshots, is listed as "size not reported" instead of measured. It is a disk tool, not a system monitor: for CPU, memory or network readings, use Stats or iStat Menus. Full Disk Access is optional. I am the developer, so weigh this section accordingly; the product page has the full list of what it does and does not do, and a 7-day trial.

## Choosing a warning line

A readout tells you the number. An alert tells you before it matters, so the useful setting is the line. Set it above the largest thing you do regularly: a video export, a virtual machine, an Xcode build. Leave room for macOS updates, which need space to download and install. If you see the alert often, raise the line less and find the cause instead. A daily comparison of what grew, which Legroom keeps for 1, 7 and 30 days, or a disk map from the analyzer guide, will point at it.

## Frequently asked

### Can macOS show free disk space in the menu bar without an app?

Not that I could find. Apple's guides describe the Finder status bar, the Storage pane in System Settings and Disk Utility, and none of them is a menu bar item. A small app is the way to keep the number in view.

### Why do Finder, Storage settings and Terminal show different free space?

Two reasons. Apple's Disk Utility help says available space can include purgeable space, which macOS clears when it needs room, and tools count it differently. And units differ: macOS reports decimal gigabytes (1 GB is 1 billion bytes), while df -h uses binary units. df -H uses decimal.

### Is there a free app that shows free space in the menu bar?

Yes. Stats is free and open source, and its Disk module can show free space as text. Activity Bar is free and can show used, free or total disk space, with its popups and widgets in a paid Pro tier. Mister Plimsoll is free and warns you when a volume passes a percentage you set. Legroom is mine: its menu-bar readout and low-space alerts stay free after the 7-day trial.

### Does Legroom need Full Disk Access to show free space?

Its page says Full Disk Access is optional, asked for only if you choose to give it. Without it, Legroom skips the folders macOS protects, such as Desktop, Documents and Downloads, and says which ones it could not read. I did not check what permissions the other apps ask for.

### Will a free-space readout make my Mac faster?

No. Showing the number does not change anything, and Legroom does not speed up a Mac either. It frees disk space and does nothing else to performance. A nearly full disk can cause its own problems, which is the reason to watch the number.

### What should I do when the low-space warning appears?

Find what is big before deleting anything: start with Storage settings, then use a disk map or a list of the largest items. Empty the Trash, and leave purgeable space and system folders alone. The disk space analyzer guide compares the tools and covers what is safe to delete.

Title: Best health tracking apps that keep your data on your phone (2026) | Purplelink
